en: The Bodhisattvabhūmi, from the Yogācārabhūmi: the Stage of the Bodhisattva.
[Tibetan 1] From the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*—the Stage of the Bodhisattva.
The Stage of the Hero. Fascicle One.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Homage to the noble Maitreya.
These ten dharmas summarize the Mahāyāna path of the bodhisattva, together with its fruit.
What are the ten? They are: the basis, the signs, the side, and...

The basis, the signs, and the positions; the resolute intention, the abidings, the births, the full acquisitions, and the stages.
Practice and final establishment are not the last.
Regarding that, what is the basis?
Here, it is the bodhisattva’s own lineage, the initial generation of the mind of awakening, and awakening...
All factors of the side [of enlightenment] are called the "basis. Why is that?
Because herein, the bodhisattva, relying upon and abiding in the lineage (*gotra*), [attains] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Because one becomes destined for the manifest and complete awakening of enlightenment and comes to possess spiritual power,
the lineage is therefore called the "basis endowed with the capacity."

In this regard, the bodhisattva, relying upon and abiding in the initial generation of the mind of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*), applies himself to generosity (*dāna*) as well as to ethical discipline (*śīla*).
They also apply themselves to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. In this way, these six perfections constitute merit.

Because it applies oneself to the accumulations, the accumulation of wisdom, and all the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*) is [the beginning] of a bodhisattva.
That application to the bodhisattva conduct is called the "basis. In this regard,
the bodhisattva, relying upon and abiding in that very application to the bodhisattva conduct, [attains] the unsurpassed, perfect...
Because it leads to the complete perfection of perfect enlightenment,
that application to the bodhisattva conduct is the basis for the complete perfection of great enlightenment.

It is called "that which is to be known. One who does not abide in the lineage—that is, one who lacks the lineage—may indeed give rise to the thought [of awakening] and remain correctly established in effort;
yet, even so, the unsurpassed [perfect enlightenment]... [is not attained].
They lack the fortune to fully perfect complete enlightenment. Therefore, by this enumeration,
it is shown that even if a bodhisattva has not yet generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), [they still possess the potential].
Even if one has not yet applied oneself to the conduct of a bodhisattva, lineage should be understood as the foundation. Furthermore, even if one abides in the lineage,
if one does not generate the mind [of awakening] and does not engage in the conduct of a bodhisattva...
If one does not apply oneself even to these [virtues], then although one possesses the potential,
awakening will not be swiftly accomplished. It should be understood that by reversing this, it will be swiftly accomplished.
Furthermore, this lineage is called the support (*ādhāra*), the sustenance (*upastambha*), the cause (*hetu*), the reliance (*niśraya*),
the proximate cause (*upaniṣad*), the precursor (*pūrvaṅgama*), and the abode (*nilaya*). Just as it is with the lineage,
so it is with the first production of the thought of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*) and all the conduct of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattvacaryā*).
In that regard, what is the lineage (*gotra*)? Briefly stated, the lineage is of two kinds:
that which abides in its natural state (*prakṛtistha*) and that which is acquired through cultivation (*samudānīta*). Among these, the lineage abiding in its natural state is...

That which is the excellence of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) of Bodhisattvas is such that it has been transmitted through a succession of others, beginningless in time, and obtained through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Among these,
the acquired lineage (*samudānīta-gotra*) is that which is obtained through the prior cultivation of roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla*).
In this context, both [meanings] are intended.
Furthermore, that lineage (*gotra*) is also called the seed (*bīja*), the element (*dhātu*), and the nature (*prakṛti*).
Moreover, when the fruit has not yet been fully realized, it is subtle and exists without the fruit.
The grossly manifested fruit, together with its fruit,
[is such that] Bodhisattvas endowed with that lineage indeed surpass all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, let alone others.

003/12/. It should be understood that all sentient beings possess a supreme distinction. Why is that? Because, in brief, there are these two kinds of purification: the purification of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Among these, [the purification] of all śrāvakas—

The lineage of the Pratyekabuddhas is purified through the purification of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), but not through the purification of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, the Bodhisattva lineage is purified both through the purification of the afflictive obscurations and through the purification of the cognitive obscurations.

It is purified by means of purification; therefore, it is said to be "completely remaining" and "supreme" in every respect. Furthermore, in four ways, the [wisdom] of a bodhisattva is superior to that of a śrāvaka—
The distinction [of the Bodhisattva] from the Pratyekabuddhas should be understood. By which four?
By those consisting of faculties, practice, skillfulness, and fruit.
In this regard, this is the distinction consisting of faculties: by nature alone, the Bodhisattva...
The Pratyekabuddha has sharp faculties, the Śrāvaka has middling faculties, and [the ordinary person] has dull faculties. In this regard, the distinction is one produced by practice.
The śrāvaka and the pratyekabuddha practice for their own benefit;
the bodhisattva, however, practices for his own benefit as well as for the benefit of others—
for the welfare of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for its purpose, benefit, and happiness.

004/06/. Among gods and humans, there is a distinction made by skillfulness. 004/07/. The *śrāvaka* and the *pratyekabuddha* exercise skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), and the truths (*satya*). The *bodhisattva*, however, [exercises skillfulness]... 004/08/. ...regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, dependent origination, the possible and the impossible, the truths, and skillfulness. 004/09/. Furthermore, the *śrāvaka* and the *pratyekabuddha* exercise skillfulness regarding the aggregates, elements, bases, dependent origination, the possible and the impossible, and the truths; the *bodhisattva* exercises skillfulness regarding these same things, as well as skillfulness regarding the immeasurable and the unconditioned. 004/10/. In those [five sciences] and in all other branches of knowledge, there is this distinction regarding the result:
the śrāvaka attains the fruit of śrāvaka-enlightenment;
the pratyekabuddha attains pratyekabuddha-enlightenment; and the bodhisattva [attains] [unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment].

He attains the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. These six become the signs of the lineage (*gotra*) of the perfections (*pāramitā*) for a bodhisattva; by means of these, others recognize him as a bodhisattva.

"This being" refers to a sentient being. These are the lineage-signs (*gotra-liṅga*) of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), and the lineage-signs of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Among these, this is the lineage-sign of the bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity: here, the bodhisattva—
A sentient being is by nature inclined toward generosity;
when objects to be given are available, they are constantly and continuously disposed to share with others, and they give with a joyful mind, not with a dejected one.
Moreover, he shares even a small portion;
he bestows gifts clearly and not meagerly, and he does not feel shame at not giving.
He speaks in praise of giving to others and encourages them toward generosity.
When he sees a donor, he becomes uplifted and joyful.
[He acts thus] toward his teachers, those who are more senior, those worthy of offerings, and those deserving of honor.

Rising from his seat, he offers it [to others]. Whether asked or unasked, regarding various duties of sentient beings, he provides instruction on what is right concerning this world and the next. He protects those who are terrified by fears such as kings, thieves, enemies, fire, water, and so forth.

And he bestows fearlessness upon those beings; according to his ability, he protects them from that manifold, extensive, and fierce danger. Furthermore, wealth belonging to others placed in his hand is not misappropriated by him.

...he does not act with malice toward others; he does not deceive his own heir, nor does he mislead him. [He does not misappropriate] gems, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, silver, emerald, and musāragalva.
He correctly awakens the deluded one whose mind is perverted regarding various objects such as red-colored items or those with rightward spirals, thinking:
"Who else will again deceive him? By his very nature..."

Furthermore, he is inclined toward magnificent enjoyments; his mind inclines toward all magnificent articles of enjoyment. He is devoted to magnificent occupations, not to those that are meager or restricted in scope. — Nivemaṇi.
In the world there are calamities, such as the calamity of women, the calamity of intoxicants, [the calamity of gambling],
and the calamity of watching actors, dancers, and the like; from such calamities as these,
he very quickly attains detachment (*vairāgya*).
Venerable sir, he manifests a sense of shame and dread of blame. Even upon obtaining vast wealth, he does not become puffed up or greedy, much less so when it is small. Thus—

These and other such qualities should be understood as the signs of the lineage (*gotra*) of a bodhisattva’s perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). Now, these are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

In this case, a bodhisattva is naturally endowed with actions of body, speech, and mind that are mild, unwholesome, yet not excessively fierce and not excessively harmful to sentient beings; even after having committed a sinful deed, [he remains thus].
Very quickly, he experiences remorse;

he does not find delight or take pleasure [in harmful actions]. By nature, he is one who does not harm sentient beings with his hands, clods of earth, sticks, weapons, or the like, and he is naturally affectionate.

He becomes beloved by sentient beings. Toward those worthy of honor, he is at all times established in the practice of greeting, saluting, rising from his seat, joining his palms in reverence, and performing acts of respectful service. He is also skillful and urbane.
[Tibetan]

He is preceded by [a friendly disposition], has a bright facial expression, is free from frowning, and is the first to speak. Toward sentient beings who have been helpful, he is grateful and appreciative of what has been done for him. And toward sentient beings who are in need, he is straightforward.
He practices correctly. He does not entice others through deceit or guile.
He acquires wealth through righteous means and not through unrighteous means. And he performs his duties with diligence—even in the performance of his activities... [he remains] diligent.
He goes toward others even before himself; and he is excessively harmed by the infliction of harm upon others— that is to say, by killing,
binding, beating, flogging, reviling, threatening, and so forth— whether having seen it or heard of it.
He values the undertaking of the Dharma and values the future life;
he perceives danger even in the slightest fault, let alone in a great one. Furthermore—
In matters that must be performed by others, he acts as a companion; that is to say, in agriculture, commerce, cattle-rearing, royal service, writing, calculation,
accounting, reckoning, and sealing, as well as in winning over his master, winning over his family, and [winning over] friends.

In propitiating friends and kings, in the acquisition, protection, accumulation, investment, and expenditure of wealth, and in matters such as bringing and giving away daughters in marriage, eating and communal feasting,
he acts as a companion in such related affairs. He does not engage in quarreling or strife.
In disputes, quarrels, or other matters involving the harassment of others— those things which lead to misfortune, suffering, and harm for oneself and others—
he restrains them from such improper actions, namely, from the ten unwholesome deeds.

From the wholesome paths of action, he becomes subject to others and obedient to others because of his equal patience and ethical discipline. Having abandoned his own affairs, he is employed by others in their own affairs according to their will.

He possesses a moist heart and a gentle mind; he does not long maintain a state of malice or a state of resentment. Rather, at that very moment, his mind turns toward goodness. He also comes to hold the truth in high esteem.

He does not deceive others with false speech; he neither delights in nor engages in creating dissension among the friends of others; he does not speak impulsively words that are incoherent, purposeless, or meaningless; and he is one who speaks kindly.
He is not harsh even toward his own retinue of servants and so forth, let alone toward others;
he is fond of the virtues of others and is one who proclaims their true praise. These and other such qualities constitute the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
By means of that [perfection], the signs of the lineage are to be understood.
In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Here, a bodhisattva, by nature, [does not harbor ill will] toward others...
Having received harm, he does not manifest a mind of malice, nor does he act to retaliate. And when being exhorted to reconciliation, he accepts that exhortation.

He accepts [an offense], yet he does not harbor resentment, nor does he maintain it for a long time, nor does he carry a grudge. These and other similar qualities should be understood as the signs of the lineage (*gotra*) of a bodhisattva’s perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
008/05. In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).

008/06. Here, a bodhisattva is by nature industrious; rising early in the morning, he goes to bed late in the evening, not seeking the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, or the pleasure of lying on his side.

One excessively indulges in pleasure. Furthermore, when a task has arisen, one applies oneself with deliberation, overcoming the desire not to act and laziness, for the sake of accomplishing that task.
This is the undertaking of all tasks.

Furthermore, he possesses firm resolve regarding these [tasks], and without having performed them or fully accomplished them, he does not entirely relax his vigor nor fall into despondency midway. Moreover, with respect to sublime and supreme goals, his mind does not experience contraction.

Nor does he disparage himself, thinking, "I am capable and have the strength to attain these [realizations]. Thus, he becomes one who has conceived enthusiasm; he is a hero when entering a great assembly, or when engaging in challenge and counter-challenge with others, except in other circumstances.
Or, even regarding difficult tasks and great undertakings that are conducive to the goal,
he does not fall into excessive weariness, let alone those that are minor. These and others of a similar kind are the signs of the lineage of a bodhisattva’s perfection of vigor.
These are to be understood.

In this regard, these are the signs of the lineage (*gotra*) of a bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*): here, a bodhisattva by nature applies close attention to the meaning of the Dharma.

He becomes abundant in non-distraction. Upon seeing or hearing of forest retreats, wilderness dwellings, and lodgings frequented by no people, devoid of evil persons, and conducive to solitary seclusion;
"O, how pleasant is renunciation and seclusion! Thus,
he generates an intense eagerness for renunciation and seclusion, and by his very nature...

His afflictions become mild, his hindrances mild, and his underlying corruption mild. Furthermore, when he has gone into seclusion and is reflecting upon his own welfare, evil and improper thoughts do not excessively agitate his mind, nor do they completely overwhelm it.

They remain [in this state]. Even toward those on the side of enemies, they very swiftly establish a mind of loving-kindness, let alone toward friends or neutral parties. And having heard of or seen the suffering of sentient beings who are afflicted by various kinds of misery, [they act accordingly].

Or he generates a mind of great compassion. And for the sake of removing the suffering of those sentient beings, he exerts himself according to his ability and according to his strength. By nature, he is one who desires the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.
He possesses desire and is steadfast in the face of calamities— whether in the misfortune of kinsmen,
the loss of wealth, execution, imprisonment, or exile—
and in such similar adversities; he is also wise in the grasping of the teachings (dharmas).
He is capable of retaining and upholding [the teachings]. He is endowed with the power of mindfulness;
he is able to recollect even what was done long ago and spoken long ago, and he causes others to recollect them as well. These and other such qualities belong to a bodhisattva.

The lineage-signs (*gotra-liṅga*) of the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) of this [bodhisattva] should be understood. Among these, the following are the lineage-signs of the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*): here, the bodhisattva, for the sake of entering into all fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*) as objects of cognition, [exerts himself].
He is endowed with innate wisdom (*sahaja-prajñā*).

He is neither dull nor sluggish, being by nature free from delusion. Furthermore, regarding the various abstentions from the bases of negligence, he possesses the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*). Thus, these...
Such qualities as these are to be understood as the signs of the lineage (*gotra*) of a bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
These are the coarse, inferential signs of a bodhisattva’s lineage.
The signs are to be known [through inference]. However, regarding the determination of the true nature of reality, only the Blessed Buddhas are those who perceive it directly.
And because that lineage of the bodhisattvas is by its very nature thus endowed with qualities— auspicious, excellent, and possessed of pure dharmas—
it is therefore difficult to realize and supreme.

For the sake of attaining the inconceivable, immovable, and unsurpassed state of a Tathāgata, one applies oneself by way of its cause; it cannot be attained otherwise. To that extent, a bodhisattva is naturally endowed with these pure qualities.

As long as one is not defiled by the four secondary afflictions that are antagonistic to pure qualities— whether in their entirety or in part— and as long as one remains undefiled, one does not appear within these pure qualities, nor among those in the states of woe.

And at one time, he is reborn [in such states]. Even when a bodhisattva is reborn in the miserable destinies (apāya), a great distinction based on his spiritual lineage (gotra) should be understood as existing between him and those beings reborn in the miserable destinies who do not possess it. Here, after a long period of time, the bodhisattva—perhaps at some point—

At times he is reborn in the states of woe; yet once reborn there, he is quickly liberated from those states of woe. Furthermore, he does not experience such intense suffering pertaining to the states of woe as do other beings born in those states of woe. By that [virtue],...
Furthermore, touched by even a slight and painful sensation, he gives rise to an intense sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Toward those beings who have been born there and are suffering,
he acquires a mind of compassion, namely, by means of that very [sensation].
(5b) Impelled by the lineage and by the cause that is the great compassion of a Buddha— such as this,
one should understand the distinction of a bodhisattva when reborn in the miserable states from other beings who have been reborn in those same miserable states.

In this regard, what are those four secondary afflictions (upakleśa) that are antagonistic to the bodhisattva’s qualities of gentleness? First, due to previous negligence and the habituation to the afflictions (kleśa), there is the intensity of the afflictions and the protracted nature of the afflictions; this is the first secondary affliction.
For one who is deluded and unwholesome, this reliance upon evil friends is the second secondary affliction. For one who is overcome by teachers, husbands, kings, thieves, or adversaries,
this lack of autonomy and mental confusion is the third secondary affliction.
The dependence on a livelihood for one who lacks the necessary requisites is this fourth secondary affliction.
For these four reasons, even one who is thus endowed with a noble lineage [may fall away].

A bodhisattva is unable to awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. By which four [factors]? Here, from the very beginning, a bodhisattva does not obtain a spiritual friend who possesses the unerring path to enlightenment.

The Teacher, whether a Buddha or a Bodhisattva— this is the first cause. Furthermore, even after having found a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), a bodhisattva may grasp things erroneously and train erroneously in the bodhisattva trainings.

This is the second cause. Furthermore, even after a bodhisattva has found a virtuous friend and is training unerringly in the bodhisattva precepts, he becomes lax in that application, being indolent and lacking in enthusiasm.
Endowed with continuous vigor— this is the third cause. Furthermore,
another [cause] is that even after having found a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra),
the bodhisattva trains without error in the bodhisattva trainings and exerts himself in that application.

One possesses vigor, yet one's faculties are unripened and one's accumulations are incomplete due to a lack of long-term cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). This is the fourth cause; even when the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) exists, it is because of the deficiency of these causes that [one does not attain] enlightenment.

Non-attainment (*aprāpti*). However, through its presence, attainment occurs. But when the lineage (*gotra*) is absent, it should be understood that there is a total non-attainment of enlightenment in every respect and in all ways.
[End of] the first chapter, the Foundation, in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The first chapter on the lineage (*gotra*) is completed.
Herein, the first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*) of a bodhisattva is the beginning of all awakening...

Among the correct aspirations (*samyak-praṇidhāna*) of sentient beings, that [first one] is the primary one, which encompasses all other correct aspirations. Therefore, from the very beginning, it has the nature of a correct aspiration. Indeed, that bodhisattva [directs] the mind toward awakening...
While thus directing his mind, he forms a mental resolve and speaks these words: "O, may I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and may I become a benefactor for all sentient beings."
"May I establish [beings] in ultimate, final nirvāṇa and in the wisdom of a Tathāgata.
Thus, while seeking both his own awakening and the welfare of sentient beings, he generates the mind [of enlightenment]. Therefore, that generation of the mind is [the aspiration].

It does not lack a formal aspect (*ākāra*). Indeed, that production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) aspires by taking awakening and the welfare of sentient beings as its objects; it does not do so without an object.
Therefore, that production of the thought of enlightenment has awakening as its object and the welfare of sentient beings as its object. That production of the thought of enlightenment...
Because he is the precursor for gathering all the roots of merit conducive to enlightenment,
he is skilled, endowed with the quality of supreme skill, auspicious, supremely auspicious,
excellent, supremely excellent, and the support for all sentient beings.

It is the opposite of misconduct of body, speech, and mind. Furthermore, among all other wholesome right aspirations regarding mundane and supramundane matters, this right aspiration is the foremost of them all.

The unsurpassed treasure is the first production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva. Thus, this first production of the thought of enlightenment should be understood by way of its intrinsic nature, its aspect, its object, its qualities, and its excellence.
Even for one who is still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), it should be understood that [the bodhicitta] possesses five characteristics.
And from the very moment that bodhicitta arises, the bodhisattva has entered the Great Vehicle of unsurpassed enlightenment; he is thus called a "bodhisattva."
It comes to be reckoned by way of conventional designation and linguistic usage.
Therefore, that production of the thought of awakening is comprised within "entry. And having produced it, the bodhisattva...
The Bodhisattva awakens to that very mind as the supreme, perfect enlightenment through a gradual process, not without having first generated it. Therefore,
that generation of the mind is the root of supreme, perfect enlightenment regarding those who suffer.
And that compassionate bodhisattva, with the intention of protecting sentient beings, generates that thought. Therefore, that generation of the thought is the outflow of compassion.
Relying upon and established in that generation of the thought, the bodhisattva [practices] the factors conducive to enlightenment...

He applies himself to all those dharmas and to the performance of deeds for the benefit of sentient beings within the training of a bodhisattva; therefore, that production of the thought of enlightenment is the foundation of the bodhisattva's training. Thus, this first production of the thought of enlightenment is [to be understood] by way of its summary.
It should also be understood from the perspective of its root, its outflow, and its basis.

Furthermore, that first production of the thought of enlightenment (bodhicittotpāda) of a bodhisattva is, in brief, of two kinds: that which leads to deliverance and that which does not lead to deliverance. Among these, that which leads to deliverance—

That which, once arisen, continues to the very end and does not turn back is "leading to liberation" (*nairyāṇika*). On the other hand, that which, once arisen, does not continue to the very end but turns back again is not so.
Furthermore, the turning back of that arising of the mind is also of two kinds.

It is both absolute and non-absolute. Among these, the absolute is that mind which, once turned away, does not arise again for the sake of enlightenment. The non-absolute, however, is that mind which, though turned away, arises again and again for the sake of enlightenment.

That generation of the mind should indeed be understood by means of four conditions, four causes, and four powers. What are the four conditions? Here, a son of good family or a daughter of good family [hears] of the Tathāgata...
When a bodhisattva sees the inconceivable and marvelous manifestation of a miracle, or hears of it from someone who is trustworthy, then,
having seen or heard it, he thinks: "Oh, how great is this majestic power!"
For one who is established in or has set out toward awakening, such power as this is seen, and such a miracle as this is manifested.

And it is heard. Taking that very sight or hearing of such power as the dominant condition, one who is resolved upon great enlightenment (mahābodhi) generates the mind set on great enlightenment. This is the first condition.
For the arising of the thought [of enlightenment], he neither sees nor hears of such power;
rather, with reference to unexcelled perfect enlightenment, he hears the True Dharma—the Bodhisattva-piṭaka—being taught. And having heard it...

Furthermore, he gains deep faith. Having gained deep faith, he makes the hearing of the true Dharma his primary focus and, being resolved upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata, generates the aspiration to attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This is the second.

This is the condition for the arising of the thought [of awakening]: he does not hear the Dharma, but rather perceives that the disappearance of the true Dharma of the Bodhisattvas has arrived before him. Having seen this, it occurs to him: "It is not..."

"Alas! For the sake of removing the suffering of conceited beings, the establishment of the Bodhisattva’s true Dharma leads to their welfare. What if I were to generate the resolve for the long endurance of the Bodhisattva’s true Dharma, that is to say, for the sake of these very beings?"

Thus, for the sake of removing the suffering of sentient beings, he makes the upholding of the true Dharma his primary focus and, being resolved upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata, generates the mind for the attainment of the wisdom of the Tathāgata. This is the third.

This condition for the arising of the mind is as follows: he does not see the disappearance of the true Dharma as already present; rather, in the final age and at the end of time, he sees the inferior physical bases of sentient beings belonging to that final age, namely:
[He sees beings] defiled by ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), namely: those abounding in delusion (*moha*),

those abounding in lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), those abounding in envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*), those abounding in suffering (*duḥkha*), those abounding in depravity (*dauṣṭhulya*), those abounding in affliction (*kleśa*), and those abounding in misconduct (*duścarita*).
Having seen those who are full of frivolity, full of negligence, full of indolence, and full of lack of faith, he further thinks to himself:

"Alas! This great age of corruption has arrived. In such a defiled time as this, it is not even easy to give rise to the thought of the enlightenment of an inferior śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, let alone that of the unsurpassed [enlightenment]."
"In supreme perfect enlightenment. What if I were now to generate the thought [of awakening], so that others, following my example, might also generate it?
Having thus made the generation of the thought of awakening his final act at the time of death, he—mahā-...
Having resolved upon enlightenment, one generates the mind directed toward great awakening. This is the fourth condition for the arising of the mind.
What are the four causes? They are the excellence of the bodhisattva’s spiritual lineage (*gotra*).

The first cause for the arising of the mind is being embraced by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends. The second cause for the arising of the mind is [the presence of] the perfections. Compassion toward sentient beings is the third cause for the arising of the Bodhisattva’s mind.

Fearlessness toward the suffering of saṃsāra, toward the suffering of difficult practices— even those that are long-lasting, diverse, intense, and uninterrupted— is the fourth cause for the arising of the [bodhi]citta.
In this regard, the perfection of the lineage (*gotra*) of a bodhisattva should be understood as being obtained through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The perfection of the spiritual friend (*mitra*) of a bodhisattva is to be understood by way of four aspects.

[It] should be understood as follows. Here, a bodhisattva’s friend from the very beginning is not dull-witted, is not of a sluggish nature, is wise and discerning, and has not fallen into wrong views. This is the first perfection of a friend. Furthermore, he does not [indulge] in negligence.

He encourages him in what is right and does not provide him with occasions for negligence; this is the second perfection of a friend. He does not encourage him in misconduct and does not provide him with occasions for misconduct; this is...

The third is the perfection of friends: one who does not discourage [the practitioner] from superior qualities— such as faith, aspiration, undertaking, vigor, and skillful means— and who does not lead them toward inferior ones.

Among those to be trained, he causes them to undertake the qualities of faith, aspiration, formal commitment, vigor, and skillful means; that is to say, by turning them away from the Mahāyāna toward either the Śrāvaka-yāna or the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, or by turning them away from that which consists of meditative cultivation.

Having turned away from that which consists of reflection by means of that which consists of reflection; having turned away from that which consists of hearing by means of that which consists of hearing; having turned away from the work of service by means of that which consists of ethical discipline; and having turned away from that which consists of generosity—thus, from such categories of qualities that are more excellent [he turns away].
He does not dissuade others from [superior qualities] and instead encourages them toward such inferior qualities as these; this is the fourth perfection of a friend.
For four reasons, a bodhisattva becomes abundant in compassion.

Among sentient beings, there exist those world-systems in which suffering is not found within the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions. Yet that bodhisattva is reborn in a realm where suffering exists, wherein suffering—
Patience is perceived when one does not [perceive] suffering;
yet one sees another person touched, afflicted, and overcome by some kind of suffering, while oneself is also touched, afflicted, and overcome by some other kind of suffering. Furthermore...

Furthermore, he perceives himself, or another, or both, as being touched, afflicted, and overwhelmed by suffering that is long-lasting, diverse, intense, and uninterrupted. Thus, for that bodhisattva, his own lineage—
Based on this reliance and by virtue of being naturally good, compassion— whether weak, middling, or intense— arises through these four objects and supports,
except in cases where it has been developed through prior practice.

For four reasons, a bodhisattva, having placed compassion for sentient beings foremost, does not fear or tremble even before the long-lasting, diverse, intense, and uninterrupted sufferings of saṃsāra, let alone those that are inferior.
By nature he is of a virtuous temperament (*sāttvika*), steadfast, and strong; this is the first cause. He is wise and possesses correct contemplation (*samyag-upanidhyāna*).
Ethical discipline strengthened by analytical reflection— this is the second cause. Being endowed with an intense resolve for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—
this is the third cause regarding sentient beings.
And he becomes endowed with intense compassion. This is the fourth cause.
What are the four powers? They are the internal power and the external power.

The power of the cause (*hetu-bala*) and the power of application (*prayoga-bala*). Among these, that inclination toward unsurpassed perfect enlightenment which falls within one's own capacity is called the bodhisattva’s internal power for the arising of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*). [The power] from another’s capacity—

However, the aspiration that has been generated for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is called the "power of others" (*para-bala*) for the sake of the arising of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*). It is the former wholesome [root] of the bodhisattva associated with the Mahāyāna.
The practice of the Dharma consists, at present, in the swift generation of the mind [of awakening] merely by beholding Buddhas and Bodhisattvas or merely by hearing their praise;
how much more so by beholding their majestic power or the True Dharma.
Or by hearing [the Dharma]. This is called the power of the cause for the arising of the thought [of awakening].
It is the long-term cultivation of wholesome qualities by a bodhisattva in this very life, beginning with attending upon superior persons, hearing the true Dharma, and reflecting upon it.
This is called the power of application for the arising of the thought [of awakening].
In that regard, if a bodhisattva, relying upon the four conditions and the four causes— both combined and individual— and by means of internal power, [generates the thought of awakening...]
That mind arises through the power of the cause and through both powers combined; thus it is firm, substantial, and immovable.

It arises. However, that mind should be understood as having a firm emergence when it arises through the power of another’s application or through its own power. There are four causes for the turning back of a bodhisattva’s mind. Which are they?
There are four [obstacles]: one does not possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); one is under the influence of evil friends (*pāpamitra*);
one has little compassion for sentient beings; and one is fearful of the long-lasting, diverse, intense, and uninterrupted sufferings of *saṃsāra*.

He becomes excessively afraid, terrified, and falls into a state of panic. These four causes for the turning back of the mind should be understood in detail as the opposites of the four causes for the arising of the mind,
as previously explained.
These two are the uncommon, marvelous, and wonderful qualities of a bodhisattva who has firmly generated the first thought of awakening. What are the two? They are:
he embraces all sentient beings as his own kin, yet... [he does not...]

Furthermore, one is defiled by the fault of attachment to wife and children. In this regard, the fault of attachment to wife and children consists of compliance and hostility caused by their benefit or harm. These two, however, do not exist for the bodhisattva.

These two noble intentions toward sentient beings proceed from a bodhisattva who has firmly generated the first thought of awakening: the intention for their welfare and the intention for their happiness. Therein, the intention for their welfare is that which [leads them] away from unwholesome states...

The desire to establish others in a state of virtue after having raised them up from it; the disposition of happiness which is the desire to provide afflicted beings who are destitute, helpless, and without refuge with things that are beneficial and free from defilement.

[018/22] These two are the applications of a bodhisattva who has firmly generated the first thought of awakening: the application of high resolve (*adhyāśaya-prayoga*) and the application of practice (*pratipatti-prayoga*).
Therein, the application of high resolve is that which consists of his very desire for [the welfare and happiness of others].
The daily strengthening of one's resolute intention; the application of practice;
and the daily application toward the maturation of oneself in the qualities of a Buddha.
And, relying solely upon the application of resolute intention according to one's capacity and strength, there is the application of bringing about benefit and happiness for sentient beings.
These two belong to a bodhisattva who has firmly generated the first thought of awakening.

It is a great gateway for the influx of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*): the application to one’s own welfare for the attainment of unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*),
and the application to the welfare of others for the liberation of all sentient beings from all suffering, just as...
There are two gateways for entry. Likewise, there are two great accumulations of wholesome dharmas, two immeasurable aggregates of wholesome dharmas—and so forth.
These two belong to a bodhisattva who has first generated the mind of enlightenment. First...

Based on the generation of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), there is a distinction in the gathering of wholesome qualities for the sake of awakening; compared to other gatherings of wholesome qualities, there is a distinction in the cause and a distinction in the fruit. That indeed is the bodhisattva’s gathering of wholesome qualities...

Grasping is the cause of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and that [enlightenment] is its fruit. No other accumulation of merit by all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is such a cause, let alone that of other sentient beings. Therefore...
The bodhisattvas’ appropriation of virtue is superior to all other appropriations of virtue, both by way of its causal nature and its fruit.
These two [aspects] belong to a bodhisattva who has firmly generated the first thought of enlightenment.

019/19/. These are the benefits of generating this thought. Simultaneously with the generation of the thought, one becomes worthy of offerings from all sentient beings, becomes a venerable person, a field of merit for living beings like a father, and [the source] of merit that is indestructible.
He takes possession [of it]. In this regard, this is the merit that is free from harm (*avyābādhyapuṇya*).
Endowed with which, a bodhisattva is protected by a protection twice that of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). When this protection is ever-present for him, [he is thus guarded].
Neither beasts of prey, nor yakṣas, nor humans, nor non-humans, nor local spirits are able to cause harm even to one who is asleep, intoxicated, or heedless. Furthermore,
when this bodhisattva has changed births, by that [power]...

Through the accumulation of merit, one becomes free from affliction and is naturally healthy; one is not touched by long-lasting or severe illness, and [is thus able to act] for the sake of sentient beings.
When he exerts himself with body and speech in deeds to be performed for the sake of sentient beings, and while teaching the Dharma, his body does not become excessively fatigued;
his mindfulness is not lost, nor is his mind impaired. This is due to his very nature.
To that extent, a bodhisattva abiding in the lineage possesses slight corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*).
However, one who has generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) becomes to a much greater degree one with slight corruption—
that is, with corruption of body and corruption of speech.

And because of the corruption of their minds, even those mantra-words and vidyā-words that are effective at pacifying calamities, afflictions, and misfortunes for sentient beings— even when they have not been mastered and are in the hands of other beings— become effective when they are in the hands of those [beings]. Who [could prevent this]?

Furthermore, [these qualities] are established. Moreover, they are endowed with an abundance of patience and gentleness; they endure the injuries inflicted by others and do not inflict injury upon others.
Even when perceiving another being harmed by a third party, they feel extreme [compassion].

He is oppressed by them. Furthermore, his secondary afflictions—anger, envy, deceit, hypocrisy, and so forth—having their force destroyed and becoming weakened, may occasionally manifest, but they quickly vanish. And in whatever village or field he dwells, that—
The evils of fear, terror, and famine, as well as calamities wrought by non-human beings—whether unarisen, they shall not arise; or if already arisen, they shall be pacified.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of enlightenment [should encounter such things] at any time...
He is reborn in the hells,

in the realms of misery; yet he is released from those hells more quickly and to a greater degree than before, experiences less intense painful sensations, and generates a much stronger sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
And toward those beings, he maintains a mind of compassion for the sake of acquiring merit that is free from affliction. Thus,
through the acquisition of merit free from affliction, the one who has first produced the thought of enlightenment [attains] many such benefits.
The bodhisattva experiences [this].
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the Foundation (*ādhāra*) of the Yoga-sthāna, this is the second [chapter].
The Chapter on the Generation of the Thought of Enlightenment is completed.
Now, for those Bodhisattvas who have thus generated the thought of enlightenment, the [practice of] the Bodhisattva...
What is conduct (*caryā*)? In brief, it is the synthesis into one of all that in which bodhisattvas train, how they train, and who trains; this is called the bodhisattva-conduct.

Furthermore, in what do bodhisattvas train? They train in seven points. What are the seven points? One’s own welfare, the welfare of others, the meaning of reality, spiritual power, the ripening of sentient beings, and one’s own [attainment of] Buddhahood.
The maturation of the Dharma and unexcelled, perfect enlightenment constitute the seventh point. The summary verse states:
Self-interest and the interest of others, the meaning of reality, power, and maturation.
The supreme enlightenment of sentient beings and of one's own buddha-qualities is accompanied by darkness.
What is the welfare of oneself and others? In brief, it consists of ten [types].
The welfare of oneself and others should be understood as follows: it is exclusive; it is connected with others;
it consists of benefit and consists of happiness; it is comprised of causes and comprised of results;
and it is of this world, of the next world, ultimate, and non-ultimate.

In this regard, whatever constitutes a purely selfish aim or a purely altruistic aim must be fully understood and abandoned by the Bodhisattva, because such aims exceed the proper conduct of a Bodhisattva and are inconsistent with it; furthermore, one should train in what remains.

In this regard, this is the purely selfish interest of a bodhisattva which must be fully understood and abandoned by him: namely, the pursuit and enjoyment of wealth by one who desires his own pleasure; or, on the other hand, being stingy with the Dharma.

The seeking and upholding of the teachings spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; and for one desiring heaven, the undertaking and practice of ethical discipline, the arousal of vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom for the sake of heaven; [and] the fruit of worldly material gain.
Or again, for one who desires [worldly things], there is worship of a Tathāgata’s shrine for the sake of worldly gain;
or for one desiring profit, it is for the sake of profit, producing profit for oneself.
For the sake of others, it is the proclamation of various non-existent qualities in order to cause them to be uplifted.

For one who desires to accept service from others, it is the gathering of a group through unrighteous means rather than through righteous means for the purpose of accepting service from others; [and] from others, [the acceptance of] slaves...
He liberates beings from the state of slavery so that they may themselves become slaves; having liberated beings bound by fetters from their bonds,
he binds them himself for his own purpose.

For the sake of accomplishment, he liberates from the fear of punishment and the like those beings who are terrified by such fears from others, precisely so that they themselves may no longer grasp at fear. Furthermore, there is for the bodhisattva a dwelling in happiness in the present life.
That which is devoid of reflection upon the welfare of sentient beings should be understood as a purely self-interested aim.
Such categories of purely self-interested aims of a bodhisattva should be understood by the bodhisattva as things to be fully known and then abandoned.

Furthermore, it should be understood that for a bodhisattva, generosity, patience, and compassion— whether they result in awakening, are dedicated toward awakening, or are for the sake of heaven— are always self-interest solely insofar as it is connected to others.
Setting aside these aforementioned aspects,
it should be understood that for Bodhisattvas, all other forms of their own welfare— being the opposite of those— are invariably connected with the welfare of others.
In this regard, this is the exclusively altruistic aim of a bodhisattva, which a bodhisattva, having fully understood it, must abandon: giving to one who holds perverted views,

to one who holds the view that there is no [karmic] arrival [of results], to one who sees no fruit [of action], and to one whose ethical discipline has fallen away— [all of whom lack] correct practice.

The teaching of the Dharma to others by one who is separated [from the higher stages]; and for a Bodhisattva skilled in the mastery of meditative absorption, the application of the wholesome dharmas belonging to the lower stages after having transcended those lower stages— this is because he, by means of the meditative absorptions...
Having dwelt in meditative absorption and emerged from it, the Bodhisattva who has attained mastery is reborn wherever he desires within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).

In all ten directions, through various emanations, he performs beneficial activities for various sentient beings. And for the Sage, the Tathāgata, who has accomplished his own purpose, [this occurs] by relying upon all the unique qualities of a Buddha, such as the powers and the grounds of self-confidence.
When sentient beings are limited in their capacity, the performance of immeasurable purposeful action is to be understood as a purely altruistic aim. Among these, the former two types of altruism,
as previously described, must be fully understood and abandoned by the bodhisattva, whereas the latter alone is to be practiced.
Furthermore, in other cases, one should train to a much greater extent for the sake of others alone. Setting aside these modes, and by way of their opposite,
all the benefit for others of bodhisattvas is connected with their own self-interest.

In that regard also, a bodhisattva should train. What is the benefit for oneself and others that follows from the welfare of a bodhisattva? It should be understood as being fivefold in its aspects: it is characterized by blamelessness, and it is...
The characteristic of the grasper is threefold: pertaining to this life, pertaining to future lives, and pertaining to peace.
In that regard, whatever wholesome undertaking or accumulation of the wholesome a bodhisattva performs—whether small or great—either by himself or for another who is small...
Whether it be small or great, he encourages others toward the acquisition of wholesome qualities and the accumulation of merit;

he disciplines them, establishes them, and settles them therein. This should be understood as the faultless, auspicious benefit for both self and others that follows from the bodhisattva’s own welfare.

Whatever happiness a bodhisattva brings about for himself or for others— excluding that which is afflicted— whether it be the happiness of material requisites or the happiness of dwelling in meditative absorption,
this is the characteristic of a bodhisattva’s assistance, [namely] benefit.

The welfare of oneself and others should be understood as follows: there is the bodhisattva’s welfare of self and others that is beneficial in this life but not in the next; there is that which is beneficial in the next life but not in this one; there is that which is beneficial both in the next life and in this one; and there is that which is beneficial neither in the next life nor in this one. Furthermore, that [welfare]...

This fourfold benefit for oneself and others should be understood as corresponding respectively to the four undertakings of the Dharma (*dharma-samādāna*). What are the four undertakings of the Dharma? There is an undertaking of the Dharma that pertains to the present...
There is that which is pleasant in the present but has a ripening of suffering in the future. There is that which is painful in the present but has a ripening of happiness in the future. There is...

There is that which is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant ripening in the future; there is that which is painful in the present and has a painful ripening in the future. The analysis of these should be understood exactly as in the Sūtra. In that regard, Nirvāṇa is [the state of] Nirvāṇa...

And those mundane and supramundane factors conducive to nirvāṇa that bring about its attainment— this, in brief, should be understood as the bodhisattva’s benefit-related and pacifying self-interest and interest of others, which is most distinguished and unsurpassed.
What is the bodhisattva’s pursuit of happiness for the sake of self and others?
In brief, it should be understood as being comprised of five kinds of happiness.
Among these, the five kinds of happiness are: the happiness of the cause, the happiness of feeling...

Pleasure is that which is the antidote to suffering; pleasure is the pleasure of the cessation of feeling; and the fifth is unafflicted pleasure. In this regard, the category of pleasure consists of two factors: the faculty and its object, as well as that which is caused by them.

Whatever contact is to be experienced as pleasant, and whatever action has a desirable fruit— whether in this present life or in a future life— all that, taken together and summarized, is called "causal happiness. There is nothing beyond this.

There is nothing beyond this. Independent of the cessation of suffering, the experience that arises through these three causes subsumed under causal happiness—which brings benefit to both body and mind—is called "experienced happiness" (*vedita-sukha*). That [is as follows].
Furthermore, in brief, it is of two kinds: with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*).

Among these, that which is without-outflows consists of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) and the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). That which is with-outflows, moreover, belongs to the three realms, being associated with the desire, form, and formless realms. That...
Furthermore, the entire triple world is, according to its application, sixfold by way of the division of bases:
[that] born of eye-contact, up to that born of mind-contact.
[026/01] It is born of contact (*saṃsparśaja*). Furthermore, that is of two kinds and six types:

bodily (*kāyika*) and mental (*caitasika*). Among these, that which is associated with the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) is bodily, while that which is associated with the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) is mental.
Because various kinds of sufferings— such as cold, heat, hunger, thirst,
and so forth— which arise in many diverse ways, are pacified by counteracting those very sufferings of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so on, in that very [state of suffering]...

The notion of pleasure that arises when there is merely the subsiding of [suffering] is called pleasure as an antidote to suffering (*duḥkha-prātipakṣika*). The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*) is called the pleasure of the cutting off of feeling (*veditopaccheda-sukha*). It is unafflicted (*avyābādhyā*).
Furthermore, happiness, in brief, should be understood as being of four kinds:

the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of tranquility, and the happiness of perfect awakening. [This arises] from going forth from the home to the homeless life with right faith.

For one who has gone forth, the liberation from the suffering of various worldly attachments is called the bliss of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-sukha*). Through the seclusion resulting from the abandonment of sensual desires and evil, unwholesome states, there is the joy and bliss born of seclusion in the first *dhyāna*.

It is called the bliss of seclusion. In the second and subsequent dhyānas, it is called the bliss of tranquility because of the subsiding of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*). And [in the final stage], it is due to the absolute dissociation from all afflictions (*kleśa*) and the perfect awakening to the reality of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-vastu-yathābhūta-abhisambodha*).
That which is happiness is called the happiness of perfect awakening (*saṃbodhi-sukha*).

Among these, causal happiness is happiness because it is the cause of happiness, but not by its own nature. The happiness of sensation is happiness not because of its status as a cause, but rather by its own nature.
In this way, pleasure that is the antidote to suffering is neither due to its being a cause nor by virtue of its own nature;
rather, it is pleasure simply from the subsiding of suffering and from the removal of suffering. It is not the pleasure of the interruption of feeling that is the cause.
Entities do not [become suffering] by virtue of their intrinsic nature, nor because of the removal of pain;
rather, whatever is felt here, that is considered to be suffering.

Happiness arises from the temporary cessation of abiding in ultimate suffering. The final [type of] happiness, comprised of the happiness free from affliction, is the happiness of perfect enlightenment; and in the future, it is likewise that very same ultimate suffering—

Because of the absolute pacification of space and because of the absolute transcendence of all factors of the afflictions and the underlying corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*) residing within the basis (*āśraya*) in this very life, there remains a bliss that is free from affliction; of that very [bliss], the final—
Because it is conducive, because it belongs to that side, and because it brings about that [state], it should be understood as unafflicted happiness.
In this regard, whatever happiness belongs to the side of benefit, that alone is [the happiness of a bodhisattva].

One should bestow [this] upon sentient beings, but not that which belongs to the side of harm. Furthermore, having thoroughly understood with correct wisdom that pleasure belonging to the side of harm is as it truly is,
one should deter sentient beings from it and, according to one's ability, cause it to be removed.

One should strive for the sake of liberation. Even that which is accompanied by suffering, if it is beneficial, should be provided to sentient beings who are unwilling, by the Bodhisattva together with suffering itself and together with dejection, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

By relying on skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), even that which is followed by pleasure but is harmful must be removed and extracted from beings who desire it, together with their pleasure and their mental joy.

By means of this reliance. For what reason? That [action] should be known as certain to lead to the future happiness of sentient beings; for it is that which, together with suffering, brings about benefit, and together with happiness, removes what is harmful. And for this very reason, the bodhisattva...

A wise being who desires the welfare of sentient beings should be known as one who, in reality, also desires their happiness. He who bestows welfare should also be known as one who bestows happiness; for in this way, welfare stands in the place of the cause, while happiness is the fruit.

It is like a dwelling place; therefore, it should be understood that he is indeed accompanied by happiness toward sentient beings. Whatever action is accompanied by benefit, therein lies the karma that results in a desired fruit.
In this present life and in future lives, that which is comprised of causal happiness,
that which is the antidote to suffering, that which is the happiness of the cessation of feeling,
and that which is the happiness free from affliction— this is exclusively for the Bodhisattva who is without hesitation.

One should bestow this upon sentient beings; for it is both beneficial and blameless. Furthermore, one should not bestow that pleasure of sensation comprised of the contact between sense faculties and their objects, nor that causal pleasure which leads to affliction, is defiled, or is accompanied by fault.
That which is unbeneficial and unwholesome, he should not provide to others. However, that which does not lead to affliction, or is unafflicted, blameless, beneficial, and wholesome—
that a bodhisattva should provide to sentient beings according to his ability and according to his strength.
Moreover, one should practice in that very same way oneself, train accordingly, and experience it firsthand.
This is to be understood as the benefit and happiness resulting from the welfare of self and others for bodhisattvas; there is nothing beyond this, nor anything more than this.

In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s benefit for self and others as comprised of cause and fruit? In brief, it should be understood that there are three kinds of causes and likewise three kinds of fruits: the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*), and merit (*puṇya*).
The cause is the fruit of merit; the cause of knowledge is the fruit of knowledge.

What is maturation (*vipāka*)? Briefly stated, there are eight kinds of maturation: excellence of lifespan, excellence of complexion, excellence of lineage, excellence of sovereignty, and excellence of being authoritative...

eloquence, great renown, human status, and strength—this is the eighth. Longevity and long endurance constitute the Bodhisattva’s perfection of life-span. Handsomeness, loveliness, amiability, and excellence of complexion—

Perfection of birth: being reborn into high families is the perfection of family. Perfection of sovereignty: possessing great wealth, a great faction, and a great retinue. Furthermore, he becomes trustworthy and reliable for sentient beings whenever they arise...

In those legal disputes, one should stand as an authoritative witness, free from deceit and guile, without using false weights such as brass or fraudulent scales. And regarding property that has been deposited—

He will be free from malice and non-deceptive; on that basis, he becomes one whose speech is accepted by sentient beings. This is called "having acceptable speech. Furthermore, great fame and renown become celebrated for him in the world, namely:
Whether it be heroism, vigor, or fortitude;
whether it be discernment, skill, or good character; or whether it concerns excellence in any particular art, craft, or field of activity—on account of such a cause, he is a teacher.

He becomes one who is to be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by the great body of people. This is called "great renown. The state of being a man, endowed with the male faculty, is humanhood. [Being] free from much illness...
029/11. A constitution free from disease and great vigor constitute the natural perfection of strength.

029/12. What is the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*)? Non-violence toward sentient beings and an intention of non-violence are the causes for the perfection of longevity. The gift of light and pure clothing is the cause for [the perfection of] complexion.

The cause of excellence is the subduing of pride toward sentient beings; this is the cause of excellence in family. Giving to those in need and to those lacking necessities is the cause of excellence in sovereignty. Speaking the truth, as well as being free from slander, harsh speech, and frivolous talk—

The habitual practice of idle chatter is the cause for one's speech not being accepted. For one who possesses the aspiration to establish various virtues within themselves in the future, worship of the Three Jewels and worship of the guru is the cause for attaining great authority. [Furthermore,] there is delight in human states of existence.

And there is an aversion to the female state. For one who perceives the defects therein, and for others, through two causes: by way of causing [others] to attain human status, and by way of creating a desire for women among those who delight in the female state. And [the defect of] women—

Through the quality of liberation from existence, it is the cause of human-hood for those humans who have been acquired and brought forth so as not to lose their male faculty. By means of the body, it consists of performing services and providing assistance for sentient beings.
Whenever duties arise, one should perform them according to one's power and strength, in accordance with the Dharma and without violence,
providing food, refreshments, gruel, drinks, and nourishing sustenance.

The provision of food and drink that provide sustenance for sentient beings is the cause for the accumulation of strength. Thus, these eight kinds of causes should be understood as the causes for the eightfold maturation (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, this cause is, in brief, nourished by three factors for the production of a fully developed, nourished, and sublime maturation. What are the three factors? Purity of mind, application, and...

Purification and the purification of the field. In that regard, there is the purity of intention through the dedication of those roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; and there is the intensity of intention through a profound, flavorful, and sublime [aspiration].

That which consists of approaching with affection, the great joy felt at the sight of a fellow practitioner of the Dharma, and the frequent application of thought and reflection upon that very same conformable Dharma every day and at every moment— this is...
This is called the purification of the mind. In this regard, it consists of long-term practice, uninterrupted performance, and skillful performance;

as well as praising others for that wholesome quality when they have not yet undertaken it, or [praising them] when they have already undertaken it. Furthermore, [it involves] encouraging them toward its completion.

Speaking in praise for the sake of gladdening them, and establishing and settling them in that very same root of virtue— this is called the purification of the application (*prayoga-viśuddhi*). In this regard, it is because the application is correctly accomplished in brief.
Furthermore, because one abides in the fruit of that very right application, the purification of the field is to be understood.
In that regard, what is the fruit of maturation? It is being endowed with a full lifespan, O Bodhisattva.
A being applies themselves to the side of the wholesome for a long time and accumulates a vast store of roots of virtue for their own benefit and for the benefit of others.

This is the fruit of the perfection of lifespan: a Bodhisattva endowed with excellence of complexion becomes dear to the great body of people; because he is dear, he becomes approachable. And by means of that form of great wisdom—

Because he has become accessible, the great mass of people considers his word worthy of being heard and put into practice. This should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of physical appearance (*varṇa-saṃpad*). A bodhisattva who is endowed with a noble family...
That being becomes esteemed by the great body of people, and is both honored and praised. Because he is esteemed, honored, and praised,
whatever matter he encourages beings toward, they are seized by his splendor and [follow] therein.
In that regard, they practice swiftly; they do not hesitate, nor do they falter in their lack of activity.
This should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of lineage.
A bodhisattva endowed with sovereign power gathers sentient beings through generosity.

He brings them to maturity. This should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of sovereignty. A bodhisattva whose speech is authoritative wins over sentient beings through pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency between words and deeds.

He gathers [beings] and brings them to maturity. This should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s authoritative speech. A bodhisattva known for his greatness becomes a companion to sentient beings in their various tasks and duties.

He becomes a benefactor. Because sentient beings have their minds bound by that benefit, out of respect and gratitude for him, they readily follow his commands with honor and diligence. This is [the perfection] of great majesty (*maheśākhyatā*) for the sake of awakening.

The fruit of this being should be understood as follows: having become a human, the bodhisattva is endowed with the male faculty for all virtues, all resolute endeavors, and all analytical investigations of the knowable; and he is fearless.
He possesses unobstructed movement in approaching, conversing with, dwelling together with, sharing enjoyments with, and being in private with all sentient beings at all times.

This should be understood as the fruit of manhood for a bodhisattva. Endowed with strength, the bodhisattva becomes untiring in the application of generating wholesome qualities and in the application of benefiting sentient beings; he is one who has initiated vigor.
Furthermore, one becomes firm in vigor and possesses swift super-knowledge (*abhijñā*).
This should be understood as the fruit of a bodhisattva’s perfection of power.
Thus, this is the [explanation] of the eightfold maturation of bodhisattvas.

Whatever kind of fruit there may be that is conducive and suitable for the benefit of sentient beings and for the arousal of the qualities of a Buddha— indeed, when a bodhisattva is established in such a fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), he is himself capable [of bringing it about].

He becomes capable of accomplishing various and abundant aims for sentient beings. Furthermore, those who are to be trained by him become compliant and ready to act according to his wishes, namely, with respect to the undertaking of their own welfare, provided that he himself...

This bodhisattva may be capable, yet his disciples might not be compliant. In this way, his performance of the welfare of others would neither be abundant nor skillful, such that he would be unable to accomplish the aims of others.
If this bodhisattva himself were incapable and lacking the power [to act],
while his disciples were those who could be directed toward the performance of beneficial tasks, even so,
the bodhisattva’s performance of the welfare of others would not be abundant nor skillful.
Because of this, he would be unable to accomplish the welfare of others. Therefore,

when both [conditions] are present and both perfections are attained, the Bodhisattva’s performance of the welfare of sentient beings becomes abundant and effective, whereby he is able to accomplish the welfare of others.

Having become such, that bodhisattva swiftly brings his own buddha-qualities to maturity, as well as sentient beings in the three vehicles, and personally realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

He is awakened; and he liberates those beings who have reached maturity. By this method, because the eightfold fruit of maturation of the bodhisattvas exists for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, therefore, whoever—
For sentient beings, cyclic existence is barren and purposeless; for them, however, it becomes non-barren and of great significance.
In this regard, what is merit? What is knowledge? Merit, in brief, consists of three perfections: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, and the perfection of patience.
Knowledge, moreover, is one perfection, which is...

Furthermore, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation should be understood as belonging to the side of merit and the side of knowledge. This is because, by relying on vigor, one gives gifts, undertakes ethical discipline, guards it, and practices loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].

And he cultivates the immeasurables. This is the category of merit consisting of such exertion; furthermore, it is the vigor by relying upon which one applies oneself to the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, or to skill in the aggregates.
He cultivates skillfulness regarding the elements (dhātu), skillfulness regarding the sense bases (āyatana), skillfulness regarding dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda),
and skillfulness regarding what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna). He understands suffering as suffering,
its origin as its origin, its cessation as its cessation, and the path as the path.
He examines from the perspective of the path: he contemplates, as they truly are, phenomena that are wholesome or unwholesome,
blameworthy or blameless, to be cultivated or not to be cultivated, inferior or superior, dark or bright,
and those phenomena that have arisen dependently with their specific distinctions.

One discriminates and examines. This is called the energy belonging to the side of knowledge (*jñāna-pakṣya-vīrya*), which, relying upon meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), either gives gifts, undertakes and guards moral discipline (*śīla*), or cultivates the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*). This is it.

Such is the meditative absorption (dhyāna) belonging to the side of merit. Furthermore, relying upon that meditative absorption, one applies oneself to the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
or else, one should speak of skillfulness regarding the aggregates (skandha-kauśalya), as previously described.

Just as in the case of vigor, this is called the meditative concentration belonging to the side of knowledge (*jñāna-pākṣya-dhyāna*). Furthermore, this merit and knowledge, in brief, are of six kinds. A-³⁴.
This measure, however, should be understood according to each individual classification.
What is the cause of merit and knowledge? In brief, three causes of merit and knowledge should be known: the basis for the acquisition of merit and knowledge...
That desire which does not lead to accumulation, the favorable and non-adverse condition,
and the prior cultivation of merit and knowledge. In this context, the "non-adverse condition" refers to the non-presence of adverse conditions.

It is the state of being set aside; it is the presence of a non-perverted condition; it is the state of being near. In this context, that which arises by relying on a bad friend (pāpamitra), such as a perverted teaching of merit and knowledge, or the grasping of what is perverted through a perverted mental attention (manasikāra).
This is called the presence of contrary conditions. By the opposite of this, through the white side (the virtuous category), the presence of non-contrary conditions is to be understood.
And for one who is engaged in the attainment, maintenance, and increase of merit and knowledge—

The avoidance of those obstacles and their non-arising is called the "non-deficient condition" for a bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom. Due to the deficiency of even one of these three causes, there is neither merit nor wisdom.
Birth is to be understood [in this way].
What is the fruit of merit and knowledge? Relying upon merit, the bodhisattva wanders through cyclic existence unharmed and is not excessively afflicted by sufferings.

Being unoppressed, the Bodhisattva is able to accomplish the welfare and benefit of sentient beings according to his wish. Relying upon knowledge, he correctly accumulates merit and not falsely; [he possesses] diverse and immeasurable skillfulness.
And by means of that activity, up until one awakens to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment— thus,
in brief, this fruit of merit and gnosis should be understood as fourfold according to its application, and it is immeasurable.

[This is] by way of these various types and distinctions. In this regard, whatever is maturation (*vipāka*), whatever is the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), and whatever is the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*)—all of this is dependent upon merit (*puṇya*) and has the power of merit; it is merit.
Furthermore, it is based on knowledge and originates from knowledge; therefore, both of these are primary for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. [This refers to] merit.

Furthermore, supreme knowledge is unsurpassed. Due to the deficiency of either merit, knowledge, or both, this bodhisattva would not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening. Thus, this is the bodhisattva’s [cultivation of] cause and fruit.
One should understand that the welfare of oneself and others is comprised [within this].

In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s welfare of self and others pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadhārmika*), and what is that pertaining to future lives (*sāmparāyika*)? [It consists of] appropriate engagement in the fields of craft and work...
The acquisition of enjoyments through [favorable] circumstances and human effort,
as well as the moderate enjoyment of those very enjoyments once acquired; and that which, in this present life, pertains to the ripening of the maturation of previous karma whose fruit was intended.

The enjoyment of the fruit: for a bodhisattva skilled in the withdrawal from meditative absorption, the reliance upon that [absorption] in this very life is for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*), and not for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others. The reliance upon meditative absorption—

The basis is that which constitutes the nirvana in this very life for one who has become a Tathāgata, as well as those conditioned phenomena— both mundane and supramundane— which lead to the attainment of nirvana in this very life. This is called the bodhisattva’s [nirvana] in this very life.
One's own welfare is indeed one's own purpose. Just as it is for a bodhisattva, so too should the welfare of others be understood for those beings who have been disciplined by a bodhisattva.
In that regard, there is the excellence of enjoyments in another world within the desire realm, and...

The excellence of the personal existence in the future life consists in that which is rebirth in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless realms (*ārūpya*) in the future. And regarding that excellence of the personal existence and enjoyments in the future life,
as well as the rebirth in the meditative absorptions and formless realms, [it is] together with suffering in the present life.

Together with mental distress, through repeated careful consideration, there is the cultivation of causes. This should be understood as the bodhisattva’s benefit for himself and others pertaining solely to future lives. Furthermore, that which pertains to the present life, together with...
