The cultivation of causes for the attainment of enjoyments and the excellence of the personal existence, together with pleasure and mental joy, which here belongs to the category of non-decline, [refers to] the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the formless attainments (ārūpya).
This is an offense. This should be understood as the benefit for oneself and others pertaining to both the present life and future lives.
What is the ultimate benefit for oneself and others? And what is the [non-ultimate]...
Non-final [attainment] refers to the excellence of enjoyments and personal existence within the desire realm, together with their causes and results;
as well as the mundane purity of ordinary persons, together with its causes and results.
Final [attainment] refers to the welfare of oneself and others, which consists in the complete abandonment of all afflictions by the noble ones.
The eightfold path and those worldly wholesome dharmas acquired by relying upon it— this is called the ultimate benefit for oneself and others. In this regard,
there is both ultimacy and non-ultimacy due to three causes.

It should be understood [in three ways]: by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), by way of retrogression (*parihāṇi*), and by way of the exhaustion of the enjoyment of the fruit (*phalopabhogaparikṣaya*). Among these, (17a) by way of intrinsic nature, *nirvāṇa* is ultimate; all that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is non-ultimate. The Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*)—

Because it is subject to decline and because its enjoyment of the fruit is exhausted, it is not ultimate. Other wholesome, contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are non-ultimate, as they are subject to decline and the exhaustion of the enjoyment of their fruit.

Thus, this is the tenfold benefit for oneself and others of the bodhisattvas, both in brief and in detail. In this regard, bodhisattvas should train according to their ability and according to their strength; there is nothing beyond this, nor anything more than this, even in the past time.
Furthermore, those who in the future have trained, or will train, for the sake of their own and others' welfare—
all of them do so within these very ten kinds of welfare for oneself and others; there is nothing beyond this, nor anything more than this.
In the Bodhisattvabhūmi, within the Foundation (Ādhāra) Yoga Station, the third chapter: "The Benefit of Oneself and Others."

What is the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*)? Briefly, it is twofold: (1) the state of being as it is (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*), concerning the actual nature (*bhūtatā*) of phenomena (*dharma*); and (2) the state of being as far as they extend (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), concerning the totality (*sarvatā*) of phenomena. This is the state of being as it is (*bhūtatā*).

The totality of all phenomena (*sarvatā*) should be understood as the complete meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*). Furthermore, that meaning of reality is fourfold according to its various classifications:
that which is established by worldly consensus, that which is established by reasoning, and that which pertains to the purification of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi*).

The sphere of knowledge (*jñāna-gocara*) and the sphere of knowledge consisting in the purification of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara*). In this regard, for all worldly beings, with respect to a given object, there is seeing by means of an intellect that has entered into conventional designations, worldly conventions, and traditional transmissions.
There is a state of equality, namely: as with earth, one recognizes "this is earth itself, not fire.
As it is with earth, so it is with fire, water, wind, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, food, drink, and vehicles.

Regarding clothing, ornaments, and personal articles; household utensils and furnishings; perfumes, garlands, and ointments; dancing, singing, and instrumental music; light; the attendance of women and men; fields, shops, houses, and property; pleasure and pain—[these are the objects of contact]. Duhkha...
"This is pleasant, not painful; this is pain, not pleasant.
In brief, "this is this, not that; it is thus, not otherwise"—such is the object of certain conviction for all ordinary people.

That which is grasped through a convention handed down by tradition, established by one's own conceptual construction, and not having been reflected upon, weighed, or examined— this is called reality established by worldly consensus (*loka-prasiddha-tattva*).

What is the reality established by reasoning (*yukti-prasiddha-tattva*)? It is that which is [established] for the wise, those learned in the meaning of reason, the discerning, the logicians (*tārkika*), and the investigators (*mīmāṃsaka*),
who abide on the level included within reasoning and possess their own intuitive intelligence.

Based upon the means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception, inference, and authoritative scripture— which belong to the level of ordinary persons and involve the pursuit of investigation—
one establishes through the reasoning that proves by logical proof that the object of knowledge, which is the domain of well-ascertained cognition, is [as it appears].
That has been established. This is called reality established by reasoning (*yukti-prasiddha-tattva*).
What is reality that is the object of the knowledge purified of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara-tattva*)?

The range and object of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, by means of their untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), the untainted knowledge that brings about attainment (*anāsravāvāhaka*), and the worldly knowledge obtained subsequent to the untainted (*anāsrava-pṛṣṭhalabdha-laukika-jñāna*)— this is called the knowledge of the purification of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna*).

The reality of the sphere of activity: by means of that object of focus, knowledge is purified from the obscuration of afflictions, and one abides in a state of non-obscuration for the future. Therefore, it is called the reality that is the sphere of activity for the knowledge that purifies the obscuration of afflictions.
Furthermore, what is that reality? It is the four noble truths:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
For one who investigates and realizes these four noble truths, [there arises...]
And that knowledge arises regarding those [truths] which have not yet been realized. Furthermore,
that realization of the truths belongs to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who perceive only the aggregates (skandha) and do not perceive a self as a distinct entity separate from the aggregates.

It arises from the repeated practice of seeing the non-existence of a person (pudgala) as distinct from the aggregates (skandhas), by means of wisdom associated with the arising and passing away of conditioned phenomena produced through dependent origination, wherein [the person] is not apprehended.

What is the reality that is the domain of the knowledge purified of the obscuration to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara*)? The obstruction of knowledge regarding the knowable is called an "obscuration.
The domain or object of the knowledge that is liberated from that obscuration to the knowable is [that reality].
The reality that is the objective domain of the knowledge purified of the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) should be understood.
Furthermore, what is that? It is that which has been entered by Bodhisattvas and the Blessed Buddhas for the sake of entering into the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya). Well—

And that which is the objective domain of the pure gnosis— which, starting from the ineffable intrinsic nature of all phenomena, is equal to the object of knowledge that is non-conceptual regarding the intrinsic nature of designations and verbal expressions— that is the supreme, unsurpassed suchness.
The thorough discernment of all phenomena, which has reached the furthest limit of the knowable, proceeds correctly;
it does not turn back, nor does it regress.
Furthermore, that characteristic of reality (tattva-lakṣaṇa) should be understood as being established as non-dual in nature. Duality refers to existence (bhāva) and non-existence (abhāva).
In this context, existence is that which is established as having the nature of conceptual designation (prajñapti-vāda-svabhāva).

And in that very same way, it has been clung to by the world for a long time. It is the root of all the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of the world; namely, such as "form" (*rūpa*), or "feeling" (*vedanā*), "perception" (*saṃjñā*), "mental formations" (*saṃskāra*), or "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); or "the eye" (*cakṣus*), or "the ear" (*śrotra*).
Or the nose, tongue, body, and mind; or earth, water, fire, and air; or form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects; or the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate.
Whether as "done," or as "arising," or as "passing away"; whether as "dependently originated," or as "past," or as "future," or as "present";
whether as "conditioned" or as "unconditioned"—this is the world.

The world beyond; both the sun and the moon; whatever has been seen, heard, thought, or cognized; what has been attained, sought after, or investigated by the mind and reflected upon; or even, ultimately, Nirvana.
Thus, this kind of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), which is established through conventional designations (prajñapti-vāda-nirūḍha) regarding phenomena,
is called "existence" (bhāva) by the world.
In that regard, "non-existence" (abhāva) refers to that which pertains to this very designation, namely, "this is form."

39.19–21. Thus, the absence of a real entity (*nirvastukatā*) and the absence of signs (*nirnimittatā*) regarding the conventional designation "even unto *nirvāṇa*," and the total non-existence and non-occurrence of that basis for conventional designation upon which such designation proceeds.
This is called non-existence (*abhāva*). Furthermore, that which is liberated from both that previous existence and this non-existence— from both existence and non-existence— is the *dharma*.
The entity comprised of characteristics is non-dual. That which is non-dual is the middle way, free from the two extremes, and is called "unsurpassed.
And in that reality, for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, there is...
Pure knowledge is to be understood. Furthermore, in that regard, the knowledge of Bodhisattvas is to be understood as being characterized by the path of training.
And that wisdom is the great means for a bodhisattva to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that?
Because, by means of that conviction in emptiness, the bodhisattva—in those various [situations]—[is able to... [Tib. 22b]
Engaging in various births for the sake of ripening sentient beings and his own buddha-qualities,
he wanders through saṃsāra and understands saṃsāra as it truly is.
Furthermore, he does not [cling] to that saṃsāra through such aspects as impermanence and so forth.

He causes [the mind] to become thoroughly disenchanted. If he did not understand cyclic existence as it truly is, he would be unable to maintain equanimity toward the mind regarding all afflictions, such as attachment, aversion, and delusion. And being unable to maintain equanimity, he would remain afflicted.

If the mind were to wander in saṃsāra, it would never bring the Buddha-qualities to maturity, nor would it [bring] sentient beings [to maturity]. However, if one should cause the mind to become weary of saṃsāra through aspects such as impermanence and so forth, then in that case, the bodhisattva will very quickly...

[If] he were to enter parinirvāṇa— were a bodhisattva to enter parinirvāṇa very quickly— even in that case, he would not bring the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma) to maturity, nor would he bring sentient beings to maturity. How much less could he realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?
By means of that very resolve for emptiness, the bodhisattva,
while applying himself [to practice], neither fears nirvana nor does he long for nirvana.
If the bodhisattva were to fear nirvana, [he would fall] into another [extreme of] nirvana.

His equipment would not be fulfilled because his mind is terrified [of nirvana], as he does not perceive its benefits and is devoid of the serene faith and resolve that arise from perceiving the qualities inherent in it— such being the case for a bodhisattva. However, if [the bodhisattva]...
A sentient being who dwells frequently in the aspiration for nirvāṇa would enter parinirvāṇa too quickly.

Because of entering parinirvāṇa so quickly, they would not bring the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma) to maturity, nor would they bring sentient beings to maturity. In that regard, [the bodhisattva] perceives cyclic existence as it truly is...
For one who does not fully understand, there is the wandering in saṃsāra with a defiled mind;
and for one whose mind is weary of saṃsāra, there is the swift attainment of nirvāṇa; and that which [arises] from nirvāṇa...

For one whose mind is terrified and who, due to the non-completion of those provisions, dwells frequently in the aspiration for nirvāṇa, there is a swift parinirvāṇa. This should be understood as a non-expedient for a bodhisattva regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Furthermore, there is the wandering in saṃsāra by one who thoroughly understands saṃsāra as it truly is, with an undefiled mind; and there is the non-hastening toward nirvāṇa by one whose mind is not distressed by saṃsāra through such aspects as impermanence and so forth; and [that which pertains] to nirvāṇa...

For one whose mind is undaunted, through the fulfillment of those provisions and by seeing the qualities and benefits in nirvāṇa, yet without falling into excessive longing for it, there is no premature extinction. This is the great skillful means of a bodhisattva for [attaining] unsurpassed [enlightenment].

for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment. And this means is based upon that conviction in supreme emptiness. Therefore, that cultivation of conviction in supreme emptiness is the path of training for a bodhisattva.

It is said that a great skillful means has been grasped, namely, the realization of the Tathāgata’s knowledge. Indeed, by means of that deeply penetrated knowledge of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*), that bodhisattva [realizes] the ineffable intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

Having understood these things as they truly are, he does not conceptualize any phenomenon in any way whatsoever; he perceives nothing other than the mere thing (*vastu-mātra*) and mere suchness (*tathatā-mātra*).
Yet, it does not occur to him that "this is a mere thing" or "this is suchness."
And [it is said]: "only as a designation. Yet that Bodhisattva acts for the sake of the ultimate meaning.
Acting for the sake of the supreme meaning, he perceives all phenomena through wisdom exactly as they are—equally identical with that suchness. Everywhere seeing with equanimity, his mind is even.
He attains supreme equanimity,
relying upon which the bodhisattva, while applying himself to skill in all branches of knowledge,
does not turn back despite all exhaustion or the onset of all sufferings; he quickly [attains his goal].
With body untiring and mind untiring, he fully accomplishes that skillfulness.

He attains the empowerment of the great power of mindfulness, yet he does not become arrogant because of that skillfulness, nor does he practice the "teacher's fist" (withholding knowledge) toward others.
He possesses a mind that is not discouraged regarding all forms of skillful means; he is energetic and his progress is unimpeded; he applies himself with firm armor, just as—
Just as he experiences specific sufferings while wandering in saṃsāra,
so too does he increase his enthusiasm for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Just as he attains specific distinctions in his physical form, so too does he [attain] emanations—
He becomes more and more gentle toward sentient beings. To the extent that he attains a specific realization of knowledge, to that same extent he increasingly avoids provoking others,
engaging in disputes, idle chatter, and the afflictions and secondary afflictions, as well as lapses in conduct.
Having thoroughly understood [the mind] again and again in relation to its active manifestations, he maintains equanimity toward the mind.
Just as he increases in virtues, so too does he become one whose goodness is concealed; he does not seek to be known by others, nor does he seek gain.

042/12. Honor. These and many other such benefits accrue to the bodhisattva who relies upon that knowledge—benefits that belong to the side of enlightenment and are conducive to awakening. Therefore, whoever [seeks] to attain enlightenment...
Whosoever have attained, whosoever will attain, and whosoever are attaining— all of them do so by relying upon this very knowledge, and not upon anything else, whether inferior or superior. Thus,
the bodhisattva who has ascended to the way free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) acts in this manner.
It is of great benefit for the ripening of one's own Buddha-qualities and for the ripening of the qualities of the three vehicles in others; thus one becomes correctly established.
Furthermore, one becomes correctly established in this manner.

He becomes free from craving for enjoyments and for his own person. And he trains himself in that state of freedom from craving for the sake of abandoning enjoyments and his own person among sentient beings, solely for the benefit of sentient beings. Furthermore, he is restrained and well-restrained by means of the body.

He trains in the restraint of speech for the sake of a natural distaste for evil and a natural state of goodness and virtue. He becomes patient toward all harms and misconducts from others, and he trains in patience for the sake of having little anger.
And for the sake of not harming others, he applies himself to all branches of knowledge, whether as a student or as one already skilled;
this is for the purpose of removing the doubts of sentient beings and for their benefit.
For the sake of bringing [the practice] to completion and for his own acquisition of the causes of omniscience,

he becomes one whose mind is inwardly established and well-concentrated; and he trains in the stability of the mind for the sake of purifying the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and the five [supernormal powers].

And for the sake of sporting with the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, and for the sake of dispelling the fatigue born from application to all forms of skillfulness,
he becomes discerning and a knower of the supreme reality; and this is for the sake of knowing the supreme reality.
He trains in the Mahāyāna for his own final nirvāṇa in the future.
That bodhisattva, thus correctly engaged, attends to sentient beings who possess virtues with offerings, gains, and honors.

Toward sentient beings who possess faults, he remains present with a mind of supreme compassion and a mind of sympathy. According to his ability and according to his strength, he applies himself to their abandonment of those faults. Toward sentient beings who cause him harm, he maintains a mind of loving-kindness.

He remains present with a state of mind that is straightforward; and according to his ability and according to his strength, being free from deceit and free from guile, he provides for their welfare and happiness. Regarding those who have done him harm, [he abandons] any state of enmity arising from the fault of his own underlying intention or application.

For the sake of abandonment, he stands ready to repay his benefactors with a return service equal to or greater than what was done for him. Furthermore, he fulfills their righteous expectations according to his ability and according to his strength, even when he is not capable.

And when requested, he demonstrates diligence and exertion toward those various tasks and duties; he does not reject them at once. [He thinks: "How might this person be made to understand that I am incapable, not that I am unwilling to act? Thus, in this way—

The correct application of a bodhisattva who has ascended to the method free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca-naya*) and relies upon the knowledge of supreme reality (*paramatattvajñāna*) should be understood as follows.
In that regard, by what reasoning is the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpyasvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena [established]?
This designation of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena—
namely, "form" or "feeling," and so forth as before,
up to and including "nirvāṇa"— should be understood as being merely a conceptual designation (*prajñaptimātra*).
It should be understood that there is neither an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor anything other than that which is distinct from it,
which is the range of speech or the object of speech. This being so, there is no intrinsic nature.

Of phenomena, it exists in such a way as it is described; yet, moreover, it is not non-existent in every respect. Furthermore, while it does not exist in that manner, it is not entirely non-existent in every respect. How so?

It exists. It exists as that which is free from the grasping of the superimposition of what is non-existent, and free from the grasping of the denial of what is existent. Furthermore, this ultimate intrinsic nature (*pāramārthika-svabhāva*) of all phenomena belongs exclusively to non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

The sphere of activity is to be understood as follows: if, moreover, those phenomena (*dharma*) upon which a verbal expression operates regarding a given object were to possess that very nature as their essence, then that object would consist of many diverse intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). Such being the case, there would be many kinds of numerous intrinsic natures.

[These] would belong to a single phenomenon (dharma) and a single entity (vastu). For what reason? Because, with respect to a single phenomenon and a single entity, many various kinds of designations (prajñapti), metaphorical usages (upacāra), and conventions are made by means of numerous expressions.
Furthermore, no fixed rule is found among the many various types of conventional designations (prajñapti-vāda) such that, by means of any single conventional designation,
that phenomenon (dharma) or that entity (vastu) would possess identity with it, consist of it, or be of its nature.
There would be an intrinsic nature [of things] through other remaining designative expressions. Therefore,
all phenomena and all entities do not possess identity with, nor are they composed of, nor are they identical to, all designative expressions, whether complete or partial.

Furthermore, if phenomena such as form were to possess the nature of conceptual designation and verbal expression as previously described, then first there would have to be a real entity, and subsequently, based upon that, the metaphorical application of conceptual designation and verbal expression would occur according to one's inclination.
Prior to the application of the conventional expression of designation, when the application of the conventional expression of designation has not yet been made,
that dharma would be devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). If it were devoid of intrinsic nature—
If there were no basis for designation, a conventional expression devoid of a real entity would not be tenable.

Furthermore, if the metaphorical application of conventional expression did not exist, it would not be tenable for a phenomenon—that is, a real entity—to have the nature of a conventional expression. Moreover, if [it were the case that] even previously...

If a designation (*prajñapti-vāda*) were applied through the application of a designation even when it has not been made, then that phenomenon (*dharma*) would be of the same nature as that object (*vastu*). This being the case, even without that application of the designation "form" (*rūpa*),
there would be a phenomenon designated as "form" by the application of the designation "form."
Regarding a known object, the cognition of "form" (rūpa) would arise; yet it does not so arise.
For this reason and by this logic, the ineffable intrinsic nature (nirabhilāpya-svabhāva) of all phenomena is to be understood. As it is with form, so it is with [the other aggregates].
The factors beginning with sensation (vedanā), as they have been described, should be understood to extend ultimately to the limit of nirvāṇa.
These two should be declared to have strayed from this Dharma and Vinaya.

And whoever, through the superimposition of what is unreal, adheres to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena such as form— the nature of which consists in the expression of designations (*prajñaptivādasvabhāva*) regarding things such as form; and whoever likewise [adheres] to the signs (*nimitta*) and so forth of those expressions of designations—

By denying that entity— which is the basis for the signs of conventional designations and which exists as the ultimate reality by virtue of its ineffable nature— one destroys it by asserting that "it does not exist at all. First, regarding the faults in the superimposition of what is non-existent:

These have already been previously examined, set forth, clarified, and explained. It should be understood that by means of those faults, one becomes lost to this Dharma and Vinaya through the superimposition of what is non-existent upon entities such as form (*rūpa*). Furthermore, as follows:
One who denies even the mere existence of a thing (*vastu-mātra*) regarding phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) is a total nihilist and has strayed from this Dharma and Vinaya.
I shall likewise explain the mere existence of a thing for phenomena such as form.
For one who denies [the existence of things], neither reality nor designation is possible;
both of these are untenable. For example, when the aggregates such as form exist—

The designation of a person (pudgala) is tenable when [the aggregates] exist, but not when they do not exist. The designation of a person would be without a basis (nir-vastuka). This being so, the metaphorical application of the discourse designating phenomena such as form is tenable only with respect to the mere existence of those phenomena such as form.

Without [an object], there is no conventional designation or metaphorical expression that is devoid of a real basis (*nirvastuka*). In that case, since the objective basis (*vastu*) for the designation does not exist, the designation itself, being without a foundation (*niradhiṣṭhāna*), cannot exist either. Therefore, some [people] [reject] those sutras associated with the Mahāyāna which are difficult to comprehend.

Having heard profound teachings associated with emptiness that explain the intended meaning, and failing to understand the meaning of what was spoken as it truly is, they engage in improper conceptualization and,
by means of mere ratiocination applied incorrectly, hold such views.
They speak thus: "All this is merely a conceptual designation (prajñapti-mātra);
this is the reality (tattva). He who sees it thus sees correctly.
For them, because that very basis of designation—the mere thing (vastu-mātra)—does not exist, that [designation] itself...

Designation does not exist at all in any way; how much less could designation-only be the reality? Therefore, by this line of reasoning, they have repudiated both reality and designation, as well as both together.

He exists. Because he denies both conventional designations and reality, he should be understood as a preeminent nihilist. Being such a nihilist, he is one with whom the wise who practice the holy life should neither speak nor dwell; he brings ruin even upon himself.

He causes [others] to fall; even the world that follows his views is brought to ruin. And it was with this in mind that the Blessed One said: "It is better for some person here to have a view of a self than for some other person to have a wrongly grasped emptiness. Why is that?
For this reason: a person who holds the view of a self (pudgala-dṛṣṭika) is merely deluded regarding the object of knowledge;

he does not, however, deny all objects of knowledge. On that account, he would not be reborn in the miserable states (apāya), nor would he [be hindered] from seeking the Dharma for the sake of liberation from suffering.
One should not deceive or mislead others; one should establish them in the Dharma and in truth, and one should not be lax regarding the precepts of training.
Furthermore, by means of emptiness wrongly grasped, one may become deluded regarding the objects of knowledge;
one may even deprecate all that is to be known. On that account, one is reborn in the states of woe, and one brings ruin to another who is righteous and seeks liberation from suffering.
One would also become lax regarding the precepts of training. By disparaging such a matter, one becomes lost to this Dharma and Vinaya.
Furthermore, how is emptiness wrongly grasped? Whoever...

Whether it be a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, they do not accept that by which something is empty, nor do they accept that which is empty. This is called emptiness wrongly grasped in such a manner. Why is that? Because [they reject] that very thing by which it is empty.

Because of the non-existence [of a thing], that which is empty would be untenable as emptiness due to its existence. Furthermore, if there were a total absence of everything, where, what, and by what would there be emptiness? Nor is it logical for something to be empty of itself. Therefore, it is thus:
Emptiness is wrongly grasped.
Furthermore, how is emptiness rightly grasped? When one perceives that whatever is not present in a certain place, that [place] is empty of that [thing].

Furthermore, whatever remains there, one understands it as it truly is: "That exists here. This is called the entry into emptiness, which is according to reality and non-perverted. That is to say, with respect to the entity designated as "form" and so forth, as previously described.
The dharma whose nature consists of the conventional designation "form" and so forth does not exist.
Therefore, that entity designated as "form" and so on is empty of the nature of conventional designation. Furthermore, what [exists] therein as form and so on?
In the entity designated as such, the remainder— namely,
that very form and so forth— is the basis for the conventional expression; and both of these are...
One understands things as they truly are, namely: that there is only the mere thing (*vastu-mātra*) which exists,
and that regarding the mere thing there is only a mere designation (*prajñapti-mātra*),
neither superimposing what is non-existent nor denying what is existent, neither adding anything extra nor subtracting anything.

One does not diminish it, nor does one elevate it, nor does one add to it. One understands that suchness—the ineffable intrinsic nature—exactly as it is, just as it truly is. This is called emptiness well-grasped and thoroughly penetrated by right wisdom.
This, first of all, is the conformable reasoning that establishes through proof by which the ineffable intrinsic nature of all phenomena is to be understood. Furthermore,
according to authoritative scripture as well, all phenomena are of an ineffable intrinsic nature.
These should be understood as they were stated by the Blessed One in the *Bava-saṃkrānti-sūtra*, elucidating this very meaning through the singing of verses:
"For by whatever name each and every phenomenon is expressed..."
"That [entity] is not found therein; for that is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena.
How, then, does this verse elucidate this very meaning?
It refers to the fact that for a phenomenon designated as "form" and so forth, there is no such thing as "form" and so on [as a substantial entity].

Name: By means of such names as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, those phenomena designated as form and so on are expressed—specifically as "form," or "feeling" (*vedanā*), and so on, up to "nirvāṇa. In that regard, there are no [phenomena] designated as form and so on...

Phenomena themselves consist of form and so forth, and within them no phenomenon consisting of anything other than that form and so forth exists. Furthermore, regarding those phenomena designated as "form" and so forth, that which exists by way of an ineffable object—
This very [nature] should be understood as the ultimate reality, the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*svabhāva-dharmatā*).
And it was said by the Blessed One in the *Arthavargīya* verses:
"Whatever conventionalities there may be in the world..."
The Sage does not approach any of those [dharmas];
for since he does not approach them, by what means would he grasp them?
Not manifesting attachment toward what has been seen or heard—
how does this verse illuminate this very meaning? It refers to those designations such as "form" and so forth, which are applied to the entities designated as form and the rest.
These are called conventionalities (*saṃvṛti*). By means of those designations (*prajñapti*), he does not approach the idea that there is an identity between those conventionalities and that entity.
For what reason? Because he possesses no view characterized by superimposition or denial. Therefore, he...
Because that view, which manifests as a perversion, is absent, he is said to be "one who does not adhere. Being thus one who does not adhere, what would he take up?
Without that view, there could be no superimposition or denial regarding that object. [He is] non-appropriating...
Giving correctly, he possesses right view; that which is known by him is what has been seen.

Whatever subsequent verbal report regarding that very same object of knowledge there may be, that is what has been heard. Toward that which has been seen and heard, he does not produce craving, nor does he increase it; rather, he turns away from it.
By means of that object, he abandons [defilements] and dwells in equanimity; thus, he does not take pleasure [in them]. Furthermore, it was said by the Blessed One concerning Saṃtha-Kātyāyana:
"In this case, Saṃtha, a monk does not rely upon the earth..."

He meditates neither on water, nor fire, nor wind; not on space, nor consciousness, nor the sphere of nothingness, nor the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; not on this world, nor the other world, nor both;
not on the sun and moon, nor on what is seen, heard, thought, or cognized.

Whatever has been attained, sought after, mentally reflected upon, or investigated—that he meditates upon without relying on any of it. How does he meditate? He meditates without relying on earth, and so on in detail until all [elements].

He does not meditate by relying [on anything]. Here, Saṃtha, for a monk, whatever perception of earth there is regarding the earth has been eliminated; likewise, the perception of water regarding water, and so forth in detail.
050/01. To the extent that every perception of everything is eliminated, 050/02. a monk who meditates in this way does not meditate depending on earth, and so on in detail 050/03.
until he does not meditate depending on "everything is everything. Thus he meditates—
The gods, together with Indra, with Īśāna, and with Prajāpati, pay homage from afar to that monk:
"Homage to you, O noble being; homage to you, O supreme among men!"
"We do not understand upon what you are meditating.
How, then, does this scriptural passage elucidate this very meaning?
It refers to that notion such as "earth" which occurs with respect to an object designated as "earth" and so forth.

It is the designation through names and conventions. With respect to an object designated as "earth" and so forth, it is both superimposing and negating. It is superimposing when it apprehends an object as having an intrinsic nature consisting of that [designation]. It is negating when it apprehends the destruction of the ultimate reality of the mere object.
It is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*). And that perception has been eliminated for him.

Elimination is said to be abandonment and relinquishment. Therefore, from the perspective of authoritative scripture—namely, the supreme and most reliable scripture of the Tathāgata—it should be understood that [the nature of things] is ineffable.
"All phenomena are entities. [Objection: Since all phenomena thus possess an ineffable intrinsic nature, for what reason is verbal expression employed?
For indeed, without verbal expression, that ineffable nature of phenomena could not be communicated to others.
It cannot even be heard; for if there is neither speaking nor hearing, that ineffable intrinsic nature cannot even be known. Therefore, speech is employed for the sake of hearing and knowing.

Because that very suchness (tathatā) is not thus fully understood by the foolish, there proceeds an eightfold conceptualization (vikalpa) based upon that, which generates the three things and brings about the production of all sentient beings and the receptacle world (bhājana-loka). That—

Just as there is the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), so too there is the conceptualization of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*), the conceptualization of grasping at a whole (*piṇḍa-grāha-vikalpa*),

the conceptualization of "I" (*ahaṃ iti vikalpa*), the conceptualization of "mine" (*mameti vikalpa*), the conceptualization of the pleasant (*priya-vikalpa*), the conceptualization of the unpleasant (*apriya-vikalpa*),
and the conceptualization that is the opposite of both. Furthermore, this [conceptualization]...
What are the eight kinds of conceptualization that serve as the generators of these three objects:
namely, the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), the conceptualization of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*), and [the conceptualization of existence]...?

And the conceptualization of grasping at a whole (*piṇḍa-grāha-vikalpa*): these three types of conceptualization produce the basis for the proliferation of conceptualization, the object that serves as the support for the proliferation of conceptualization, which is designated by names such as "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth. Depending upon that object, there arises the designation of names and concepts.

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is grasped by verbal expression and permeated by names, notions, and verbal expressions, ranges over that very same object, proliferating (*prapañcayan*) in many ways and in numerous diverse forms. Among these, there is the conceptual construction of "I," and...
And the conceptual construction "this is mine"— these two conceptual constructions produce the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
which is the root of all other views, and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*),
which is the root of all other forms of conceit. In that regard, the [conceptualization] of what is pleasant...
The conceptualization of the small, the conceptualization of the unpleasant, and the conceptualization that is the opposite of both,
give rise to attachment, aversion, and delusion respectively. Thus, these eight kinds of conceptualization lead to the manifestation of this threefold reality.
It proceeds as follows: namely, the basis of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is the object of proliferation (*prapañca-vastu*);

and [the basis of] views, the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*), and passion, hatred, and delusion. Among these, the view of a self-existent body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) have their support in the object of proliferation that is conceptual construction.
Furthermore, attachment, aversion, and delusion are based upon the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the conceit "I am" (asmimāna).
By means of these three entities, the entire side of the active process (pravṛtti-pakṣa) of all worlds is fully elucidated without exception.

In this context, what is the conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*)? It is the conceptualization such as "this is form" with respect to an entity such as form; this is called the conceptualization of intrinsic nature.
What is the conceptualization of distinction (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*)? It is the [conceptualization] regarding that very same entity designated as "form" and so forth, such as:

"this is material," "this is immaterial," "this is visible," "this is invisible," and likewise, "this has resistance," "this is without resistance," "this is with outflows," or "this is without outflows."
Conditioned, unconditioned, wholesome, unwholesome, indeterminate, past, future, and present— by such immeasurable categories of distinction as these, by which [it is characterized].

That conceptualization of specific qualities which is based upon the conceptualization of intrinsic nature and which conceptualizes that particular object is called "conceptualization of specific qualities" (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*).
What is the "conceptualization of grasping as a whole" (*piṇḍa-grāha-vikalpa*)? It is that which [occurs] with respect to that very same [object], such as form (*rūpa*), etc.

Regarding an object designated [as such], it proceeds accompanied by the notions and mental constructions of a self, a sentient being, a living soul, and a creature; it proceeds based on the cause of grasping at a composite whole with respect to many aggregated phenomena,
as in the cases of a house, an army, a forest, food, drink, vehicles, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding garments and so forth, that which is accompanied by the designation and convention of "that" is called the conceptualization of grasping at a whole (*piṇḍa-grāha-vikalpa*).
What is the conceptualization of "I" and "mine"? It is that thing...

That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and subject to grasping (*sopādānīya*), which has for a long time been habituated to, adhered to, and familiarized as "self" or "belonging to self"— from that habituation to such grasping, there arises, in dependence upon its own object which serves as a basis for views, [false] discrimination.
052/14. Furthermore, there is the conceptual construction [of the self]. This is called the conceptual construction of "I" and "mine.
052/15. What is the conceptual construction of the pleasant? It is the conceptual construction that has as its objective support a beautiful and agreeable thing.

What is the conceptualization of the unpleasant? It is the conceptualization that has as its object an impure and disagreeable thing. What is the conceptualization that is the opposite of both the pleasant and the unpleasant? It is that which is pure...

Conceptualization has as its object a thing that is beautiful, ugly, both, or devoid of both. Briefly stated, these two consist of conceptualization itself and the thing that serves as the basis for conceptualization and the object of conceptualization.

Both of these should be understood as being beginningless and mutually causal: past conceptualization [serves] for the manifestation of the object that is the basis of present conceptualization, and present [conceptualization],
in turn...
A thing that has appeared as an object of conceptualization (*vikalpālambana*) is the cause for the manifestation of a present conceptualization that takes it as its object. In this regard,
the lack of full comprehension (*aparijñāna*) of the conceptualization at present is [the cause] for the [future] thing that serves as its object.
And because that [consciousness] arises,
there necessarily follows the manifestation of the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) which has it as its basis and depends upon it, as well as its locus.
Furthermore, how does the thorough knowledge of this conceptualization come about?
It occurs through the four investigations and through the fourfold thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).

What are the four investigations? They are: the investigation of names, the investigation of things, the investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature, and the investigation of the designation of specific qualities.

In this regard, the search for names (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*) is when a bodhisattva perceives in a name merely the name itself. Likewise, the search for things (*vastu-paryeṣaṇā*) is the perception of a thing as merely a thing. [The search for designations of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñapti-paryeṣaṇā*) is] the perception of the designation of intrinsic nature as merely the designation of intrinsic nature.

The investigation of the designation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prajñapti*) consists in the vision of it as such. Regarding the designation of specific qualities (*viśeṣa-prajñapti*), the investigation of the designation of specific qualities consists in the vision of it as being merely the designation of specific qualities. He perceives the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) as distinct from the name and the thing (*vastu*).
And it is closely connected. One penetrates the designation of intrinsic nature and the designation of specific qualities, which are based on the close connection between names and things.
What are the four thorough cognitions of reality as it is? They are: the search for names...

The thorough knowledge of reality as it is consists of: that which pertains to the search for the object, that which pertains to the search for the designation of intrinsic nature, and that which pertains to the search for the designation of specific qualities.

What is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is regarding the search for names? It is when that bodhisattva, having searched for the state of being a mere name within a name, thoroughly knows that very name as it truly is: "This is the name; this is its referent."
A thing is established [with a name] only for the sake of designation (*saṃjñā*), for the sake of view (*dṛṣṭi*),
and for the sake of conventional usage (*upacāra*). If the name "form" were not established for the thing designated as "form," no one would perceive that thing as "form."

One should perceive in this way: not perceiving through superimposition, one should not become attached; while not becoming attached, one should not speak of it. Thus, that which is thus understood according to reality—
This is called thorough knowledge of reality as it is, pertaining to the search for names.
What is thorough knowledge of reality as it is, pertaining to the search for things?
It is when a bodhisattva, having searched for the mere-thingness of a thing within a thing, [realizes] all...
One perceives that entity designated as "form" and so forth as being dissociated from verbal expression and inexpressible. This is the second thorough knowledge of reality as it is,
pertaining to the search for entities (*vastveṣaṇāgata*).

What is the thorough knowledge of reality as it is regarding the search for the designation of intrinsic nature? It is when a bodhisattva, with respect to a thing designated as "form" and so forth, [realizes that] within the designation of its intrinsic nature, it is merely a designation.

Having investigated designations of intrinsic nature, one penetrates and understands, as it truly is, the appearance of that very intrinsic nature in a thing which lacks that intrinsic nature, by means of those designations of intrinsic nature. For him, [it is like] a magical creation, a reflection, or...

For one who perceives that intrinsic nature as being like an echo, a mirage, the moon in water, a dream, or an illusion— appearing as such yet not consisting of it— this is the third thorough knowledge of reality as it is, which has an extremely profound objective domain.

What is the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are regarding the search for the designation of distinctions? It is that by which Bodhisattvas, having searched for the mere nature of designation within the designation of distinctions, [realize] the distinction in that entity designated as "form" and so forth.
One perceives the designation (prajñapti) as non-dual in meaning. That entity (vastu) is neither an existent (bhāva) nor a non-existent (abhāva).
It is not an existent because it is not established by way of an expressible nature;
yet it is not a non-existent because it is established by way of an inexpressible nature.

Thus, it is not material from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), nor is it non-material from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), because there is a metaphorical designation of "material" therein. Just as existence and non-existence, and the material and the non-material,
so too are the distinctions such as visible and invisible.
All synonyms for designations (prajñapti) are to be understood in this same manner. Thus,
this specific designation [is to be understood] in this way by way of non-duality.

One understands reality as it is. This is called the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*) pertaining to the search for the designation of specific distinctions (*viśeṣa-prajñapti*).
In that regard, there is this eightfold false conceptualization (*mithyā-vikalpa*) of fools... [triple]...

The producer of the objective basis (*vastu*) brings about the world. Due to the deficiency and non-occurrence of the fourfold thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*), this [world] proceeds. Furthermore, from that false conceptualization (*mithyāvikalpa*), affliction (*saṃkleśa*) arises.

From affliction comes the wandering in saṃsāra; from the wandering in saṃsāra, the suffering consisting of birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth, which follows upon saṃsāra, proceeds. And when the Bodhisattva possesses the fourfold thorough knowledge of things as they truly are—

Relying on this, those eight kinds of conceptual construction are thoroughly understood. Through that correct thorough understanding in the present life, there is no further manifestation in the future of the entity that has fallen into conceptual proliferation— the basis and the object of those constructions.

It comes to be. Because that [object] does not arise and does not manifest, there is also no manifestation in the future of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that takes it as its object. Thus, the cessation of that conceptual construction which possesses a real basis (*savastuka*) is the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It should be understood that in this way, the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is the Mahāyāna parinirvāṇa of the bodhisattva. Furthermore, in this very life (*dṛṣṭe dharme*),
because his knowledge of the sphere of the supreme reality-meaning is purified, all—

In this regard, that bodhisattva attains mastery: namely, through various emanations by means of the miraculous power of emanation; through various transformations by means of the miraculous power of transformation; and in the knowledge of all that is to be known, as far as...
And he remains as a *preta* at will; and he passes away without external intervention according to his own desire.
Having thus attained mastery, he becomes superior to all sentient beings and unsurpassed. Such is that Bodhisattva who possesses mastery in all respects.
The five supreme benefits are to be understood as follows: one attains the highest tranquility of mind through the serenity of one's dwelling,
rather than through the mere subsiding of the afflictions.

Furthermore, his knowledge and vision regarding all fields of learning proceed unimpeded, completely pure, and fully perfected. Moreover, he does not become weary from wandering through cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings. Such is the case for the Tathāgatas.

And he penetrates all intentional teachings (*saṃdhāya-vacana*). Furthermore, due to his lack of dependence on others, he cannot be turned back from his resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) in the Mahāyāna.
Indeed, for these five kinds of benefits, there are five kinds of...

This should be understood as the action [of the bodhisattva]. It is the supreme dwelling in happiness in the present life for a bodhisattva who is dedicated to the application toward awakening; it is the benefit of mental tranquility that results from the destruction of physical and mental exhaustion caused by exertion.

This should be understood as the activity [of the bodhisattva]. It should be understood as the activity that constitutes the benefit of the bodhisattva’s unimpeded knowledge regarding all fields of learning (*vidyāsthāna*), which is the maturation of all the qualities of a Buddha. The maturation of sentient beings is—
The function of this should be understood as the benefit of not becoming weary of the cycle of existence for the sake of sentient beings;
it consists in the dispelling of the doubts that arise one after another among those to be trained,
and the long-term preservation of the guidance of the Dharma.

056/17/. It is the upholding [of the teaching] by means of thoroughly understanding, revealing, and removing those counterfeit forms of the True Dharma that cause the disappearance of the dispensation. This should be understood as the function of the benefit of entering into all intentional speech (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*). All—
The subduing of opponents, firmness of vigor, and non-retrogression from one's vow— this should be understood as the activity of the aspiration for being unshakeable and not dependent on others.
In this way, whatever constitutes the duty of a bodhisattva is all encompassed by these five activities of benefit. Furthermore, what is that duty? It is as follows: a—
Defiled self-happiness, the ripening of the Buddha-qualities, the ripening of sentient beings,
the upholding of the True Dharma, and unwavering resolve.
And for one who possesses ardent vigor, there is the suppression of the arguments of opponents.
Among those four meanings of reality, the first two should be known as inferior, the third as middling, and the fourth as supreme.
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the Foundation (*ādhāra-yogasthāna*),
this is the fourth chapter: "The Meaning of Reality" (*tattvārtha-paṭala*).

In this regard, what is the power (*prabhāva*) of the bodhisattvas? In brief, it is the accomplishment of all aims through mere wish by one who has attained mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), based upon that mastery over meditative concentration, for one whose mind is pliant and well-cultivated.
The noble power (*prabhāva*) is said to belong to one whose mind is free from attachment. Furthermore, the great fruitfulness and great benefit of the dharmas is called their power.
That which [arises] for the Buddhas from the previous accumulation of the great equipment of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*)— [End of fragment]
Furthermore, the innate nature of wonder and marvel belonging to the bodhisattvas—
this too should be understood as another innate power of theirs.
Indeed, this [power], according to its various classifications, pertains to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
It is of five kinds: the power arising from supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), the power consisting in the proclamation of the Dharma, innate power, power shared with Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
and power not shared with them.

In this regard, the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are: the domain of miraculous power (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*), the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), knowledge of the minds of others (*cetaḥ-paryāya*), recollection of former abodes (*pūrve-nivāsānusmṛti*), the vision of death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapāda-darśana*), and the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*). These are the powers of the supernormal knowledges.

It is said: therein, the six perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom—are called "all phenomena. The power inherent in those phenomena is called "the majesty of all phenomena."

In this context, what is supernormal power (*ṛddhi*)? Briefly, it is of two kinds: that consisting of transformation (*pāriṇāmikī*) and that consisting of emanation (*nairmāṇikī*). Furthermore, each of these two types is manifold according to its various subdivisions.
In that regard, what are the various types of transformative supernatural power (*pāriṇāmikī ṛddhi*)? They are as follows:
shaking, flaming, pervading, manifesting, transforming into something else, going and coming, contracting, and expanding.
Entering into all forms and bodies, approaching those of the same class,
appearing and disappearing, and exercising mastery over the supernatural powers of others.

Overpowering, the granting of eloquence, the granting of mindfulness, the granting of happiness, and the emission of rays— such as these are called "transformational" (*pāriṇāmikī*). In that regard, "trembling" refers here to the Tathāgata who has attained mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
With a mind rendered pliant (*karmanya*), a bodhisattva can cause even his monastery to tremble,
as well as his house, village, town, city, field, the world of hell-beings, the world of animals, the world of hungry ghosts, the world of humans, and the world of gods.

Furthermore, [he perceives] a world-system consisting of a single four-continent world, a thousandfold world-system, a two-thousandfold world-system, a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system,
a hundred such systems, a thousand such systems, a hundred thousand such systems, up to immeasurable and incalculable [world-systems].
He causes the trichiliocosm to tremble.
There, fire blazes from his upper body, while cool streams of water flow from his lower body; he blazes from his lower body, and [cool streams of water flow from his upper body].
From his body, streams of cool water flow forth in succession. He also enters the fire-element;
his entire body blazes forth.
From his entire blazing body, various rays of light issue forth—blue, yellow, red, and so on.
They are of the colors of white, madder-red, and crystal.
Therein, as for the pervasion: even that house is suffused with light, as well as the monastery, and so on as before, up to immeasurable and incalculable [worlds].

He pervades world-systems with his radiance as before, just as in the case of the earthquake. Therein, the manifestation is as follows: [he appears] seated comfortably and so forth, having arrived [before] śramaṇas, brahmins, śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and asuras.
To assemblies of *garuḍas*, *kiṃnaras*, and *mahoragas*,
the Tathāgata or a bodhisattva displays the lower realms below, as well as gods and humans above, and other Buddha-fields.
He manifests buddha-fields, and within them he displays Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— even those as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— having transcended even that many buddha-fields,
to whichever name a particular buddha-field is designated. Therein...
And whatever is the name of the Tathāgata in that Buddha-field,
he displays that Buddha-field and that Tathāgata, and that very name.
He designates it, and from that point he also demonstrates and designates what lies further back than that;
and beyond that, as much as he desires and for as long as he desires.
In that regard, if he intends to effect a transformation, such as [transforming] earth into water—

That which is resolved upon becomes exactly so and not otherwise. If one resolves upon fire or wind, that too becomes exactly so and not otherwise. If one resolves upon water or earth, or resolves upon fire or wind—if it be fire...
He resolves upon earth as water or wind;
if he resolves upon wind as earth, he resolves upon water or fire;
if he resolves upon fire as earth, or if he resolves upon wind as earth...

It is liberated. One resolves that water [is] fire; all that becomes exactly so and not otherwise. Just as there is no action of transformation into something else among the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) through their mutual transformation, so it is with visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
It should be understood that if one resolves upon substances such as grass,

cow dung, or clay as being food, drink, vehicles, clothing, ornaments, utensils, equipment, perfumes, garlands, or ointments; or [resolves upon] stones, pebbles, potsherds, and so forth [as such things].
And he resolves that [the earth] consists of jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, and coral.
Or, beginning with Himavat, the king of mountains, he resolves that all mountains are gold. All of that, too, is exactly so.
It is so and not otherwise. Likewise, one resolves that beings who are beautiful in color become ugly in color, and those who are ugly in color become beautiful in color.
Furthermore, for those who are devoid of both, one resolves that they become either beautiful in color or ugly in color.

Or both together, as in the case of beauty and ugliness. Likewise, with respect to being maimed or not maimed, being emaciated or stout, and so forth— whatever may be the case— that which is capable of being otherwise resolved upon than its actual specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
All that becomes exactly as one resolves it.
Therein, there is coming and going through walls, through mountains, and through...
He moves through walls with an unimpeded body; in detail,
he approaches and returns from as far as the Brahma-world,
and even further upward until the ultimate limit, or horizontally across immeasurable and infinite worlds.
He goes to and comes from incalculable trichiliocosm world-systems, either with a coarse body composed of the four great elements,
or by means of a speed like that of the mind, having resolved upon the distant as being near.
It goes and it comes.
Therein, as for contraction and expansion: even the Himavat, the king of mountains, he contracts to the size of an atom; and even an atom [he expands].
He extends [his power] over Himavat, the king of mountains. There,
before a great and diverse assembly, he performs the entry of all forms and bodies, including villages, towns, grass, forests, the earth, and mountains.
He causes that physical body to enter his own body, and that entire assembly perceives itself as having entered into that very same body. In this regard,
the approach to a common assembly is the approach to an assembly of kṣatriyas.
He enters. Once he has entered, whatever excellence of complexion they possess, such is his; whatever their height and girth, such is his;
whatever their protection of voice, such is his.

It comes to pass that whatever matter they discuss, he discusses that same matter; and even that matter which they do not discuss, he does not discuss. Furthermore, he provides them with superior, reasoned instruction.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse, he vanished. They did not even perceive his disappearance, wondering, "Who was this that vanished?
Was it a god or a human? Just as it was with the assembly of kṣatriyas, so it was [with the others].
The assemblies of brahmins, householders, and śramaṇas; the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa, the Yāma, the Tuṣita, and the Nirmāṇarati [heavens].

The gods who wield power over the creations of others (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), the Brahma-body gods (*brahmakāyika*), the ministers of Brahmā (*brahmapurohita*), the great Brahmās (*mahābrahman*), those of limited radiance (*parīttābha*), those of immeasurable radiance (*apramāṇābha*),
those of supreme radiance (*ābhāsvara*), those of limited purity (*parīttaśubha*), those of immeasurable purity (*apramāṇaśubha*), and those of pervasive purity (*śubhakṛtsna*).
The [heavens] Kṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa,
Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha. Therein, before a great assembly, he manifests and disappears.
A hundred times, a thousand times, or even more than that, he vanishes;
and again, in that very same way, he manifests and displays himself.
In this regard, his exercise of mastery extends to the entire realm of sentient beings.
It carries out all activities, such as going, coming, and staying.
If it occurs to him, "Let him go," he goes; "Let him stay," he stays; "Let him come," he comes; "Let him speak," he speaks.

In this regard, the Tathāgata’s surpassing of the supernatural powers of others means that, having surpassed the performance of supernatural power by all other possessors of such power, he accomplishes his purpose according to his will. A Bodhisattva who has reached the final stage— [is able to do so alone].

Except for a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva of equal spiritual lineage who is bound to one more birth (*carama-bhavika*), he surpasses all other Bodhisattvas in the performance of miraculous powers (*ṛddhy-abhisaṃskāra*). As for those other Bodhisattvas...
Excepting those who have entered a higher stage and those bodhisattvas of an equal class,
he surpasses all other possessors of supernatural power (*ṛddhimat*) regarding the manifestation of their supernatural powers (*ṛddhy-abhisaṃskāra*).
In that regard, the gift of eloquence provides eloquence when eloquence has been exhausted. In that regard,
the gift of mindfulness provides mindfulness regarding phenomena when mindfulness has been lost.
He applies mindfulness.
In that regard, the gift of happiness consists of those [beings] for whom he teaches the Dharma while speaking it.

They listen. To them, he provides such physical and mental assistance—the bliss of tranquility—by which they, free from hindrances, listen to the Dharma; and that [assistance] lasts only for that duration.
Through yoga, however, it is not permanently; he pacifies disturbances caused by an imbalance of the elements, those resulting from external circumstances, and those unleashed by non-human beings.
In that regard, the emission of rays is performed by a Bodhisattva or a Tathāgata through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).

He emits such rays from his body; some of them, having gone to immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions, cause the cessation of the hellish sufferings of beings in the hells. Some...

Having gone to the sublime abodes of the world of the gods— where the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas dwell with their respective palaces— he exhorts them to come here. Likewise, he exhorts the bodhisattvas residing in other world-systems.
In the immeasurable and innumerable world-systems throughout the ten directions, the Tathāgata briefly exhorts [beings] to come here by means of immeasurable, innumerable,
and diverse kinds of light rays for the sake of infinite sentient beings.
It performs a manifold, immeasurable, and incalculable benefit for beings.
Furthermore, all these varieties of transformative supernatural power (*pāriṇāmikī ṛddhi*),
when analyzed individually, are each immeasurable and incalculable.

[The phenomena] are to be understood in this way. Otherwise, the transformation of an existing entity from its natural state into something else is called *pariṇāma* (transformation). Therefore, this is called "transformative supernatural power" (*pāriṇāmikī ṛddhi*).

In that regard, what is transformational supernatural power (*nairmāṇikī ṛddhi*)? Briefly stated, it is a transformation devoid of a real basis (*nirvastuka*). When it is produced at will by means of the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), it succeeds;
this is called transformational supernatural power. And it is manifold—
It is of three kinds: the transformation of the body, the transformation of speech, and the transformation of objects.
Furthermore, that transformation of the body is either similar to oneself or dissimilar to oneself.
Or he creates for himself or for another a body that is either similar or dissimilar. Furthermore,
that bodily creation— whether similar or dissimilar to oneself or others—
creates sense-faculties that are concordant with the faculties (*indriya-sabhāga*) as well as the bases of the sense-faculties (*indriyādhiṣṭhāna*), but not the [actual] sense-faculties themselves.
064/05. He also creates emanations that resemble sense objects (*viṣaya*). For example: 064/06.
food, drink, and so forth; jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, and so on—whatever external requisites are comprised of form, odor, taste, and tangible objects—those he creates. 064/07. [End of section]

Free from that [previous form], he creates everything similar to it according to his desire. Furthermore, that [creation] is of many various kinds, resembling himself, and takes on the appearance of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas.

The form of a human, the form of an animal, a hungry ghost, or a hell-being; the form of a śrāvaka, the form of a pratyekabuddha, the form of a bodhisattva, or the form of a tathāgata. If he is exactly as the bodhisattva is, then he is exactly like that.
The emanation is perceived as distinct from oneself. That emanation of his is of the same class (*sabhāga*) as himself;
otherwise, the emanation is of a different class (*visabhāga*) from himself. If he emanates another being who has become a god, it is similar to that [god].

That emanation of his is similar to him. If he were to emanate something dissimilar, it would be of a different class from another, such as being like a god; in this same way, it should be understood up to being like a Tathāgata.

In this regard, what is the emanation of many bodies? Here, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva simultaneously [manifests] for immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems throughout the ten directions.

He performs a purpose by means of those variously colored emanations. Furthermore, he sustains certain emanations such that they continue even after the Bodhisattva or Tathāgata has passed away. Certain emanations [are sustained] by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
It is merely for the purpose of manifesting to sentient beings that it is like an illusion.
Furthermore, some things— such as food, drink, vehicles, clothing, and so forth— are real, [as are] jewels...
065/01. Furthermore, things such as pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, and coral are manifested;
it is exactly thus and not otherwise. By whatever wealth or utensil the function of wealth or utensils is performed—this, first of all, is the manifestation of the body regarding objects.
And [there is] pride.
Furthermore, there is the transformation of speech which is endowed with a beautiful tone;
there is that which is possessed of clarity and excellence, pertaining to oneself and pertaining to others.

[It is] unconnected, comprised within the teaching of the Dharma, and comprised within the movement of those who are heedless. In that regard, the excellent voice of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is [like] an emanated speech.

His speech is profound, possessing the resonance of thunderclouds; it resembles the voice of the kalaviṅka bird, captivating the heart, lovely, and endearing. That speech is refined, well-articulated, beautiful, distinct, intelligible, and worthy of being heard.
It is contrary [to worldly things], independent, and boundless. In that regard,
if a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva so desires, they may manifest a clear voice for the various [beings]—
gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth.

With his perfectly full voice, he made himself heard by the entire assembly of *garuḍas*, *kiṃnaras*, *mahoragas*, *śrāvakas*, and *bodhisattvas* who were seated and gathered together, extending as far as the circle of the assembly for a distance of one *yojana*. He addressed them all with wisdom...

He makes himself heard by those who are far away as well as those who are near and seated [around him]. Wishing, he makes himself known by his voice throughout the Sahasrikā and Cūḍikā world-systems, or the Dvisāhasra,
or the Trisāhasra, up to immeasurable and incalculable [world-systems] in the ten directions.
He makes the world-system aware with his voice; and from that sound, the teaching of the Dharma issues forth in manifold ways for the benefit of sentient beings.
In that regard, the verbal emanation connected with oneself is that which,
by means of speech that has been emanated by oneself, either teaches the Dharma or [restrains] one who is heedless.
He exhorts.
Furthermore, that which is connected to another is when one teaches the Dharma with speech produced by another,
or when one exhorts one who is heedless.
In that regard, unconnected verbal emanation is that which issues forth as speech from space,
or from an emanated being, but not from the mental continuum of a sentient being.
In that regard, the emanation of the teaching of the Dharma is that which occurs here and there for those who are deluded.
[This is] for the purpose of demonstrating the reasoning regarding the gifts.

In that regard, "incitement through emanation" refers to that which produces a sense of shame in those who are heedless— those who are not deluded and have attained serene confidence— regarding their heedlessness.
And for the purpose of instigating others toward heedfulness.
This aforementioned manifold emanation should be understood, in brief, as bodily emanation,
vocal emanation, and the emanation of objects.
Thus, this is the emanated supernatural power (*nairmāṇikī ṛddhi*). Furthermore, this should be understood as immeasurable and incalculable, due to the distinctions among each of its various types.
Moreover, both these two kinds of supernatural power belong to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
In brief, it accomplishes two tasks: either, having won over sentient beings through the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), it causes them to enter the teaching of the Buddha;
or, it provides manifold assistance of many various kinds to those who are suffering.
[He] bestows [these] upon those sentient beings.
In that regard, what is the knowledge of former abodes (*pūrva-nivāsa-jñāna*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
Here, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva, by means of himself, [knows] of himself...
To that extent, he recollects his former abodes: "Those beings were named such-and-such, where I was born with such-and-such a name," and so on in detail as described in the Sūtra;
he recollects everything, including the entire body of beings, just as he does for himself.
He recollects himself; likewise, he causes others to recollect [it];
and he himself causes others to recollect those beings as well.

Regarding the bodies in the past: he himself recollects them and causes others to recollect them. "Those beings named so-and-so, in whom I formerly existed, were called by such-and-such a name," and so on in detail. Of those beings as well, [he recollects] all their former [lives] in exactly the same way.
He recollects his various dwellings just as he does in the present life;
he recollects even the subtle, whether it be little or much, whatever was previously performed after having intended it, and which has not been lost from memory.

He also recollects [events] without interval, in a continuous sequence that is not interrupted; he recollects them exactly in the order in which they were performed. He also recollects even that which is measured, for which it is possible to calculate a number by means of the reckoning of eons (*kalpa*).

He also recollects that which is immeasurable and incalculable, for which it is impossible to calculate a number by means of the method of counting eons. In brief, his knowledge of former abodes proceeds unhindered wherever he desires and in whatever manner.

068/01/. Here, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva, by means of the divine ear, [hears] the divine [sounds] and human...

In that regard, divine sounds [are heard] upward as far as the beings who have reached the world-system of Aghanistha; provided that he does not direct his attention beyond that point. However, if he does direct his attention, then he hears others even further beyond, in the world-systems above.
In that regard, human sounds are those produced by sentient beings belonging to the animal realm throughout all four continents.
In that regard, noble sounds are those of the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas.
[It is] from Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas,
or having heard it from them, by those who proclaim it to other sentient beings—
namely, by those who demonstrate it, encourage it, inspire it, and gladden it.

Distant sounds: setting aside those sounds that issue forth in whatever village, field, or monastery the Tathāgata or a bodhisattva dwells, [he hears] all others, even those as far as immeasurable and incalculable [worlds].

Whether it be a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva, having observed the physical conduct— whether virtuous or non-virtuous— of sentient beings in the ten directions, they act toward those beings as is appropriate and as is fitting.
