In that regard, what is the knowledge of the mental dispositions (*cetaḥ-paryāya-jñāna*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? Here, a Bodhisattva or a Tathāgata [knows] the ten... of others.

In immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions, he knows the minds of sentient beings even when they are obsessed by afflictions; he knows them even when free from the obsession of afflictions, yet still accompanied by the latent tendencies of afflictions, and even when the afflictions have been eliminated.

He knows the mind that is continuous yet free from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), as well as the mind that is wrongly directed. For example, he knows the mind of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*), and whatever mind is characterized by worldly attachment (*sāmiṣābhiprāya*), even if it is not afflicted (*akliṣṭa*) and is rightly directed (*samyak-praṇihita*).

He also knows the superior mind; conversely, he also knows the inferior mind—for example, that of all beings born in the desire realm, down to even the beasts and birds. He also knows the middling mind.

For example, [he knows] the minds of all beings born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). He also knows the sublime mind, such as that of beings born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), whether it is associated with pleasure or associated with suffering.
He also knows a mind associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

By means of a single knowledge of others' minds, he simultaneously knows whatever mind has arisen for a single sentient being— of whomsoever it may be, in whatever manner, of whatever kind, and to whatever extent.

He understands it as it truly is. By means of a single knowledge of others' minds, he simultaneously understands, as it truly is, the minds of many sentient beings— whatever [minds] they have, however [they are], of whatever kind they are, and to whatever extent they are present.

He knows it. Furthermore, this supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) belongs to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the sake of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of sentient beings, and for the sake of knowing their various inclinations (nānādhimukti).

It is for the sake of knowing the various elements and temperaments, and for the sake of correctly directing [beings] toward the diverse paths that lead toward the city of Nirvana according to their needs. This should be understood as its function.
071/04. Among these, what is the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas?
Here, a Tathāgata or a Bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, the attainment of the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*). [He knows: "The outflows have been destroyed by me, or by others."
"Is there exhaustion [of the outflows] or not? He understands, as it truly is, the means for attaining the exhaustion of the outflows for himself and for others.
Just as he understands the means, so too he understands what is not the means, as it truly is, regarding the attainment of the exhaustion of the outflows.

He understands the overestimation (*abhimāna*) of others as it truly is, and he understands the absence of overestimation as it truly is. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva understands all of this, yet he does not personally realize the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

Therefore, he does not personally realize that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) directly. For this reason, the bodhisattva does not abandon the object that has outflows together with those outflows;
rather, he courses within that object of outflows and yet is not defiled. This is how it is.
It should be understood that among all [supernatural] powers, this is the greatest power. Indeed,

by means of that knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves are not afflicted, and they point out [the path] to others, [removing] their overweening pride (*abhimāna*).
And they cause [them] to perish; this should be understood as his karma.
In that regard, what is the power of the Dharma? It is the power of generosity, and the powers of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Furthermore, this—
The power of the dharmas such as giving and so forth should be understood, in brief, by way of four aspects: through the abandonment of opposing factors, through the maturation of the accumulations,
through the benefiting of oneself and others, and through the yielding of fruit in the future.

Giving a gift, the bodhisattva abandons stinginess, which is the opposite of giving. That gift of his becomes a provision for his own enlightenment. And by means of giving, one of the articles of attraction, he brings sentient beings to maturity.

He accumulates merit: before giving, he is well-disposed; while giving, he clarifies his mind; and after having given, he is without regret. By means of a joyful mind in these three times, he [purifies] himself—
He benefits others by removing their hunger, thirst, cold, heat, fatigue, frustration, fear, and suffering; furthermore,

One possesses great wealth, a great faction, and a large retinue, and one takes delight in giving. Thus,

When a bodhisattva undertakes the ethical discipline of restraint in body and speech,

And by means of the articles of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), he brings sentient beings to maturity. Abandoning immorality, fear, blame, and enmity, he benefits himself, sleeping in peace and waking in peace. Likewise...
For one who possesses ethical discipline, there is freedom from remorse, joy, and so forth, up to mental concentration.
In this way, he benefits himself. Furthermore, by not harming all sentient beings in any manner whatsoever, he bestows fearlessness upon them. Thus...

One greatly benefits others. On that basis, after the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world among the gods; and one takes delight in ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Thus, the power of ethical discipline has these four aspects; there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
The patient bodhisattva abandons impatience, which is the opposite of patience. That patience becomes a provision for awakening.
Furthermore, through the very practice of consistency in purpose, he brings sentient beings to maturity and matures himself as well.
Furthermore, by protecting others from great fear through that patience,
he benefits both himself and others. On that basis, in future lives, the bodhisattva becomes one who has little enmity, little dissension, and little suffering.
Abounding in mental distress, yet free from remorse in this present life, he passes away;

And he finds delight in patience. Thus, this is the fourfold cultivation of patience;

When a bodhisattva has initiated vigor, he dwells in vigor—

He abandons the opposing factor, which is laziness. That vigor becomes the equipment for awakening and serves as its support. Furthermore, through the very quality of consistency in purpose (*samānārthatā*), he brings sentient beings to maturity. And one who has initiated vigor experiences ease.

Dwelling unmixed with evil and unwholesome states, he perceives successive stages of distinguished attainment; through joy and gladness, he benefits himself. And being devoted to the side of the wholesome, he does not [neglect] others.

One harms others through body or speech; yet, when others exert vigor, one generates enthusiasm for them. In this way, one also benefits others. One becomes strong in causal power and, in the future, takes delight in human effort. This is the fourth—

The mode [of practice] is the power of vigor; there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this. When a bodhisattva enters meditative absorption, he [overcomes] the affliction that is the adversary of dhyāna, as well as speech, discursive thought, joy, bliss, the perception of form, and so forth.

He abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*). That meditation (*dhyāna*) of his becomes the equipment for awakening (*bodhi-sambhāra*) and its basis. This is the purity of knowledge, the purity of the accomplishment of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and rebirth among the gods.

In that regard, what is maturation? Briefly, maturation should be understood through six aspects: by way of its intrinsic nature, and also by way of the person to be matured...

Through the cultivation of wholesome dharmas, there arises a pliancy and fitness of body and mind that is conducive to the purification resulting from the abandonment of the afflictions and the obstructions to the knowable; this is the culmination of correct application, established in which one [serves] the Teacher or...

Whether the Teacher has been approached or not approached, one becomes capable and empowered to realize either the immediate abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) or the abandonment of the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). When it has reached the state where it is immediately ready to be split open, it is said to be "fully ripened. Just as when earthenware vessels such as jars, pots,

It is said to be "fully ripened. Just as fruits such as the mango or the jackfruit are called "ripe" when they have reached their final state for consumption and are ready to be eaten immediately thereafter, so too is this.
That culmination of right application which results from the cultivation of wholesome dharmas and leads to immediate purification is the nature of maturation.

In that regard, the persons to be matured are, in brief, fourfold: those of the śrāvaka lineage are to be matured in the śrāvaka vehicle; those of the pratyekabuddha lineage in the pratyekabuddha vehicle;

Even a person who abides in the lineage (gotrastha) must be brought to maturity for the sake of proceeding to a good rebirth by the Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Thus,

In the future time as well, there will be nothing superior to these, nor any other cause more extensive than these, for the sake of either affliction or purification. In that regard, what is the fruit? In brief, there are five fruits.
The fruit of maturation, the fruit of outflow, the fruit of dissociation, the fruit of human effort, and the dominant fruit. For unwholesome dharmas, maturation ripens in the miserable realms.

The wholesome outflows [lead] to a good rebirth; that is their fruit of ripening (*vipāka-phala*). Furthermore, from the practice of the unwholesome, there arises an abundance of the unwholesome and a preponderance of the unwholesome. From the practice of the wholesome, there arises an abundance of the wholesome and a preponderance of the wholesome, as before.
Or, the conformity of subsequent results to the similarity of the action is the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

The cessation of afflictions through the noble eightfold path is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). Furthermore, that which is the cessation of afflictions by means of the mundane path—[that is the fruit of disjunction].
It does not follow excessively for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, that is not the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*). Furthermore, in some cases, in this very life...
Whatever gain is obtained through diligent human effort based on a craft or occupation—
whether by agriculture, or by trade, or by royal service; or by means of writing, calculation, accounting, numeration, and sealing— [such as] salt and so forth...
...and brings about such results as these; this is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Visual consciousness is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) of the visual faculty.
In the same way, up to mental consciousness is [the dominant fruit] of the mental faculty, and likewise for the vital breaths.

103/07/. Non-separation from the life-faculty (jīvitendriya). Thus, whatever fruit is produced by each of the twenty-two faculties through its own respective predominance (ādhipatya), that should be understood as the predominant fruit (adhipati-phala). And that predominant [fruit]...

This should be understood among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), as set forth in the *Vastu-saṃgrahaṇī*. For in this way, the bodhisattva, having understood the Buddha’s word as a mode that correctly elucidates cause and fruit, [abides] in the proper state—
The lineage of the power of knowledge regarding possible and impossible places is purified and increased gradually through repeated cultivation.
Furthermore, neither what has not been done nor what was done by another ripens for anyone. Nor...

Even after hundreds of eons, actions performed by oneself do not perish with respect to their yielding of fruit. Thus, the Bodhisattva elucidates the Buddha’s word regarding the non-arrival of what was not done and the non-perishing of what was done.
Having known things as they truly are, one gradually purifies and increases the lineage of the power of knowledge regarding the fact that actions are one's own.
In this regard, how does a bodhisattva seek out what has been heard? Here, the bodhisattva—

A bodhisattva, having established intense reverence, seeks the Dharma in well-spoken and well-articulated teachings. In brief, such reverence for what is well-spoken is present in this bodhisattva, such that he—
For the sake of hearing even a single well-spoken word, one should enter even a ground made of iron that is heated and blazing with the utmost joy and reverence, if necessary.

Otherwise, one would not even obtain the hearing of well-spoken words, let alone the meaning of abundant well-spoken words. Furthermore, the love and respect that a bodhisattva has for his own physical body and person are surpassed by that which he has for all others.
Regarding the requisites for the body, such as food and drink, and the love and respect one feels for hearing well-spoken words: compared to the former love and respect,
the latter love and respect does not even equal a hundredth part.
It does not approach even a thousandth part, nor a numerical fraction, nor a calculation, nor a comparison,
nor even a resemblance. Thus,
having conceived reverence for well-spoken words, he listens to the well-spoken teaching without weariness.

He is insatiable and full of faith; he abounds in clarity, possesses a moistened mental continuum, and has an upright view. Out of a desire for virtues and a desire for the Dharma, he approaches the Dharma-preacher, not out of a desire to find fault.

With a respectful intention, and not with the arrogance of pride; seeking what is wholesome, and not for the sake of self-exaltation; thinking, "I shall establish both myself and others in roots of virtue," and not for the sake of gain or honor.
Having thus perfected his approach, he listens to the Dharma without affliction and without distraction.
How does he listen without affliction? He is free from the affliction of arrogance.

Having established reverence for the Dharma,

He hears it free from affliction. In this way, the bodhisattva hears the Dharma without being afflicted. In that regard, how does the bodhisattva hear the Dharma without distraction?

He hears by means of five aspects: with a mind intent on understanding, a one-pointed mind, an attentive ear, a receptive mental disposition, and attending with his entire being—he hears the Dharma. In this way, a bodhisattva seeks out what has been heard.

What does a bodhisattva seek? A bodhisattva seeks the word of the Buddha for the purpose of accomplishing it through the correct practice in accordance with the Dharma, and for the purpose of explaining it extensively to others.

A bodhisattva seeks the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*) for the sake of thoroughly understanding, as it truly is, the poorly spoken and poorly articulated nature of that very treatise, for the sake of refuting the arguments of others, and for the sake of inspiring faith in those who lack faith in this teaching.

105/16. And for the further increase of those who have faith in giving. 105/17. A bodhisattva seeks the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*) in order to produce confidence within himself regarding those who are devoted to refined speech, by means of the precise determination of well-expressed words and phonemes.
105/19. For the sake of entering into the conventional usage of various etymological explanations for a single meaning,
the Bodhisattva seeks the science of medicine (cikitsā-śāstra) for the purpose of pacifying the various kinds of diseases of sentient beings and the great multitude.

And for the sake of benefiting his own body, a bodhisattva seeks out worldly arts and crafts in order to acquire wealth with little difficulty for the benefit of sentient beings, and in order to inspire great respect in sentient beings.
And for the sake of benefiting and gathering others through the sharing of knowledge of the arts (*śilpa-jñāna*),
the bodhisattva seeks all these five fields of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*) as a great accumulation of wisdom (*mahājñāna-sambhāra*) for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
For the sake of fulfillment. For if one does not train in this way in all respects, one will not gradually attain the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience. As for that which...
It has been explained what a bodhisattva seeks, how he seeks it, and for what purpose he seeks it. In that regard, what does the bodhisattva teach others, and how?

He teaches. For what purpose and by what cause does he teach? In this regard, he teaches exactly that which he has investigated; he teaches others precisely for that purpose for which he himself has investigated it. Furthermore, he teaches by means of two aspects.
106/09/. He delivers a discourse that is both conformable and pure. In this regard, 106/10/.
how does he deliver a conformable discourse? He teaches one who is standing with a suitable deportment, and not one with an unsuitable deportment; nor does he teach one seated on a higher seat.

this should be understood in detail according to the Sūtra. For what reason? Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are those for whom the Dharma is the highest authority. Indeed, when the Dharma is being honored...

Others develop an intense reverence for the Dharma; they become respectful toward listening to it and do not harbor contempt. He teaches all of them, and he teaches everything without interruption. [He is free from] stinginess regarding the Dharma.

Not acting with the "teacher's fist" (ācāryamuṣṭi) regarding the teachings, he instructs the words and syllables in their proper sequence. Having instructed the words and syllables in their proper sequence, he analyzes them according to their meaning in that same sequence. Regarding the meaning...

He teaches the Dharma and its meaning in a coherent manner, not one that is disconnected from the goal. He demonstrates what should be demonstrated; he encourages others to undertake what should be undertaken;

He gladdens those who are to be disciplined. Not obscure, and moreover associated with the four noble truths; for all assemblies, whatever the assembly may be and whatever the discourse may be, [he speaks] according to what is appropriate for that assembly.

In this way he speaks with her. It should be understood that, by means of these fifteen aspects, the discourse of Bodhisattvas toward sentient beings is compliant with all aims for the benefit of others.

He becomes one who reflects, not relying on the literal phrasing (*vyañjana*). He understands the provisional teachings (*kālāpadeśa*) and the definitive teachings (*mahāpadeśa*) as they truly are. Through initial entry, he enters into reflection;

He brings it to a state of solidity. Avoiding the inconceivable, the bodhisattva does not fall into delusion or mental distraction. Constantly, continuously, and with reverence, he applies himself to reflection upon a meaning previously unknown.

One discerns, attains, and realizes the object that has been understood; one does not lose it, nor does one forget it. Furthermore, by means of reasoning, as one investigates, enters into, and examines something, one does not become dependent on another. Regarding those [objects],...

Thus [one should reflect].

Not rejecting those teachings, a bodhisattva who relies on the meaning and not on the letter avoids blame, protecting himself unharmed and uninjured; for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have all their intentional terminology [in mind].

He enters into the [Buddha’s] words. Skilled in the provisional teachings (*kālāpadeśa*) and the definitive teachings (*mahāpadeśa*), the bodhisattva is unable to be shaken or moved from the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*).
In some way or another, it can be achieved. From the very beginning, as the bodhisattva enters into reflection, he attains a patience (*kṣānti*) never attained before.
Furthermore, having well-attained that very patience, he brings it to a state of firmness (*sāratā*).

By means of these eight aspects, the bodhisattva enters into cultivation; thus, the bodhisattva becomes one who has entered into the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānudharma-pratipatti) as comprised by reflection.

When a sentient being, for the sake of purifying their intention, gives while neglecting a task that has arisen for the benefit of sentient beings, that intention of theirs is pure; he does not give by neglecting a task for sentient beings that has already presented itself.

Furthermore, he does not give his own body, limb by limb, to the gods belonging to Māra’s host when they have approached as supplicants with the intention of causing harm; [he does so] lest there be excessive injury and destruction for them.

As it is with the gods belonging to Māra’s host, so should it be understood regarding those beings commanded by them. Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not give his own body in its various parts to those who are insane or whose minds are deranged; for they do not possess their own [sound] minds.

They remain [in that state]; they do not seek out objects with purpose, nor is there anything other than idle chatter. Because their minds lack self-mastery, he does not give to them. These are the modes...

117/02/. Setting aside the opposite case, a bodhisattva first gives away his own body to those who request it, either by placing himself under their control or by relinquishing it limb by limb and member by member. Thus, first, regarding the internal [gift] of a bodhisattva—
117/05/. Of what kind of object should it be understood that there is both giving and non-giving?
117/06/. Furthermore, regarding external objects, a bodhisattva does not bestow upon those who ask such things as poison, fire, weapons, or intoxicants, which would cause harm to sentient beings.

If those things— such as poison, fire, weapons, or intoxicants— are requested by seekers for the purpose of harming themselves or others, the Bodhisattva does not give them. However, if those same things are for the benefit of sentient beings,
the Bodhisattva gives them to the seekers, whether for his own benefit or for theirs.

117/11. Or, he gives away things requested by supplicants for the sake of favoring others. Furthermore, 117/12. a bodhisattva does not bestow another's property upon others without their consent. A bodhisattva does not [approach] another's wife through a go-between.

Having gathered [these things], he bestows them upon others. He does not bestow food or drink containing living beings. Furthermore, even that which is conducive to pleasure and play, yet not conducive to the welfare of sentient beings, is not to be given by a bodhisattva.

There is also a case where a bodhisattva does not give a certain object to those who request it. For what reason? Although that object might cause them to produce merely a slight clarity of mind toward the bodhisattva, it would nevertheless result in even greater [benefit] for him.

One might perform a gift that would be useless, because by reason of it one incurs intoxication, negligence, and misconduct; through the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in the states of woe. However, if that object—such as pleasure or play—is...
It would not lead to rebirth in the miserable states, nor would it result in the accumulation of unwholesome roots. Indeed,
for the sake of inspiring clarity of mind, a bodhisattva may give such objects as pleasure and play to those who request them, even by means of that object.

Furthermore, for the sake of gathering [beings] and bringing them to maturity, what kind of object of pleasure and play does a bodhisattva not give to those who ask? And what kind does he give? That—^118—[is as follows:]...

Just as a bodhisattva does not provide instruction in the killing of wild animals, so too he does not [perform] such sacrifices as those minor sacrifices and great undertakings in which powerful living beings meet their destruction, being conquered and deprived of life. He does not perform such sacrifices.

118/04. He sacrifices for himself and does not cause others to sacrifice for him. Nor does he permit the slaughter of animals in temples of the gods. Nor does he occupy regions inhabited by a multitude of living beings, whether aquatic or terrestrial creatures. 118/06. Nor does he [occupy] places frequented by many sentient beings...
118/07. He does not give nets, nor traps, nor instruction in nets and traps, when asked for the purpose of obstructing those living beings.
118/08–09. Nor does he give [anything] for the purpose of reviling or killing [living beings].

He provides an enemy for his enemies in order to bind, punish, or imprison them. In brief, whatever a bodhisattva [knows] that causes affliction to other beings, harms other beings, or is an object of amusement and play for beings— all that [he does not provide].
118/13. A bodhisattva does not give to those who seek, even though there are these various things:
elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and mounts; garments and ornaments; excellent food and drink; and training in dance, song, and instrumental music, as well as dance—[Tib. 118/15, 64a].
Musical instruments for singing and playing, perfumes, garlands, and ointments; various household utensils and furnishings; gardens, houses, and women for service;
and training in various arts and crafts—such as these are the objects of delight.

For the sake of inspiring confidence in the minds of those who seek it, a bodhisattva bestows articles for play upon them. Furthermore, even to one who is ill and seeking it, a bodhisattva does not provide food or drink that is either excessive or unwholesome. Nor...

To beings who are greedy by nature, they provide excellent food and drink even when those beings are already satiated. Nor do they give themselves up for the sake of beings afflicted by grief, nor for their own destruction, nor for being beaten, nor for consuming poison, nor for leaping from a precipice.
Nor does he grant permission for them to act as they please. Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not give away his mother and father to supplicants in every respect;
for the mother and father occupy the position of the most supreme secret to a bodhisattva.

It is that which brings about birth, nourishes, and causes growth. Because the Bodhisattva has carried these two upon his head for a long night, he should not fall into weariness. Regarding those two...

119/02/. One’s self is subject to being pledged as a loan, held as collateral, sold, or given away. How, then, could a bodhisattva venture to bestow it upon others, much less actually give it? Nor does a bodhisattva...
An anointed king, the sovereign over his own realm of sentient beings together with their possessions,
seizes from others the children and wives belonging to others and bestows them upon other [people]. This is not the case for the entirety [of the realm].
He might bestow a village or a portion of a village, a city or a portion of a city,
or wealth, saying, "May it be yours just as it was mine. Yet the Bodhisattva [does not give away] his own son—
He bestows upon others who request them his wife, female and male slaves, laborers, servants, and dependents, even when they have not been properly informed, are unwilling, and are dejected;
yet he does so even when they have been properly informed and are well-disposed.

Having generated the desire [to give], he does not bestow [it] upon enemies, nor upon yakṣas or rākṣasas, nor upon those who perform cruel deeds; nor does he bestow his wife and children, his delicate family members, or other people into a state of slavery. Nor does he [bestow them] for the sake of awakening—

A person who is engaged in fierce deeds characterized by excessive harm to others gives the gift of their kingdom to those who beg for it; and if they have the power, they even displace such individuals from that kingdom.

119/20/. To give. And a bodhisattva does not take away wealth from his mother and father and bestow it upon beggars. As he does not act toward his mother and father, so too toward his sons, wives, female and male slaves, and laborers. Nor indeed from his mother—

Having set aside his father— and so on in detail until— having set aside his laborers and servants, the bodhisattva relinquishes objects to be given to other supplicants. Having acquired wealth through righteous and non-coercive means, he practices giving.
He gives not unrighteously or with violence; he does not give by oppressing or harming others. And in the teaching of the Blessed Buddhas, the bodhisattva—

120/03. One who, while remaining [in a state of non-transgression], gives a gift by somehow transgressing the training; 120/04. And the bodhisattva, while giving a gift, gives with an even mind toward all sentient beings, having established the notion that they are worthy of offerings (dakṣiṇīya) toward friends, enemies, and neutrals.

Whether toward those with virtues or those with faults, the lowly or the equal, the distinguished or those who are happy or suffering, a bodhisattva does not give a gift to a petitioner that is less than what has been described or promised; there is no other way.

Whether equal or superior, a bodhisattva does not, having promised an excellent thing, give something coarse or inferior; nor, when an excellent thing is available, does he give what is inferior after having promised the excellent. Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not give with a troubled mind or in anger.
120/12/. One gives a gift with a disturbed mind.
Nor, having given a gift, does one repeatedly disparage it by proclaiming, "In such and such a way, you have been favored, nourished, and rescued by me through this gift."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, when a bodhisattva gives a gift even to an inferior person, he does not give what has been cast aside or without due respect; how much less so to one who possesses virtuous qualities.
Nor does a bodhisattva [give] to those who are arrogant and established in various forms of misconduct.
With a mind weary due to the misconduct of beggars who are unrestrained in themselves, who revile, who are angry, and who abuse him, he gives a gift; yet,
toward them alone, the bodhisattva increases his [compassionate] measure even further.
Having understood that [beings] are of a nature possessed by afflictions, he gives a gift while maintaining a mind of compassion. Furthermore, he does not give a gift that is grasped by false views;
for example, he does not practice the Dharma through the giving of violence in great and cruel sacrifices.
He does not believe in it; nor does he give a gift associated with curiosity or auspicious rites.
Nor does he believe that through the mere act of giving, even if it were perfectly pure in every respect, one attains mundane or supramundane purification through detachment.
[65b] One practices giving not for anything other than as a mere accumulation for purification;
one gives without looking for a reward, and all such giving—

He dedicates [it] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Having conceived firm conviction regarding the fruit of every kind of giving and its maturation exactly as it truly is, the bodhisattva, being independent of others—

One who is led by others gives a gift; for example, the giver of food becomes strong, the giver of clothing becomes beautiful in complexion, the giver of a vehicle becomes happy and possessed of sight, the giver of a lamp [becomes so], and so forth—this should be understood in detail. And yet, [it is not] awakening...

A sentient being gives a gift out of fear of the danger of poverty; it is solely with an intention of compassion that he gives, and a bodhisattva does not give an unsuitable gift to supplicants— such as,
for example, leftovers or drink to ascetics.

Food that is mixed with or defiled by excrement, urine, spittle, nasal mucus, vomit, or purgings; or pus and blood; or that which is not announced, not tasted, such as boiled rice or gruel that is subject to being discarded—likewise.
To those who do not eat onions, [to give food] mixed with onions or contaminated with onions;
likewise to those who do not eat meat. To those who do not drink intoxicants, [to give food] mixed with intoxicants or contaminated with intoxicants. Likewise, by engaging them in unsuitable work.
A bodhisattva does not give gifts to others in such a manner;
that is, he does not give an improper gift. Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not [give] to a petitioner who has come and gone repeatedly through repeated begging or through servitude.

He gives a gift after having caused distress through the arrangement of his conduct; he does not give otherwise than merely when requested, nor does the bodhisattva give a gift based on fame, renown, or praise,
nor for the sake of a reciprocal favor from others.
It is not dependent; it gives without being dependent on the sovereignty of Śakra, Māra, or a universal monarch (cakravartin),
nor does it give for the sake of deceiving others.
He gives [this gift] with the thought: "May other kings, or royal ministers,
or town-dwellers and country-folk, or brahmins and householders, or wealthy men, guild-leaders, and caravan-merchants, recognizing me as a donor and a master of generosity, honor and revere me."

[They] might act [toward him], honor, and worship [him]. Furthermore, he does not give a gift out of miserliness; even from what is small, he gives clearly and generously, let alone from what is abundant.
Nor does he give a gift for the purpose of deceiving others. By means of this gift...

"Having first enticed him, I shall later cause him to be alienated. Nor does he give gifts to others from another for the purpose of causing division— for example, by means of a gift [offering] a village,
or a portion of a village, or a district, or a portion of a district.
"Having created a division, I shall seize [the property] from the presence of my masters and I shall attack.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva is skillful and not indolent; he is endowed with initiative, personally girded for action, and takes the lead in preparation.
Regarding the relinquishment of the object to be given, he gives it himself and causes others to give;
he does not manifest laziness himself and then command others to give.
Even when there is a great gathering of seekers, whether they are virtuous or immoral—
Having perceived that they were all seated and assembled together, starting from the eldest down to the youngest,
he distributes all those articles of offering again and again in successive order by means of the "going-and-returning" method.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not give limited gifts when abundant, vast, and extensive enjoyments are available. Nor does he give gifts to others for the purpose of harassing them, or for the purpose of reviling or inciting anger.

Or he gives a gift for the purpose of beating, threatening, reviling, killing, binding, cutting, obstructing, or banishing. Even before giving, the bodhisattva becomes well-disposed; while giving, he clarifies his mind.
Having given, he is free from regret. He does not give a gift out of deceit,
such as counterfeit gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, and so forth.

For those beings who possess hope in that regard, there is no gift— whether small or great— that has not already been mentally relinquished by the bodhisattva to all sentient beings; only afterwards does the petitioner [receive] it as their own.

Just as one might beg from a bodhisattva wealth that has been borrowed and lent out, (51) the bodhisattva gives a gift at the proper time and not at an improper time; it is appropriate for himself and appropriate for the other in this world; and he gives with proper conduct and not with improper conduct.
With a mind that is undistracted and not distracted, the bodhisattva does not mock or deride the reciter; he does not treat him with contempt,
nor does he knit his brows, but rather maintains a cheerful countenance.

His speech is preceded by a smile, and he is the first to speak. He gives gifts neither too slowly nor too hurriedly. Even without being asked, the Bodhisattva himself invites others, providing whatever each person may need.
He gives that to them and personally authorizes their taking of it. Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not give a gift of poor wisdom; when giving, he gives only the gift of wisdom.

123/18. What is the gift of wisdom (*prajñā-dāna*) of a bodhisattva? Here, when objects to be given are available, a bodhisattva first forms this thought even before the arrival of a petitioner: [Tib. 67a] 123/19–20. Thus he prepares his mind.
"If two supplicants should come to me— one who is happy, not miserable, not wretched,
having a protector, and not without refuge; and one who is suffering, miserable, wretched, without a protector,
and without refuge— then, if I have wealth..."
When there is the possibility of satisfying both and fulfilling the desires of both,
then both should be satisfied; thus, the desires of both are fulfilled.
This is what ought to be done: if there were not yet sufficient wealth for me to satisfy both [parties] and fulfill their desires, then,
setting aside the one who is happy, a gift should be given to the one who is suffering, without being miserly.

"Having abandoned one who is not pitiable— who possesses a protector and has a refuge— one should give a gift to one who is miserable, wretched, without a protector, and without a refuge. Having thus formed this mental intention, he acts according to that very formation through his deed.

He accomplishes it. However, if he is unable to fulfill the desire of a petitioner who is seeking happiness, then, based on that very same previous mental formation and conceptualization, he informs that petitioner as follows:

124/10. He sends word: "This gift, previously assigned and previously promised by me for this suffering person, has been delivered to him by me. It is not that I have any intention of not giving it to you, O gentle-faced one; therefore, [it is not my fault]. 124/12. Thus, O noble sir—
“‘One should not show a lack of affection toward us. Furthermore,
when items fit for giving are available,
there are families that are stingy, even families that are extremely stingy.”
There are families that cling to their possessions and dwell in huts and hovels, where no gift for ascetics or brahmins ever arises. The Bodhisattva,
having approached such families, greets them and speaks with affection.

Having made such an arrangement, he said: "Now, sirs, may you first be established in a great service by means of the depletion of my treasury. In my house there exist abundant enjoyments and abundant things to be given as religious gifts."
"I am one who seeks a petitioner for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of generosity. If you would satisfy the petitioner, do not reject or turn them away;
rather, having taken my wealth—which is to be given—bestow it upon them."
"Let it be as you wish. Alternatively, provide that petitioner with what he needs from us. And rejoice in the gift being given by me."
Having given their consent to him, they act accordingly, thinking, "By the depletion of our treasury, this son of good family will have his mind gratified by us. In this way,
that bodhisattva acts for the sake of removing the stain of stinginess from them in the future.
The seed has been sown. And by that gradual practice,
through that skill in means preceded by wisdom, they bestow even their own meager wealth upon others, relying on a mild degree of non-greed.

They attain the middling [level]. Relying upon the middling, they attain the superior. Furthermore, whatever teachers, preceptors, co-residents, disciples, or fellow practitioners a bodhisattva may have—
Furthermore, there are those who are impoverished and by nature greedy, or of a greedy disposition,
or even those who are not of a greedy disposition but are frustrated in their desires due to a lack of goods to give.
In such cases, the bodhisattva [offers] what has been planted in the Buddha or what has been planted in the Dharma.

Or, desiring to perform a basis of meritorious action consisting of giving that has been planted in the Saṃgha, he relinquishes it to them; he causes those objects of gift to be prepared by them and does not do so himself. In this way, that bodhisattva himself—
A much greater merit is produced.

For some fellow practitioners of the holy life, the subduing of afflictions is accomplished; for others, the fulfillment of their desire for the Dharma is accomplished. [For the sake of] sentient beings—
The gathering [of beings] and the ripening of sentient beings are accomplished. Furthermore,
when objects to be given are available, the bodhisattva, having recognized a petitioner by a mere hint or sign, [provides them] according to their desire.
He provides [others] with gifts of merit.

Furthermore, if someone approaches him thinking, "I shall deceive him through fraudulent trade," he perceives that person's intention and conceals even their misconduct, let alone his own. Much less...
In this very way, he fulfills his wish so that he may depart free from hesitation, uplifted, confident, and filled with joy. By means of that [wish], too...

Furthermore, a bodhisattva may be deceived by fraud or guile. He has not previously recognized that deception, but recognizes it afterwards. Yet, he does not subsequently reproach that person who practiced the deception on account of that matter.

He encourages [the recipient] and reminds him: "All this that has been done by me is an act of taking what was not given; I rejoice in it with my whole being. Such is the wise giving of a bodhisattva when objects to be given are available.
Furthermore,
when objects for giving are non-existent and not available, a bodhisattva who is skilled in various arts and crafts brings to mind a particular craft or field of work.

He acts such that, with little difficulty, he acquires and dwells in a great mass of wealth. Or, the Bodhisattva is one who possesses diverse speech, sweet speech, and excellent eloquence, and likewise [speaks] the Dharma to others.

126/14. He delivers the teaching: just as even among poor beings there arises a desire to give, let alone among the wealthy; and just as it arises even among the stingy, let alone among those whose nature is generosity. Or again, those which... [Tib. 68b]

Regarding those faithful families in which gifts of merit (*deyadharma*) are practiced day after day due to their extensive wealth— toward such families, he provides for whatever supplicants arrive. Having gone there himself, he [encourages them] in acts of giving and merit.

While these acts are being performed, one who is skillful, untiring, and endowed with diligence applies himself to activity through body and speech according to his ability and strength, having inspired confidence in his mind; and that gift is well-bestowed upon those who beg.

It acts [properly]. For such is that gift: it does not become something that is poorly bestowed due to the deficiency of an attendant, or something that is partial, or something done by one who does not practice [the rules], or due to the loss of mindfulness. In this way, the bodhisattva [acts].
Even when wealth is non-existent and not present, a wise person becomes a giver of gifts until they attain purity of intention. Pure—
Furthermore, a bodhisattva with resolute intention attains the transcendence of the miserable realms;
in that very same way, he attains inexhaustible wealth in birth after birth. Moreover, a bodhisattva does not [seek] a flaw in a non-Buddhist...
He gives the Dharma— whether as an oral recitation from his mouth or as it is contained in a book— to one who is seeking it.
He does not give a book to one whose nature is greed, nor to one who wishes to sell it, nor to one who wishes to accumulate it, but rather to one who seeks that knowledge for its own sake.
Furthermore, if he possesses knowledge, or if his purpose has already been fulfilled by means of the book,

he gives it to the seeker himself at their own convenience. However, if his purpose has not yet been fulfilled— for which reason that book was acquired by him— it is in this manner [that he should act].

That bodhisattva, seeing that another has [already] acquired it, or having had it written down, gives something else. If he neither sees the original nor is able to have it written down, he must from the very beginning examine his own mind: "May it not be mine..."
The mind is obsessed by the stain of stinginess regarding the Dharma. "May it not be that, even by my own intention, I am unwilling to give the written Dharma.
If, while reflecting in this way, he should know: "I possess the Dharma..."

The manifestation of the stain of stinginess: even if that bodhisattva were to form such a thought, that gift of Dharma must still be given. Even if, by means of this gift of Dharma, I were to become mute...
"In this very life, even if I were unable to endure my afflictions, I would still have to give the gift of Dharma; how much more so when I am devoid of the equipment of knowledge!
Furthermore, if, upon examination, he should realize: 'I possess no Dharma...'"

The manifestation of the stain of stinginess. Furthermore, that bodhisattva should train himself thus: "I shall give this gift of Dharma for the sake of destroying my own afflictions; it is for the accumulation of wisdom."

Whether for the sake of fulfilling [the needs of others] or simply out of affection for sentient beings, I do not yet perceive any affliction; nor do I perceive even the accumulation of wisdom in this present life.

"I see that for future lives, there is far more [suffering] from not giving than from giving. For the sake of the abundance of the attainment of the Dharma, even in future lives, [the suffering] is slight. And while not bestowing [gifts], I [act] for the sake of all sentient beings..."

"Accumulating knowledge for the sake of the welfare and happiness of that being, I act with kindness toward that being and all other sentient beings. Yet, perceiving it thus, one thinks: 'I am acting with kindness toward this single being alone.'"
If a bodhisattva does not give in accordance with reality, he is blameless, free from regret, and has not transgressed the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, how is it that he does not give? Indeed, a bodhisattva...
He is able to reject a petitioner with harsh speech, saying, "I will not give to you. However, he sends him away after having informed him through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
In this regard, such is his skillful means: even before [the request is made], the bodhisattva—[having already prepared] all...
All requisites and all things to be given are, with a pure intention, relinquished and dedicated to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the ten directions;
they are conceptualized just as, for example, a monk [dedicates his belongings] to a teacher or a preceptor.
Or, that by which he might transform his own robe— by reason of such transformation,
even though he has acquired a store of all kinds of diverse and magnificent articles for use as gifts,
the bodhisattva who dwells in the noble lineages is called one who possesses immeasurable merit.
He becomes a producer [of merit]. And that merit of his, for one who constantly applies his mind to it, increases at all times, following him throughout all periods.
He holds those objects of generosity as if they were entrusted to him by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

If he sees a petitioner and perceives that it is appropriate to bestow the gift of the Dharma upon them according to their desire, [he reflects]: "There is nothing whatsoever belonging to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas that has not been relinquished for the sake of sentient beings."

Having understood this, he fulfills the wish of the petitioner; however, if he does not perceive it as being appropriate, then, taking that very consideration into account, [he considers] the property of others...
"O gentle-faced one, it was not that this was not permitted for you to give. Having thus consoled him with gentle words, he sends him away,
or else provides him with another gift, honor, and hospitality of double or triple value.

Having done so, he sends it back so that the other may understand: "This bodhisattva does not wish to give to us out of a greedy nature; rather, he is surely not independent regarding this gift of the Dharma in the form of a book, which is why he does not give."
This too should be understood as the wise giving of a bodhisattva, undertaken with respect to the gift of Dharma. Furthermore, a bodhisattva [understands] all gifts—
the gift of Dharma, the gift of material things, and the gift of fearlessness— both by way of their synonyms and by way of their characteristics.

Giving correctly, according to reality, both in terms of the source and in terms of the distinction between cause and fruit, he understands accordingly. This also should be known as the wise giving of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, a bodhisattva, toward sentient beings who have done him harm...
One gives gifts with an intention of loving-kindness toward those who are worthy; with an intention of compassion toward those who are suffering;
with an intention of sympathetic joy toward those who possess virtuous qualities; and with an intention of equanimity toward benefactors, friends, and well-wishers.
This also should be understood as the wise gift of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva understands, as they truly are, both the obstacles to giving and the remedies for those obstacles to giving.
In this regard, there are four obstacles to giving: lack of prior practice, [lack of familiarity with] the object to be given...

129/19/. Scarcity and deficiency of dharmas; attachment to objects that are foremost and pleasing to the mind; and taking delight in seeing the fruit of the perfection of wealth in the future. Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva possesses the things to be given...

When a petitioner has properly approached him, his mind does not incline toward giving. He quickly and easily realizes through wisdom: "This fault of mine is caused by a lack of practice. Furthermore, he realizes it thus: "Surely..."

"In the past, I never gave gifts, because of which my mind does not now incline toward giving, even though wealth is available and a petitioner has properly approached. If, at this time, I do not reflect upon it..."
"I shall give; yet, in the future, I may again experience aversion toward giving.
Having understood this, he relies upon the antidote to the obstruction of giving.

130/03/. He gives having reflected with discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāya*); he does not follow after the faults produced by habituation, nor does he fall under their influence. Furthermore, if a petitioner has properly approached a bodhisattva who possesses limited wealth, [he gives].
The mind does not incline toward giving. Having very quickly discerned through wisdom the cause for the obstruction of giving— that which consists of the distress [caused by others]—
and having reflected upon it, he endures that suffering born of distress out of compassion.

Out of compassion, he gives a gift. It occurs to him: "Due to the fault of past karma, or because of being subject to others, I have experienced many intense sufferings such as hunger and thirst within cyclic existence, without having benefited others."
"Even if this gift should lead to my death at the time of passing away,
there would be suffering in this very life; nevertheless, for me, giving alone is better than the rejection of a petitioner,
let alone anyone else."
He subsists on some vegetable leaves. In this way, the bodhisattva endures that suffering caused by deprivation and gives a gift.
Furthermore, when a proper supplicant has appeared before the bodhisattva, if...

Because the object to be given is exceedingly pleasing and supreme, his mind does not incline toward giving. The bodhisattva, having very quickly discerned through wisdom that this fault is caused by craving, [thinks]: "This is suffering for me, though it appears as pleasure."

The perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) produces suffering in the future; therefore, through the thorough understanding of this perversion, the Bodhisattva abandons it and, having applied analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), gives that object. Furthermore, if a Bodhisattva, after giving a gift, [regards] the fruit of the gift...
The perception of benefits arises regarding great wealth, but not regarding unsurpassed,
perfect enlightenment. The bodhisattva, having very quickly understood through wisdom that this is a fault produced by the view of false fruits, [abandons it].
130/27. He contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they truly are, seeing their lack of essence.
All conditioned phenomena are momentary and perishable; they are like the enjoyment of a fruit.

They are fragile due to their total exhaustion and fragile due to separation. Contemplating in this way and abandoning the view of [worldly] fruits, whatever gift he gives, all of it is dedicated solely toward great enlightenment.
131/05/. He gives.
131/06/. This is the fourfold knowledge that serves as the antidote to the fourfold obstruction to giving, belonging to the fourfold expansion of the bodhisattva’s generosity.

It should be understood that penetration consists of the endurance of suffering, the thorough knowledge of perversion, and the vision of the lack of solidity in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). In this regard, by means of the threefold counteractive knowledge previously mentioned, the bodhisattva is certain and correct.
And he gives a gift. By means of the final antidotal knowledge (*pratipakṣa-jñāna*), he correctly takes hold of the fruit of merit. This also should be understood as the wise giving of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva, having gone into private seclusion within,
conceives a serene resolve with a pure intention and a profound sense of devotion; repeatedly resolving upon various, sublime, and immeasurable objects of giving, he [visualizes them] as real.
When a bodhisattva desires to bestow and present [gifts] upon those who are worthy of them,

In this way, the detailed classification of a bodhisattva’s giving of all internal and external things should be understood. 132.132/26/. [71b] Furthermore, it should be understood that there are four kinds of distinctions regarding the excellence of a bodhisattva’s giving of material things. What are these four? First, the distinction of the basis; second, the distinction of the object; third, the distinction of the mental disposition; and fourth, the distinction of the excellence of the result. Among these, what is the distinction of the basis? It refers to the bodhisattva’s giving of material things from a basis that is either superior, middling, or inferior. Among these, what is the superior basis? It is when a bodhisattva gives material things from a state of being endowed with the perfection of generosity, or from a state of being endowed with the perfection of ethical discipline, or from a state of being endowed with the perfection of patience, or from a state of being endowed with the perfection of diligence, or from a state of being endowed with the perfection of meditative concentration, or from a state of being endowed with the perfection of wisdom. This is called the superior basis. What is the middling basis? It is when a bodhisattva gives material things from a state of being endowed with the roots of virtue conducive to liberation, or from a state of being endowed with the roots of virtue conducive to penetration. This is called the middling basis. What is the inferior basis? It is when a bodhisattva gives material things from a state of being endowed with the roots of virtue conducive to wholesome rebirth, or from a state of being endowed with the roots of virtue accumulated for the sake of the śrāvaka vehicle, or from a state of being endowed with the roots of virtue accumulated for the sake of the pratyekabuddha vehicle. This is called the inferior basis. Among these, what is the distinction of the object? It refers to the bodhisattva’s giving of material things to an object that is either superior, middling, or inferior. Among these, what is the superior object? It is when a bodhisattva gives material things to those who have fallen into great suffering, such as the blind, the deaf, the mute, the mentally deranged, those afflicted by disease, the destitute, the unprotected, the wretched, and the miserable; or to those who possess little merit and few roots of virtue; or to those who have entered the Great Vehicle; or to those who are practicing the path of the Great Vehicle; or to those who have already attained the fruit of the Great Vehicle. This is called the superior object. What is the middling object? It is when a bodhisattva gives material things to those who are established in the five precepts, or to those who are stream-enterers, or to those who are once-returners, or to those who are non-returners, or to those who are arhats, or to those who are pratyekabuddhas. This is called the middling object. What is the inferior object? It is when a bodhisattva gives material things to those who are ordinary worldlings, or to those who are followers of other paths, or to those who are householders. This is called the inferior object. Among these, what is the distinction of the mental disposition? It refers to the bodhisattva’s giving of material things with a mental disposition that is either superior, middling, or inferior. Among these, what is the superior mental disposition? It is when a bodhisattva gives material things with a mind of great compassion, or with a mind of sympathetic joy, or with a mind of equanimity, or with a mind free from attachment, or with a mind of supreme faith, or with a mind of profound respect, or with a mind of pure intention, or with a mind of unflagging perseverance, or with a mind of skillful means, or with a mind of dedication toward supreme perfect enlightenment. This is called the superior mental disposition. What is the middling mental disposition? It is when a bodhisattva gives material things with a mind seeking future wealth, or with a mind seeking future status, or with a mind seeking future fame, or with a mind seeking future pleasure, or with a mind seeking future power, or with a mind seeking future liberation for oneself alone. This is called the middling mental disposition. What is the inferior mental disposition? It is when a bodhisattva gives material things with a mind of pride, or with a mind of contempt, or with a mind of deceit, or with a mind of flattery, or with a mind of malice, or with a mind of regret. This is called the inferior mental disposition. Among these, what is the distinction of the excellence of the result? It refers to the bodhisattva’s giving of material things which results in a superior, middling, or inferior excellence of the fruit. Among these, what is the superior excellence of the fruit? It is when a bodhisattva, through the giving of material things, attains a superior excellence of the body, or a superior excellence of wealth, or a superior excellence of retinue, or a superior excellence of influence, or a superior excellence of the faculties, or a superior excellence of the marks and signs, or a superior excellence of the dharmas conducive to enlightenment, or a superior excellence of the dharmas of a buddha. This is called the superior excellence of the fruit. What is the middling excellence of the fruit? It is when a bodhisattva, through the giving of material things, attains a middling excellence of the body, or a middling excellence of wealth, or a middling excellence of retinue, or a middling excellence of influence, or a middling excellence of the faculties, or a middling excellence of the marks and signs, or a middling excellence of the dharmas conducive to enlightenment, or a middling excellence of the dharmas of a buddha. This is called the middling excellence of the fruit. What is the inferior excellence of the fruit? It is when a bodhisattva, through the giving of material things, attains an inferior excellence of the body, or an inferior excellence of wealth, or an inferior excellence of retinue, or an inferior excellence of influence, or an inferior excellence of the faculties, or an inferior excellence of the marks and signs, or an inferior excellence of the dharmas conducive to enlightenment, or an inferior excellence of the dharmas of a buddha. This is called the inferior excellence of the fruit. Furthermore, it should be understood that there are four kinds of distinctions regarding the excellence of a bodhisattva’s giving of the Dharma. From this point onward, it should be understood that all other classifications of giving—beginning with "difficult giving" (duṣkara-dāna) and so forth—are derived from this very same classification of all forms of giving.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s difficult giving? It is as follows:
When a bodhisattva, possessing a limited object to be given, gives it away to others by afflicting himself and enduring suffering,
this is the first difficult gift of a bodhisattva. That which...

A bodhisattva, having dispelled attachment to a desired object— whether it be due to natural affection, long-term familiarity, or its being of supreme benefit— and having likewise dispelled greed for a preeminent and excellent gift, bestows it upon others.

This is the second difficult gift of a bodhisattva: that a bodhisattva bestows upon others objects to be given that were acquired with great hardship. This is the third difficult gift of a bodhisattva.

In this regard, what is the gift of a true person by a bodhisattva who is a true person? It is when a bodhisattva gives a gift with faith, respectfully, with his own hand, at the proper time, and without harming others. This is the gift of a bodhisattva.
It is said that the gift of a true person is the gift of a true person. In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s giving in all its forms?
It is giving without dependence, giving with clarity, giving with joy, and giving with one's own...
Constant giving, giving with a vessel, giving without a vessel, giving everything, giving everywhere,

133/09/. This is the giving of light to those who desire light. This should be understood as the eightfold gift of a bodhisattva to those who desire relief from distress. 133/10/. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s gift that brings happiness in this world and the next?

In brief, the gift of material things (*āmiṣa-dāna*), the gift of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), and the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*) should be understood as the giving that brings happiness to sentient beings both in this world and the next. Furthermore,
that gift of material things consists of what is excellent, pure, and suitable, having subdued stinginess.

It bestows the gift free from stain and the gift free from hoarding. Therein, the discipline regarding the stain of stinginess is to be understood as the relinquishing of attachment to the mind; the discipline regarding the stain of hoarding is to be understood as the relinquishing of attachment to enjoyments. This is the gift of fearlessness.

It should be understood as providing protection from fears such as lions, tigers, crocodiles, kings, thieves, water, and so forth. The gift of Dharma consists of the unerring teaching of the Dharma, instruction in the proper method, and the instigation to undertake the precepts (*śikṣāpada*). All of this—

In brief, the ninefold gift of a bodhisattva brings happiness to sentient beings both in this world and the next. Among these, the giving of material goods and the giving of protection from fear, with their various subdivisions, constitute happiness in this world. Furthermore, the giving of the Dharma, with its various subdivisions, [constitutes happiness in the next world].
133/24. [It leads to] happiness in the hereafter.

and is independent of recompense as well as independent of karmic maturation.

134/02. What is unattached giving? In this case, when a petitioner has appeared, the bodhisattva gives quickly and without delay. The petitioner does not feel such urgency in receiving as the bodhisattva feels in giving.

134/05. Regarding one who is giving: what is unattached giving? It is when a bodhisattva does not, through [wrong] views, grasp at this gift [with such thoughts]: "There is no fruit for this gift," or "Furthermore, merit arises from a gift given through violence."

Furthermore, through even a perfectly accomplished gift alone, mundane and supramundane purity comes to be. What is unaccumulated giving? It is not that a bodhisattva, having repeatedly accumulated [wealth], gives it away over a long period of time as a gift...

Having accumulated a store of dharmas, he subsequently gives a gift all at once. For what reason? Because a bodhisattva, while objects to be given are available, does not reject a petitioner who has properly approached him.

He does not venture [to do so], nor does he see it as appropriate by which he might reject it; how then could he make a collection? Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not possess a superior gateway to merit through the giving that has been accumulated.

He observes: "For what reason would a gift of equal value, given either sequentially or all at once to beggars who are equal—whether individually or collectively—result in a distinction in merit? Furthermore, [he reflects on] awakening...

The person perceives giving from accumulated wealth as indeed faulty, whereas they perceive the giving of wealth as it arises spontaneously as faultless. Why is that? Because the giver of accumulated wealth, when besought by hundreds of supplicants, [is unable to satisfy them all].
Having first dispelled their resentment, impatience, and lack of confidence,

and having subsequently generated [these positive states], he gives a gift to some of them even though unasked. Therefore, a bodhisattva does not give a gift that has been accumulated [for the sake of such a reaction].

Having given a gift, one conceives pride because of that gift, thinking: "I am the giver, the master of the gift;

What is non-reliant giving? For a bodhisattva does not [give] for the sake of fame...
One gives a gift by relying on sound, noise, and verse, considering fame— which arises from conceptual syllables, is dependent on mere words, and is like a leaf from a field—

135/08. What is non-depressed giving? Here, a bodhisattva is well-disposed even before giving; while giving, he clarifies his mind; and having given, he is without regret. Furthermore, [he gives] vast and most sublime gifts as a bodhisattva...
Having heard of the gifts of others, he does not fall into self-contempt or discouragement.
What is undepressed giving? It is when a bodhisattva, having reflected again and again, [gives].
135/14. With effort, he bestows those things among the gifts to be given that are the most excellent and superior, such as food, drink, vehicles, clothing, and so forth.
135/15–16. What is non-averse giving? A bodhisattva with an even mind—

In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality in its entirety? In brief:

A steadfast bodhisattva should be understood as one who exerts himself through his own noble wisdom (*prajñā*) after having discerned [the matter], and not by means of inciting others nor by mutual encouragement. And by him it has been accepted.
And this gift of the restraint of ethical discipline (śīla-saṃvara-samādāna) should be given to him according to this procedure.

Furthermore, for a bodhisattva thus established in the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), there are four dharmas that constitute grounds for defeat (*pārājika-sthānīya*). What are the four? [They are: being intent on gain and honor, exalting oneself, and disparaging others...

158/05/. Contempt is a bodhisattva’s offense involving defeat (*pārājika-sthānīyo dharmaḥ*). When wealth and resources are available, because of a greedy nature, [to fail to give] to those who are suffering, miserable, destitute, and helpless... 158/07/. ...in response to [their needs].

When [beings] are present, for a bodhisattva to fail to give material gifts out of cruelty, and to fail to share the teachings with those seekers who have properly approached him due to stinginess regarding the Dharma,
constitutes a defeat-level offense.

158/11/. Offense: Should a bodhisattva, being thus overcome by an outburst of anger—overpowered by anger—strike sentient beings with the hand, or with a clod of earth, or with a staff; 158/12/. [he commits an offense.]
He beats, harms, and oppresses others, maintaining an intense state of malice within himself,
yet he does not accept from others any acknowledgment of his transgression.
...the [false] Dharma. It consists of the disparagement of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, and the praising, illuminating, and establishing of counterfeit dharmas.

159/01/. Or, for one who is personally devoted to a counterfeit of the true Dharma, [the teaching] of others—[is not the true] Dharma. 159/03/. Thus, these are the four dharmas that constitute grounds for defeat, by which a bodhisattva—

159/04/. A sentient being, having committed any one or another of these [offenses], much less all of them, becomes incapable in this very life of accumulating or acquiring a vast collection of the requisites for enlightenment. He becomes incapable.
In this very life, for the sake of purifying his intention, that bodhisattva becomes a semblance bodhisattva, but not a genuine bodhisattva. Furthermore,
through weak or middling degrees of obsession, the bodhisattva— by these [factors]...

One does not abandon that undertaking of the excellence of ethical discipline by means of the four factors involving defeat; however, one abandons it through an excessive degree of obsession (*paryavasthāna*). And because a bodhisattva [commits] these four factors involving defeat—

Due to the frequent occurrence of those factors conducive to such states, one does not give rise to even a slight sense of shame (*hrī*) or dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*). Instead, one takes pleasure in them, delights in them, and perceives qualities in that very state. This is the [adhimāna].

The extent of the outburst [of the affliction] should be understood as limited. However, a bodhisattva does not abandon the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) merely by once committing an act that constitutes a defeat (*pārājika-sthānīya-dharma*), just as [a monk does not lose his vows] through the defeats.
By means of these factors, a monk [may] relinquish the Prātimokṣa restraint;
yet even a Bodhisattva who has relinquished it remains capable, in this very life, of once again undertaking the Bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline (śīla-saṃvara). It is not...

159/22. It is impossible [to lose it], just as, for example, a monk who abides in the Prātimokṣa restraint but has committed a defeat (pārājika). In brief, the relinquishment of the undertaking of the Bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline occurs for only two reasons.
And because of abandoning the vow for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
there is the intense obsession with a dharma that constitutes a defeat.

And by way of conduct: even when he has changed births, a bodhisattva does not abandon the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline and restraint (*śīla-saṃvara-samādāna*), whether being reborn below,
above, or across— everywhere— by means of that vow which the bodhisattva has made.

It is not abandoned, nor has an excessive degree of obsession regarding the rules of defeat been committed. However, having changed births, the Bodhisattva, with mindfulness lost, [seeks] a spiritual friend—
Having encountered [the conditions], he repeatedly undertakes [the vows] for the purpose of awakening mindfulness,
but not as a new undertaking.
Thus, for one established in the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline...

160/11/.
