Every day, whether for the sake of the Tathāgata at a stūpa dedicated to the Tathāgata, or for the sake of the Dharma at a stūpa dedicated to the Dharma, [one should offer] to the Bodhisattva Sūtra Piṭaka or the Mother of the Bodhisattva Sūtra Piṭaka as they exist in written form.

Whether it be for one’s own person or for the Saṅgha— whatever small or great act of worship may be performed toward the Saṅgha of those Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages throughout the ten directions— if one fails to perform even a single [act of]... at the very least, [one will experience the result].

Even by bowing with the body, at the very least, with respect to the virtues of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; or even by speaking with the voice, at the very least, uttering a single four-line verse; or even by having a single moment of serene faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.

If one passes day and night with the mind preoccupied with recollecting [the Buddha’s] qualities, one becomes guilty of an offense and a transgression. If it is due to a lack of respect, or out of laziness and indolence, one incurs an afflicted offense. If...

Due to a lapse of mindfulness, one incurs an unafflicted offense; having incurred it, one remains [in that state]. There is no offense for one whose mind is deranged. There is no offense for one whose intention is pure.

[This pertains] to one who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*). For a bodhisattva of pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*) serves the Teacher with a constant sense of duty and honors him with the highest worship, just as a monk who has attained verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*) does.
If a bodhisattva, having developed great desire, lack of contentment, or pride regarding gain and honor, tolerates [these] toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha,
he becomes guilty of an offense and commits a transgression.

One incurs an afflicted offense. There is no offense for one who has generated the desire to abandon it and exerts effort, provided they are established in its antidote by means of embracing that remedy;
nor for one who, due to an innate intensity of afflictions, is [overwhelmed].
Furthermore, because of its repeated manifestation:
when a bodhisattva sees a fellow practitioner who is senior, virtuous, worthy of honor, and superior to himself, yet is gripped by pride and harbors malice—

With an angry mind or a hostile mind, he rises and does not offer a seat. When others address him, converse with him, greet him with joy, or question him, he does not respond with an appropriate verbal reply.
If he persists while being constrained by pride, with a mind of malice or a mind of resentment,
he becomes guilty of an offense, incurs transgression, and falls into a defiled offense.
If, however, he is not constrained by pride, nor has a mind of malice or resentment, [he does not incur such an offense].

However, if it is due to laziness or indolence, or if the mind is neutral (*avyākṛta*) or there is a lapse of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃpramoṣa*), one is indeed guilty of an offense and commits a transgression (*sātisāra*), yet one does not incur an afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) offense. There is no offense if one is severely ill or has a disturbed mind (*kṣipta-citta*).
Or, there is no offense if he is asleep and the other person approaches him with the perception that he is awake,
and touches him, speaks to him, converses with him, greets him, or questions him.
There is no offense for one who is engaged in teaching the Dharma to others.
Or, in the determination of what should be spoken, there is no offense if one greets others who are different from those [previously mentioned].
There is no offense when others are teaching the Dharma and one is attentive.

There is no offense for one who listens with the ear to a definitive discourse on the discussion [of the Dharma]. There is no offense for one who complies with the flow of a discourse on the Dharma and the intention of the preacher of the Dharma. There is no offense for one who, by that means, tames those sentient beings.

There is no offense for one who, by means of discipline, causes another to rise from an unwholesome state and establishes them in a wholesome state; there is no offense for one who protects a formal act (*kriyākāra*) belonging to the Saṃgha;
there is no offense when it concerns the minds of a greater number of others.
162/07/. While guarding [the precepts], 162/08/.
a bodhisattva, being invited by others to a house or within a monastery for food, drink, clothing, and other requisites, [should act as follows].

If, being restrained by pride, or with a mind of malice or resentment, one does not go, nor accepts the invitation, one incurs an offense and a transgression; one commits a defiled offense. If one does not go due to indolence or laziness—

One incurs an afflicted offense. There is no offense if one is ill, lacks physical strength, or is deranged in mind. There is no offense if the location is remote or the path is dangerous. There is no offense if, by that means, one is to be tamed.

One may desire to discipline [another], wishing to raise them up from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state. There is no offense if another person has already made a prior commitment. There is no offense if [the action is performed] immediately.

There is no offense for one who is engaged in the side of the wholesome and, in order to guard against breaches in the side of the unwholesome, does not go [to see someone], provided it is for the sake of hearing a previously unheard teaching that is connected with the goal and conducive to the Dharma and its meaning, and which is a cause for the non-decline [of those qualities], just as in the case of the Dharma and its meaning.
The same should be understood regarding the determination of a discussion for the sake of listening.
There is no offense if one has been invited with the intention of causing harassment. There is no offense if one protects against the hostile mind of a great many others.
There is no offense for one who protects a formal act (kriyākāra) of the Saṃgha.
A bodhisattva [who accepts] gold, silver, or jewels from others...
If, while receiving excellent, diverse, and abundant varieties of pearls, lapis lazuli, and so forth—
superior and of the highest quality— one who is not pleased, but instead harbors a mind of malice and a mind of resentment, refuses to accept them and rejects them, he becomes guilty of an offense.

One incurs an offense of wrongdoing and commits a defiled transgression by neglecting sentient beings. If one does not accept [a request] due to indolence or laziness, one becomes guilty of an offense and incurs wrongdoing, yet one does not commit a defiled transgression. There is no offense for one whose mind is deranged.

There is no offense for one who perceives that the mind finds delight in accepting that gift. There is no offense for one who anticipates that remorse will arise for him later. There is no offense for one who anticipates a failure in the act of giving. There is no offense for one who is free from attachment.

There is no offense for one who perceives that it would cause poverty or ruin to the donor or the master of the gift on account of that [gift]. There is no offense for one who perceives that the item belongs to the Saṃgha or to a stūpa.
There is no offense for one who perceives that it was taken away by another from him. From these [cases], there is no offense.
If there should arise for him a cause for execution, imprisonment, punishment, loss,
or censure,
yet the bodhisattva maintains a mind of malice toward others who seek the Dharma.
If, with a mind of resentment or disturbed by envy, one does not bestow the Dharma, one commits an offense;
one becomes guilty of a transgression and incurs an afflicted offense.
If one does not give [the Dharma] out of laziness or indolence, one commits an offense; one becomes guilty of a transgression.

One does not incur a defiled offense. There is no offense in looking at the rules of non-Buddhist ascetics. There is no offense if one is severely ill or mentally deranged. There is no offense if, by that means, one intends to subdue or discipline [the person].
Desiring to cause [another] to rise from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state,
there is no offense if they do not engage with the Dharma.
There is no offense if they should accept [the teaching] while being disrespectful, lacking reverence, and possessing improper conduct.
It is an offense for one of dull faculties to cause alarm, false views, or false adherence through an exalted teaching of the Dharma or through the mastery of the Dharma.
One may cause injury and damage [to the Dharma]. There is no offense if,
while the Dharma is in one's hands, one causes it to be dispersed among others who are not fit vessels for the Dharma.
If a bodhisattva, toward beings who are fierce and of immoral conduct, maintains a mind of malice or a mind of resentment, and either neglects them or behaves with harshness—
taking their fierceness and immorality as the very reason for doing so— he incurs an offense and is at fault.

164/09/. One who is essential [to the community] incurs an afflicted offense if, out of laziness and indolence, he neglects [his duty], or if, through loss of mindfulness, he acts improperly; he becomes guilty of an offense and a transgression. 164/10/.
However, he does not incur an afflicted offense. Why is that? Because it is not...
In the engagement of a bodhisattva’s actions of body, speech,
and mind, there is present a compassionate mind and a desire to act in such a way that, toward even fierce and immoral sentient beings who are suffering—

There is no offense when [the act] is for the sake of a cause among those who are present; there is no offense for one whose mind is deranged. There is no offense if, as before, one intends to discipline that person by means of such a method. There is no offense for one who is protecting the minds of many others. There is no offense for the Saṃgha...

164/18. Those who guard their conduct and manner of action. 164/19. A bodhisattva [observes] that which has been established by the Blessed One in the Prātimokṣa and Vinaya as an offense of transgression (pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya) on account of guarding the minds of others—
For the sake of inspiring faith in those who have not yet found it, and for the sake of increasing the steadfastness of those who already possess it.
In this regard, he practices a training identical to that of the śrāvakas, without any distinction.
For what reason? Because the śrāvakas, for their part, are primarily intent upon their own self-interest; they, at least, do not...

They train themselves in the precepts for the sake of protecting others, to inspire faith in those who lack it, and to increase the faith of those who already possess it; how much more so, then, the bodhisattvas.
165/01. Those for whom the welfare of others is supreme.

165/02. Furthermore, regarding those [precepts] that are blameworthy by prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), which concern having few aims, few duties, and dwelling with little concern, for the Śrāvakas of the Blessed One—
[This] has been established by the Blessed One. In that regard, a bodhisattva does not practice a training identical to that of the śrāvakas.
For what reason? It is fitting for a śrāvaka who is supreme in his own interest and indifferent to the interest of others to [strive] for the interest of others.

165/07/. One who has set out for his own sake is of little purpose, performs few deeds, and dwells with little zeal; however, 165/08/. a bodhisattva, for whom the welfare of others is supreme, does not shine if he is of little purpose, performs few deeds, and dwells with little zeal regarding the welfare of others. For thus it is with a bodhisattva—

With the aim of benefiting others, one who has been invited [to accept robes] should seek from unrelated brahmins and householders hundreds or even thousands of robes, having carefully observed the strength and weakness of those beings. Up to...

They are to be accepted for their utility, just as robes are. Just as they are to be sought after, so too [robes] are to be woven by professional weavers with thread requested by oneself, provided there is authorization. And for the sake of others, [robes made of] silk—

Hundreds of rugs should be provided; even hundreds of thousands of millions of the finest things, such as gold and silver, should be accepted. With regard to such matters as having few possessions, few duties, and dwelling with little concern, [the Buddha spoke] to the disciples...

As an antidote to these [faults], a bodhisattva who abides in the restraint of the bodhisattva ethical discipline becomes one whose training is equal [to that of others] regarding the welfare of sentient beings;
he does not harbor a mind of malice or a mind of resentment, and he possesses great purpose and performs great deeds.

One who dwells with little concern becomes guilty of an offense, incurs a transgression, and falls into a defiled offense. Through indolence and laziness, one becomes of little purpose and little activity;
by dwelling with little concern, one becomes guilty of an offense, incurs a transgression, and [falls into a defiled offense].
He incurs an afflicted transgression.
Furthermore, there are certain natural misdeeds (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) which a bodhisattva may practice by means of such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) that he remains free from transgression.
And much merit is produced. For instance,
when a bodhisattva [encounters] a thief or a robber who has [killed] many hundreds of living beings—

He sees many people intent on committing immediate karmic offenses for the sake of some small material gain, against those great beings— the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas. Having seen this, he further...
In this way, he conditions his mind with his thought:
"Even if, by depriving this living being of life, I were to be reborn in the hells, let my rebirth in the hells be so; for this sentient being has committed an act of immediate retribution."

"Having done this, let it not be that he goes to hell. With such an intention, the bodhisattva— having recognized that living being and being either of a wholesome or neutral state of mind— feels revulsion and, out of compassion, [deprives him] of life for the sake of his future welfare.
166/12. Regarding the taking of life: there is no transgression, and much merit is produced.
166/13. This is as when a bodhisattva [deals with] those beings who are kings, or... 166/14. [who are] kings.

Or, kings or great ministers who are exceedingly fierce and merciless toward sentient beings, being exclusively intent on harming others— if he has the power, he causes them to fall from that royal sovereignty and dominion upon which they stand, and for that reason...
Those who, with a mind of compassion and an intention for welfare and happiness, produce great demerit— namely,
those thieves and robbers who seize the abundant property belonging to the Saṅgha or to a stūpa, and having taken it, appropriate and consume it.
166/21/. [There are] those who are addicted to sensual pleasures. From them, the bodhisattva seizes property, thinking:
"Lest indeed that enjoyment of property by them lead to harm and disadvantage for a long time. Having made this very condition and having seized it, he gives it away.

He restores to the Saṃgha what belongs to the Saṃgha, and to the stūpa what belongs to the stūpa. Furthermore, those who are attendants or monastery servants who, through misconduct, squander property belonging to the Saṃgha or the stūpa and make it their own personal possession—
They consume it. Having reflected upon this, the bodhisattva thinks: "May that karma and that wrong consumption not become long-lasting for them."
"Night and day, for the sake of what is not beneficial and what is not wholesome, he causes [the person] to fall from that position of authority.
Therefore, by this method, even though the bodhisattva takes what has not been given,
he incurs no offense and generates much merit."
For example, a householder bodhisattva might engage in sexual intercourse with a woman who is not married to another, who is tormented by the desire for non-celibacy, whose mind is bound to him,
and who has not been taken by another; let it not be that he [acts] out of a mind of malice.

One will produce much demerit. Having established a mind of compassion, thinking, "She shall be submissive in the application of roots of merit as desired, and in the abandonment of roots of non-merit," [one should refrain from] unchaste conduct.
Even while practicing sexual intercourse,
he incurs no offense and generates great merit. Furthermore, for a bodhisattva who has gone forth,
while guarding against the schism of the Śrāvaka teaching, in every respect—
It is not permissible for a bodhisattva to engage in unchaste conduct,
even if it is for the sake of liberating many sentient beings from death, or for the sake of liberating them from bondage to their hands and feet.

For the sake of preventing the cutting off of noses or ears, and for the sake of protecting against the impairment or destruction of the eyes— that conscious false speech which a bodhisattva would not utter even for the sake of his own life, he may nevertheless speak it for the benefit of those sentient beings.
He speaks after careful deliberation. In brief, by whatever means a bodhisattva perceives only the welfare of sentient beings and not their harm,
and he himself possesses a mind free from worldly desire, desiring solely the benefit of sentient beings— this is [the basis for his speech].
If one speaks otherwise than what is true while being fully aware and having set aside the underlying intention, one incurs no offense while speaking; rather,
one generates much merit.
Furthermore, just as when there are sentient beings who have been taken hold of by non-virtuous friends, the bodhisattva [acts] for them, [to separate them] from those non-virtuous friends...

To the best of his ability and according to his strength, he utters speech that causes distraction; and being delighted by it, he becomes one who delights in distraction. Yet, taking only a mind of compassion as his basis, he thinks: "May these sentient beings not fall into association with evil friends."
"Over a long period of time, for their disadvantage and harm"— by this formulation, even if a bodhisattva causes a breach of friendship, he incurs no offense and generates much merit.
Furthermore, it is when a bodhisattva, with harsh or sharp speech, reproves beings who are walking on a wrong path or who do not walk according to the right principle,
solely for the purpose of causing them to rise from an unwholesome state and establish them in a wholesome state by that means.
For the purpose of establishing [others in virtue], a bodhisattva who speaks harshly in this way incurs no offense and generates much merit.
This is as when a bodhisattva [acts] toward those who are devoted to dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
For those beings who are preoccupied with talk of kings, thieves, food, drink, courtesans, streets, and the like,
he [the Buddha] attends to them through dance, song, and instrumental music,
as well as through various conversations associated with frivolous chatter.
Having satisfied them with a compassionate intention and having won them over, he brings them to a state of submissiveness and obedience;
having caused them to rise from an unwholesome state, he establishes them in a wholesome state.
In this way, even a bodhisattva who engages in frivolous chatter incurs no offense.
And much merit is produced. A bodhisattva [should abandon] hypocrisy, flattery, hinting, belittling, and the desire to obtain gain by means of gain that has already been acquired.

If one tolerates factors that constitute wrong livelihood, and does not feel repugnance toward them, nor dispel them, one becomes guilty of an offense; one incurs an afflicted offense with transgression. There is no offense for one who has generated the desire to dispel them.
Because, for one who has initiated effort, the mind is overcome by the abundance of afflictions and thus [the practice] does not proceed.
A bodhisattva, with a mind seized by restlessness, being unpacified and delighting in lack of pacification, laughs loudly, plays about,
shouts "kilikila," and manifests agitation and levity toward others.
Desiring to cause laughter or desiring to provide amusement—having made this very condition the motive—one becomes guilty of an offense; one commits a transgression and incurs an afflicted offense.
Through loss of mindfulness, one incurs an unafflicted offense. There is no offense [if it occurs] otherwise.

169/09/. If, having developed the desire to dispel that [distress], it is as previously described, there is no offense. 169/10/. There is no offense if one intends to dispel, by that means, the malice that has arisen in others.
169/11/. There is no offense if one intends to remove the grief that has arisen in others.

One incurs an offense. If, due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, one does not recite [the scriptures], one incurs an unafflicted offense. There is no offense if, by nature, one has few desires, and one does not commit an offense solely for the sake of maintaining that state.

If he should be ill and lacking the strength [to do so], there is no offense, provided that by such a means he intends to tame and instruct [the person] as previously described. There is no offense for one who protects the formal procedure (*kriyākāra*) of the Saṃgha. There is no offense if, on account of that, it would lead to affliction...
If one considers pleasure, intoxication, or pride to lead to harm,

there is no offense in acting to avoid them. This applies even if the qualities [claimed] are merely counterfeits of virtue rather than genuine virtues, or if the eloquent speech is a counterfeit of true eloquence.

It is not a transgression if he is a non-Buddhist who ought to be subdued. It is also no transgression for one who is waiting for the conclusion of the discourse. [Furthermore,] it is no transgression for a bodhisattva [to employ] those beings who deserve censure or who deserve disciplinary action.
If one with a defiled mind does not censure those who deserve banishment;
or, having censured them, does not subject them to disciplinary action; or, having subjected them to disciplinary action, does not banish them—one incurs an offense and commits a transgression.

One incurs an afflicted offense through indolence, laziness, or negligence, provided one does not censure [the offender], nor banish them. One incurs an unafflicted offense [if one fails to do so] out of [compassion].
There is no offense if the person is incurable, or if they are unfit for discussion, difficult to speak with, or harbor malice.
There is no offense for one who frequently practices equanimity; there is no offense for one who is waiting for the appropriate time.
There is no offense arising from that cause involving quarreling, brawling, strife, or dispute.

Those who observe [the situation]— observing whether there will be gathering, conflict, or division— are not at fault. Those beings should be free from deceit and endowed with intense shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*),
so that they may very quickly restore themselves to their former state.
180/04/. A bodhisattva, endowed with the power of various miraculous transformations and displays,

[employs] supernatural power for the purpose of terrifying those beings who ought to be terrified, for the purpose of winning over those beings who ought to be won over, and for the purpose of protecting what has been given in faith.
If one neither terrifies nor wins over [others], one incurs an offense; one is guilty of a transgression.
One incurs an unafflicted offense. There is no offense in a case where sentient beings are for the most part deeply attached to heresy through the denigration of the Noble Ones.

Those who are possessed of wrong view [are exempt]. Furthermore, there is no offense in any case for one whose mind is deranged by an excessive [affliction], for one who is overwhelmed by intense suffering, or for one who has not undertaken the vows. It should be understood thus.
Thus, these training precepts (śikṣāpāda) of the bodhisattvas, which concern arisen matters,
have been extensively proclaimed by the Blessed One in various sūtras: namely, the morality of restraint (saṃvara-śīla),
the morality of gathering virtuous qualities (kuśala-saṃgrāhaka-śīla), and the morality of acting for the benefit of sentient beings (sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla).

Having begun from there, all those [precepts] are fully explained in this *Mātṛkā* of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, in which a bodhisattva, having generated earnestness and established the highest reverence, must practice training. From others, [he receives] restraint (*saṃvara*).

Having made the formal undertaking, one should from the very beginning be free from transgression, having generated a sense of reverence through a perfectly pure intention to train, an intention for awakening, and an intention for the welfare of sentient beings; and should one transgress, [one should act] according to the Dharma.

One must perform restoration through making amends. All such an offense of a bodhisattva is to be understood as being comprised within the category of "wrongdoing" (*duṣkṛta*). It should be confessed in the presence of anyone whatsoever, whether they belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Mahāyāna.
If there were someone capable of understanding and grasping that vocal intimation,
and if a bodhisattva [were to commit] an offense involving defeat...

If one has committed an offense through an intense outburst of passion (*paryavasthāna*), the restraint (*saṃvara*) is relinquished by that act; it must be taken up once again. If, however, one has committed an offense through a moderate outburst of passion, by that—
One should confess a misdeed (*duṣkṛta*) before three persons, or even more than that.
Having first announced the matter, one should sit down before them and say this: "Venerable sir, please attend to me; I, who am named so-and-so..."

If a bodhisattva has committed a misdeed (*duṣkṛta*) by transgressing the bodhisattva discipline regarding a matter as it has been proclaimed, the rest should be understood in the same way as when a monk confesses a *duṣkṛta*. This also applies to that which constitutes a defeat (*pārājika*).

It should be understood that for a transgression involving a mild outburst of passion (*paryavasthāna*), confession before a single person is sufficient; this also applies to other offenses. Furthermore, if a suitable person is not available before whom one might confess, the Bodhisattva should, with sincere intention (*āśaya*), resolve never to commit it again.
One should arouse a sense of shame regarding the mind and practice restraint for the future.
In this way, one who has emerged from that transgression should be addressed.
This also constitutes the formal undertaking of the bodhisattva vow.
If a person endowed with those qualities is not present,
then the bodhisattva should himself undertake the vow of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline in the presence of an image of the Tathāgata. And in this way:

It must be performed again. Having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder, having placed the right knee upon the ground, and squatting before [the preceptor], this should be recited: "I, who am named so-and-so, in the ten directions..."
In all directions, I inform all the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages; and in their presence,
I undertake all the training precepts of a Bodhisattva and the entire Bodhisattva ethical discipline of restraint.
Ethical discipline consists of the discipline that gathers virtuous qualities and the discipline that acts for the benefit of sentient beings;
it is that in which all bodhisattvas of the past have trained, and [all those of] the future [will train].

"Bodhisattvas will train; all bodhisattvas in the ten directions are training at present. This should be stated twice and thrice. Having spoken thus, one should rise. All that remains, however, is as before.
It should be understood that there is no transgression whatsoever on the path of a bodhisattva; furthermore,
as has been stated by the Blessed One, for the most part, a bodhisattva’s [transgression] is hatred—

An offense arising from this [compassion] should be understood as not being one arising from passion (*rāga*). In this regard, the following intention is to be seen: whatever a bodhisattva performs, having made affection for sentient beings and love for sentient beings the predominant factor, all that—

The duty of a bodhisattva is not a non-duty; nor is it appropriate for one performing that duty to incur an offense. However, a bodhisattva who harbors hatred toward sentient beings does not act for the benefit of himself or others, and this is not [the path to] awakening.

The duty of a sentient being is as follows: it is appropriate that an offense occurs for one who performs what is not their duty. Furthermore, the mild, medium, and intense degrees of a bodhisattva’s offenses are to be understood as they are set forth in the *Vastu-saṃgrahaṇī*.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who is thus engaged in training within his own discipline dwells in a state of ease, endowed with three perfections:
the perfection of application, the perfection of intention, and the perfection of prior causes.

In that regard, what is the perfection of application? It is when a bodhisattva acts without flaw regarding the ethical precepts, possesses completely pure conduct of body, speech, and mind, does not frequently commit offenses, and discloses his misdeeds.
This is called the perfection of application (*prayoga-saṃpat*).

What is the perfection of intention (*āśaya-saṃpat*)? It is when one who has gone forth does so with the intention for the Dharma, not with the intention for a livelihood; he is one who seeks great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
He is not one who seeks what is meaningless; he is one who seeks the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*) and liberation (*nirvāṇa*), and he does not seek what is meaningless.
Being thus intent on his goal, he dwells neither indolent, nor lacking in vigor, nor devoid of vigor;
he is not defiled by evil, unwholesome states that lead to affliction and rebirth.
[Actions] that are real, accompanied by feverish distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to birth, aging, and death in the future—
this is called the perfection of intention (*āśaya-saṃpad*).
What is the perfection of prior causes? It is when a bodhisattva, in previous births, has performed meritorious deeds and cultivated wholesome roots,
by virtue of which he is not himself deprived of robes, alms-food, bedding, and so forth in this present life.
He is capable of sharing with others the requisites for bedding, seats, and medicinal provisions for the sick; this should be understood as the Bodhisattva’s perfection of prior causes.
Endowed with these three prosperities,
a bodhisattva engaged in the training dwells in comfort.
Conversely, endowed with the three adversities, he dwells in suffering.
It should be understood that he dwells in contact [with this].
This, first of all, is called the bodhisattva’s entire morality, both in brief and in detail,
pertaining to the side of the laity and the side of those who have gone forth.
Furthermore, the detailed classification of this very same morality includes other types, such as difficult-to-practice morality (*duṣkara-śīla*) and so forth, which should be understood.
Among these, what is the difficult-to-practice morality of a bodhisattva? It is threefold:
This should be understood as being of eighteen kinds.
When a bodhisattva possessing great wealth, while abiding in great sovereignty and lordship,
renounces those enjoyments and renounces that great sovereignty—
The undertaking of the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) with sovereign mastery is called the difficult ethical discipline of a bodhisattva. Furthermore,
even when fallen into hardship, a bodhisattva who has undertaken ethical discipline— up until [the attainment of]...
Even when falling into adversity, he does not break that undertaking of the restraint of ethical discipline;
how much less would he ever cause it to be ruined? This is called the bodhisattva’s second difficult-to-practice ethical discipline.
In such and such a manner, bodhisattvas maintain established mindfulness and remain vigilant in all conduct, dwellings, and mental engagements, even for the duration of their entire lives.
He does not commit even a slight transgression, nor does he stumble in his ethical discipline; how much less so a grave one? This is called the bodhisattva’s third difficult ethical discipline.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality that faces all directions?
It should be understood as being fourfold: morality undertaken, natural morality, practiced morality, and morality endowed with skillful means.
In this regard, "undertaken morality" refers to that by which a bodhisattva has performed the threefold undertaking of morality:
the morality of restraint,
the morality of gathering virtuous qualities, and the morality of acting for the welfare of sentient beings.
In this context, natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*) is that which occurs when, for a bodhisattva who abides in the lineage (*gotra*),
bodily and vocal actions proceed with a completely pure continuum precisely because of his natural goodness.

In that regard, "practiced ethical discipline" refers to a bodhisattva by whom the threefold ethical discipline, as previously described, has been practiced in other former births. By virtue of the empowerment of that prior causal force, he does not [violate it] in any way whatsoever.
He delights in evil conduct and recoils from evil. He delights in virtuous conduct and yearns only for virtuous conduct.
In this regard, ethical discipline (*śīla*) endowed with skillful means consists of the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgraha-vastu*).
Based upon these bases, a bodhisattva’s virtuous physical and vocal actions toward sentient beings proceed.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality of a true person? It is as follows:

It should be understood as being fivefold. Here, a bodhisattva is himself possessed of ethical discipline (*śīla*), encourages others to undertake ethical discipline, speaks in praise of ethical discipline, and upon seeing a fellow practitioner of the Dharma, becomes joyful.
...he falls into an offense and remedies it in accordance with the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality in all its forms? It is as follows:
The sixfold and sevenfold [types of giving], condensed together into one, should be understood as thirteenfold. It is dedicated toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Because it is embraced by extensive rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), it is lucid; [it is free from] the pleasure of desire...

Because it avoids the two extremes of sensual indulgence and self-mortification, it is a basis for blameless joy. Because one does not renounce the training even for the duration of one's life, it is constant.
It cannot be overcome by any gain, honor, adversaries, or primary and secondary afflictions.

Because it is difficult to corrupt and cannot be taken away, it is firm. It is also endowed with the ornament of ethical discipline (*śīlālaṃkāra*). The ornament of ethical discipline should be understood as follows, as described in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*: ethical discipline of abstention through refraining from killing living beings and so forth; and ethical discipline of the wholesome...
The morality of engagement consists in gathering [beings] and accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.

The protective morality consists in guarding the morality of engagement and withdrawal. There is the morality that ripens into the marks of a Great Man, the morality that ripens into higher mind, and the morality that leads to a desirable rebirth.

[It is] that which results from maturation (*vaipākya*) and that which results from maturation for the sake of sentient beings (*sattvārtha-vaipākya*). Among these, what is the bodhisattva’s morality regarding the relief of those who are distressed and seeking help?
That should be understood as being of eight kinds. Here, the bodhisattva himself...
In this way, he reflects as follows: "Just as I am desirous of life, may no one deprive me of life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct,
speak falsehoods, utter slander, harsh words, or idle chatter."
One might engage in idle chatter, or treat one with undesirable contacts such as those of hands, clods of earth, or creepers,
or even with violent assaults. For me, who am thus seeking [the goal], [this would be the case].
If others were to treat me with hostility, I would experience distress because of that; it would be disagreeable to me. Just as we desire that others not deprive us of life, and so on in detail...

"May they not treat me with harmful contact. If I were to treat those who seek [my favor] in a contrary manner, they would be frustrated; that would be unpleasant for them. Thus, [he reflects: what...

"Since this is unpleasant for both myself and others, why should I treat others with such unpleasantness? Having reflected thus, the bodhisattva does not treat others with the eight kinds of unpleasant behavior, even for the sake of his own life.
186/10. This is called the eightfold morality of the bodhisattva for those who seek relief from distress.
186/11. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s morality that brings happiness in this life and the next?
That should be understood as being of nine kinds. Here, the bodhisattva [provides] for sentient beings...
He prohibits those matters that ought to be prohibited; he permits those matters that ought to be permitted. He gathers in those beings who ought to be gathered in;
he restrains those beings who ought to be restrained. In this regard, for the bodhisattva—
That bodily and vocal action which proceeds in a state of complete purity— this, first of all,

is the fourfold ethical discipline (*śīla*). Furthermore, there is another ethical discipline associated with generosity (*dāna*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

And that which is concomitant is fivefold. When these are condensed together into a single whole, morality becomes ninefold. And for that bodhisattva, as well as for others, it conduces to happiness in the present life and in future lives. Therefore—
This is called "happiness in this world and the next.
In that regard, what is the pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of a bodhisattva? It should be understood as being of ten kinds. From the very beginning, it is well-undertaken.

It has proceeded because it is free from misplaced remorse (*kaukṛtya*). It is free from laziness (*kausīdya*) because it does not indulge in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining on one's side, or the pleasure of lying down, and because of its application to the side of virtue day and night. It is unremitting...

It is not possessed by negligence, as previously described, due to the practice of the five factors of heedfulness. It is rightly directed because of the departure from craving for gain and honor; it is [undertaken] by making a vow for the state of a god while practicing the holy life.
And because of the acceptance of the saffron robe, it is embraced by the perfection of conduct through the manner of deportment;

that is, by way of the well-composed and appropriate engagement of body and speech in the application of the factors of the side of wholesome action. It is [also embraced] by the perfection of livelihood.
It is embraced because it is free from all faults that produce wrong livelihood, such as hypocrisy (*kuhana*) and the like;
it avoids the two extremes because it is free from devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure and self-mortification;
and it leads to liberation because it is free from the views of all non-Buddhist teachers.
Through its state of being free from [faults], the morality of bodhisattvas is not fallen away from its undertaking;
through its state of being without breach or destruction, this tenfold morality of bodhisattvas is called "pure."

Thus, this is the great aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) of a bodhisattva, which brings about the fruit of great enlightenment; relying upon it, the bodhisattva fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) and awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And until he attains perfect awakening, while training in this immeasurable aggregate of bodhisattva morality, he obtains five benefits:
he is attended by the Buddhas; he possesses great joy;...

Dying while remaining [in that state], after the dissolution of the body, he is reborn there among those bodhisattvas who possess equal or superior ethical discipline, who are his peers, fellow practitioners of the Dharma,
and who have become his spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). And by means of immeasurable merit—

He becomes endowed with the aggregate that fulfills the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). In both the present life and future lives, he attains natural ethical discipline and a state of being composed of that very ethical discipline.
And all this morality, as previously described— beginning with natural morality (*svabhāva-śīla*) and so forth—
is ninefold in its aspects and is subsumed under three types of morality.

It should be understood that [this] is by means of the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of acting for the benefit of sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). Furthermore, that threefold morality, in brief, performs three functions for the bodhisattva. First, the morality of restraint...

Ethical discipline (*śīla*) conduces to the stability of the mind; the ethical discipline that gathers what is wholesome conduces to the maturation of one’s own Buddha-qualities; and the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings conduces to the maturation of sentient beings. And this much is the [ethical discipline] of a bodhisattva—

For him, everything that is to be done is accomplished; namely, the stability of the mind for dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*), the ripening of the Buddha-dharmas with body and mind untiring, and the ripening of sentient beings. This much is awakening.
This is the morality of sentient beings. Such is the extent of the benefit of the bodhisattva’s morality;

such is the extent of the function of the bodhisattva’s morality—there is nothing beyond this and nothing more than this—in which the bodhisattvas of the past who desired great enlightenment have trained, and in which those of the future shall likewise train.

They will train; those currently existing in the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions are also training. This is the tenth [chapter], the Bodhisattvabhūmi, in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
188/18/. The Chapter on Ethical Discipline (*śīla-paṭala*). 189/01/.
The summary verse (*uddāna*) should be understood as being the same as that in the [previous] Chapter on Ethical Discipline.

189/02. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience by nature (*svabhāva-kṣānti*)? It is the endurance of harm from others and the endurance of all [harm] toward all [beings], whether based on the power of analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*) or by way of one's innate nature (*prakṛtyā*). 189/03–04. And it is the endurance of everything.
Endurance with a mind free from worldly desire and through pure compassion— this,
in brief, should be understood as the nature of a bodhisattva’s patience.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s all-inclusive patience?
That [patience] is to be seen as twofold: that which relies on the side of householders and that which relies on the side of those who have gone forth.
Furthermore, even that which relies on both sides should be understood as threefold:
patience in enduring harm from others, patience in accepting suffering, and patience regarding the Dharma.
189/11/. And there is the patience of meditative reflection and resolute conviction.
189/12/. In that regard, how does a bodhisattva endure and tolerate harm inflicted by others?
Here, a bodhisattva [encounters harm] that is intense, continuous, diverse, and long-lasting.
Furthermore, when suffering arising from the harm inflicted by others manifests before him, he trains himself with regard to this: "This is the fault of my own karma;
it is because of my own previously committed unwholesome action that I experience such a result of suffering."

"I experience this, yet I am averse to suffering. Moreover, this intolerance serves as a cause for future suffering. How could I, having undertaken such a factor that constitutes a cause of suffering, continue to abide in it?"

"Surely this is undesirable for me alone. Therefore, I would be joining myself with myself; thus, it would be an injury done to myself, and not so much to others. Furthermore, by their very nature, these [senses] are of the essence of suffering."

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belong to the continuums of oneself and others. Among these, those who are ignorant first inflict further suffering upon beings who are already suffering by their very nature.
However, for us who possess discernment (*vijñāna*), it would not be fitting [to do the same].
"We too would further inflict suffering upon others who are already suffering by their very nature; and this, even though we ourselves are currently striving for our own sake."
"It would be improper for the Śrāvakas to lack patience when it produces suffering for both themselves and others, let alone for us who are dedicated to the welfare of others.
Having reflected thus, that Bodhisattva [cultivates] the fivefold perception.

Cultivating [loving-kindness] toward friends, enemies, and neutral parties; toward those inferior, equal, or superior; toward those who are happy or suffering; and toward beings endowed with virtues or faults, he endures all injuries.

What are the five perceptions? They are: the perception of former-life friends, the perception that follows mere phenomena, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, and the perception of non-appropriation.
190/10. And how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of friendliness toward sentient beings who have done him harm? Here, a bodhisattva trains himself thus:

"That sentient being who, after the passing of a long period of time, [has not been my relative] is not easily found. 190/12. [He reflects: "No such sentient being is easily found who, after the passing of a long duration..."
"In previous births, he has been one's mother, father, brother, sister, teacher, preceptor, guru, or one in the position of a guru.
As he attends to this with proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), the perception of him as an adversary ceases.
Toward those beings who act harmfully, [the bodhisattva] disappears [from their perception], and the notion of them as friends remains established.
Relying upon that notion of them as friends, he endures and forgives their harms. And how does a bodhisattva [behave] toward beings who have acted harmfully? Regarding the Dharma—

He cultivates the perception that follows after measure. Here, the bodhisattva trains himself thus: "This is merely conditioned formations, merely phenomena, dependent upon conditions; herein there is no self or sentient being whatsoever."
Whether it be a living soul (*jīva*), a sentient being (*jaṃtu*), one who might revile, provoke to anger,
strike, mock, or abuse; or one who might be reviled, provoked to anger, struck, mocked, or abused— [for such a person], he thus applies correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).

As he practices, the perception of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*) disappears, and the perception of mere phenomena (*dharma-mātra-saṃjñā*) remains. Relying upon and established in that perception of mere phenomena,
he endures all harm from others.
He dwells [in patience] and endures. How does a bodhisattva conceive the notion of impermanence toward sentient beings who have done him harm?

191/03. He cultivates [this]. Here, a bodhisattva trains himself with regard to this: "Whatever beings there are who have been born and have come into existence, all of them are impermanent and subject to death.
And this is the ultimate injury, namely, the depriving of life."

191/06–191/08. For a wise person, it would not be fitting even to give rise to a defiled thought toward sentient beings who are subject to death and impermanence; how much less so to strike them with the hand, a clod of earth, or a staff?
Or even [to kill] by means of a weapon, let alone to deprive anyone entirely of life.

As he attends to this with proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), the perception of permanence and solidity is abandoned, and the perception of impermanence and lack of solidity is established. He, regarding that which is impermanent and lacks solidity—
Relying on perception, he endures and forgives all injuries inflicted by others.
And how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of suffering toward sentient beings who cause him harm? In this case, a bodhisattva [regards] even those sentient beings...

Even those who abide in great prosperity, he perceives as being pursued by the three types of suffering: the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); how much more so those who dwell in misfortune.

Seeing this, he trains himself with regard to this: "In this way, we must strive for the removal of suffering from sentient beings who are thus constantly pursued by suffering, and not for the infliction of suffering. For him, such is the proper reflection—

For one who attends [to this], the perception of pleasure is abandoned and the perception of suffering arises. Relying upon that perception of suffering, he endures and forgives all injuries inflicted by others.
191/24. And how does a bodhisattva cultivate the perception of embracing those beings who have done him harm? In this regard, a bodhisattva trains himself thus:
"Indeed, by me, while generating the mind for enlightenment, all sentient beings [have been embraced]."
Having accepted [them] as my wife and children, I have thought, "I must act for the benefit of all sentient beings. Therefore, it would not be fitting for me if I were to act thus.

"Taking all sentient beings as my basis, I shall act for their benefit"— if, while harboring such a thought, I were to do what is harmful and inflict injury because I am unable to endure it, I would be acting contrary to that very purpose. As he applies himself to this proper mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*), his perception of others as separate from himself (*para-saṃjñā*) regarding those sentient beings who have done him harm is abandoned.
The perception of "acceptance" (parigraha-saṃjñā) is established. Relying upon that perception of acceptance, one endures and forgives all injuries from others.
What is patience (kṣānti)? It is that which does not become angry and does not retaliate.
It does not produce passion, nor is it to be carried by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). This is called patience (*kṣānti*).
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s patience of enduring suffering?
Here, the bodhisattva trains himself with respect to this: "Indeed, by me..."

Formerly, while engaged in the pursuit of sensual pleasures and seeking those desires, he reflected that they are of the nature of suffering because they are a cause of suffering; for the sake of such sensual pleasures,
he underwent many intense sufferings.
These [sufferings] were endured and experienced while engaged in agriculture, commerce, royal service, and military duty.
Thus, that was in vain; through the fault of ignorance and a lack of discernment, I have accepted great suffering for the sake of nothing but suffering.
But now, for me who is engaged in wholesome conduct that brings about happiness,
it would be appropriate to accept and endure suffering that is a hundred thousand times ten million times greater than that, having reflected upon it; how much more so than before?
192/21. Of that which is deficient. Thus, correctly attending to [the mind] and applying himself to awakening, the bodhisattva endures suffering pertaining to all things.
192/22–23. What is suffering pertaining to all things? Briefly stated, it is as follows:
It should be understood as having eight aspects: the basis of reliance, the basis of worldly dharmas, the basis of deportment, the basis of grasping the Dharma,
the basis of the mode of life for alms-gathering, and the basis of application.
The basis of weariness, the basis of performing deeds for the sake of sentient beings,
and the basis of what is to be done.

193/02. There are four requisites. Relying upon these, one enters the religious life, receives full ordination, and attains the status of a bhikṣu within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; namely: robes, alms-food, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick.

And by means of those [resources], even if the bodhisattva receives coarse and meager wealth without it being treated with respect, he does not feel longing for it, nor does he become despondent; nor does he, on that account, slacken his vigor. Such is the basis of reliance.

193/09/. There are nine worldly conditions (*loka-dharma*): lack of gain, ill-repute, censure, suffering, the loss of that which is subject to loss, the decay of that which is subject to decay, old age—

right effort is so called because it is directed toward the attainment of the goal to be attained which is connected with the purpose, because it is continuous due to constant application, and because it is free from...
