In that context, what is the pure vigor of a bodhisattva? It is as follows:
In brief, it should be understood as being of ten kinds:

conformable, practiced, unremitting, well-grasped, applied with practice at the proper time, joined with the discernment of signs, non-depressed, not discordant, even, and directed toward great enlightenment.
204/20/. And it is transformed.

204/21/. Here, by whichever secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) a bodhisattva is excessively oppressed, for the sake of abandoning that very secondary affliction, he applies a corresponding antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
204/23. When [this] has arisen, one cultivates the meditation on the foul as the antidote to sensual desire (*kāma-rāga*).

One cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as the antidote to ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and one cultivates specific conditionality (*idampratyayatā*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as the antidote to delusion (*moha*). [One cultivates the meditation on] discursive thought (*vitarka*)...

As an antidote, he cultivates mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*). As an antidote to pride (*māna*), he cultivates the analysis of the elements (*dhātu-prabheda*). This is the category of [practices] belonging to a bodhisattva.

205/01. This is called appropriate vigor. 205/02. Here, a bodhisattva is not endowed with the vigor of a beginner, one who has only just begun their practice; that is to say, for the sake of the stabilization of the mind, [he receives] instruction... 205/03.
Through the instruction on giving, the bodhisattva’s application becomes practiced and familiar;
this is called the bodhisattva’s practiced vigor.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva’s application is not merely practiced [without guidance].

205/07. Regarding the stability of the mind in the instruction on giving: moreover, that beginner bodhisattva is one whose application in that practice is not lax, by virtue of practicing with constancy and with respect. This is the bodhisattva’s lack of laxity.
This is called diligence.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva— either from the presence of teachers or by himself—
through the acquisition of the power of great learning and through the correct grasping [of the teachings], applies himself to the stability of the mind.
He exerts vigor; this is called the "well-grasped vigor" of a bodhisattva. Furthermore, the bodhisattva who thus grasps things without error [applies himself] to calm abiding (śamatha)...

He cultivates calm abiding at the proper time; he uplifts the mind at the time for uplifting; he cultivates equanimity at the time for equanimity. This is called his "effort applied at the proper time."

Furthermore, a bodhisattva acts continuously and with earnest respect for the sake of discerning, not forgetting, and penetrating the signs of tranquility, exertion, and equanimity, as well as the signs of remaining in, and emerging from, meditative concentration.
This is called the bodhisattva’s vigor of penetrating signs.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva [exerts vigor regarding] those which are supremely vast and supremely profound...
Having heard the teachings on the inconceivable and immeasurable exertion of vigor (*vīryārambha*) of the bodhisattvas, he does not despise himself; his mind does not become cowed,
nor does he settle for a mere slight or inferior degree of excellence.
He is content with what he has attained and does not strive for more;
this is called the undaunted vigor of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva, at the proper time, practices guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, application to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, and dwelling in clear comprehension; in this manner—

206/05. He proceeds by undertaking the requisites for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If he is devoted to these, he exerts effort everywhere in a manner that is unerring and endowed with meaningful purpose. This is the non-deficient vigor of a bodhisattva.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva initiates an effort that is neither too lax nor too strenuous,
but one that carries the practice with evenness in all undertakings to be performed.
In those [beings] toward whom he acts with equal respect, this is called the bodhisattva’s even vigor (*sama-vīryatā*). Furthermore,
the bodhisattva [undertakes] all the exertions of vigor that have been performed.
He dedicates [it] toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. This is called the bodhisattva’s rightly dedicated vigor.
Thus, this [vigor], beginning with essential vigor and ending with pure vigor, is described.

And it is the vigor of the bodhisattvas which has great enlightenment as its fruit; relying upon this, bodhisattvas, having fulfilled the perfection of vigor, have awakened, will awaken, and are awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And they awaken;
and they awaken.
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the Foundation (*ādhāra-yoga-sthāna*),
207/01. The summary (uddāna) is to be understood as before.
207/02. In that regard, what is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the meditative concentration (dhyāna) of bodhisattvas?
207/03. It is that which is mundane (laukika), preceded by hearing and reflecting upon the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

207/04/. The supramundane wholesome one-pointedness of mind of Bodhisattvas is the stability of mind (cittasthiti), which belongs either to the side of calm abiding (śamatha), or to the side of insight (vipaśyanā), or to the path that carries both yoked together; this is bodhi—
The nature of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of sentient beings should be understood [in this way].
In that regard, what is the "all-inclusive meditative concentration" (*sarva-dhyāna*) of Bodhisattvas?
It should be seen as being of two kinds: mundane (*laukika*) and supramundane (*lokottara*). That...
Furthermore, it should be understood as being threefold according to its application:
meditation for dwelling in happiness in the present life, meditation for the production of the qualities of a bodhisattva’s samādhis, and meditation for performing the welfare of sentient beings.

In this regard, the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of bodhisattvas is that which is free from all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), generates physical and mental pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), is supremely tranquil, devoid of conceit (*māna*), untasted by relish (*āsvāda*), and free from all signs (*nimitta*).

This should be understood as their dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭa-dharma-sukha-vihāra*). In that regard, the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of bodhisattvas is for the sake of bringing forth those samādhis comprised within the lineage of the ten powers (*daśabala-gotra*), which are manifold, inconceivable, and immeasurable.
It proceeds. Even the names of those meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) that all *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* do not even know— let alone how they might attain them—
are [known] by the Bodhisattvas through their liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), and bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

It conduces to the actualization of qualities such as the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), and the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), which are not shared with the *śrāvakas*. This is to be understood as the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration for the purpose of actualizing the qualities of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

It should be understood that the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of a bodhisattva engaged in activities for the benefit of sentient beings is of ten types, as previously described. Relying upon which meditative concentration,
the bodhisattva assists sentient beings in their affairs that are conducive to their welfare.
He attains non-duality.
He removes suffering. He teaches the proper method to those who are suffering. Grateful and appreciative, he returns favors to those who have helped him.

He performs services for them; he protects them from fears; he dispels their grief when they are in a state of calamity; he provides requisites for those who lack them; he properly gathers a retinue; and he conforms to their minds.

He gladdens them with their true virtues and correctly restrains them. Through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), he terrifies them and wins them over. All of this, taken together as one, is called the "all-encompassing meditation" (*sarva-dhyāna*) of the bodhisattvas. Not beyond this...
208/09/. Nothing further than this exists.
208/10/. In that regard, what is the difficult meditation (*duṣkara-dhyāna*) of the bodhisattvas?
It should be understood as being of three kinds: namely, that which bodhisattvas [perform] with sublime...

Having dwelt for as long as he desired in various well-mastered meditative absorptions brought forth through cultivation, and having voluntarily turned away from that supreme bliss of meditation, he— out of compassion for sentient beings and through deliberate reflection— [engages] in the vast benefit of sentient beings.

Observing that there is activity for the ripening of sentient beings, they are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This should be understood as the first difficult meditation (*duṣkaradhyāna*) of the bodhisattvas. Furthermore, when a bodhisattva [practices] meditation...

Relying upon immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable bodhisattva samādhis that transcend the entire domain of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he brings them forth. This is the second difficult task of the bodhisattva.

Dhyāna is to be understood [in this context]. Furthermore, by relying upon dhyāna, a bodhisattva awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is to be understood as the third difficult dhyāna of a bodhisattva.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s all-encompassing meditative concentration (*sarvato-mukha-dhyāna*)?
It should be understood as fourfold: (1) accompanied by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*);
(2) born of seclusion (*vivekaja*) and born of concentration (*samādhija*), accompanied by joy (*prīti*); and (3) accompanied by pleasant happiness (*sāta-sukha*).
Accompanied [by joy] and accompanied by equanimity.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s meditation of a true person? It is as follows:
It should be understood as fivefold: that which is untasted, that which is accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
that which is accompanied by compassion (*karuṇā*), that which is accompanied by sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and that which is accompanied by equanimity (*upekṣā*).

209/06. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration of all aspects (*sarvākāra-dhyāna*)? It should be understood as being of thirteen types, when the sixfold and sevenfold [categories] are condensed together. [These are: wholesome meditative concentration, non-afflicted...

And meditation has been cultivated for the sake of creating emanations; meditation belonging to the side of calm abiding (*śamatha*); meditation belonging to the side of insight (*vipaśyanā*); meditation for the sake of correctly attending to the welfare of oneself and others;
and meditation for the sake of bringing forth the qualities of the power of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
The object of name; the object of meaning; the object of the sign of grasping the signs of calm abiding (*śamatha*); the object of the sign of equanimity (*upekṣā*);
and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) for dwelling in happiness in the present life and for accomplishing the welfare of others.
Thus, this thirteenfold meditation of the bodhisattvas is called "meditation in all its aspects.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s meditation for those who are distressed and seeking [relief]?

That should be understood as being of eight kinds: meditative absorption that presides over mantras for the purpose of pacifying calamities such as poison, lightning, venomous fevers, spirits, and planetary seizures; and [that which pacifies] those arising from an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
Meditation for the pacification of diseases;
meditation that brings forth rain when famines and great hells have appeared;
[meditation for protection] from various fears caused by humans and non-humans.

209/24/. Meditation for the sake of correctly rescuing those who have fallen into water or onto land. Likewise, 209/25/. meditation for the sake of providing food and drink to those who lack food and drink while traveling through forests and wildernesses. [Meditation] for the sake of [providing] enjoyments to those disciples who are destitute of them.

Meditative concentration for the purpose of providing resources; meditative concentration for the purpose of correctly awakening those who are heedless in the ten directions; and [meditative concentration] for those who have repeatedly arisen [in states of heedlessness].
210/02/. Dhyāna for the correct accomplishment of the tasks of sentient beings.
210/03/. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dhyāna that brings happiness in this world and the next?
It should be understood as being of nine kinds: [beginning] with the miracle of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).

210/05/. Meditation for the sake of disciplining sentient beings; meditation for the sake of disciplining sentient beings through the miracle of mind-reading and the miracle of instruction. 210/06/. Meditation that reveals the states of woe to those who commit evil deeds. [Meditation] for those whose eloquence has been lost...
The meditative absorption for bringing about eloquence in those beings who lack it; the meditative absorption for restoring mindfulness to those beings whose mindfulness has been lost;
and [the meditative absorption] for the systematic arrangement of non-perverted treatises, poetry, manuals, and compositions.
Meditative concentration for the sake of ensuring the long endurance of the Dharma; and [meditation] upon worldly arts and crafts that are conducive to welfare and beneficial to sentient beings,
such as writing, calculation, accounting, numeration, and sealing, as well as beds and seats.
The meditative concentration that provides various and diverse articles of utility, such as umbrellas, sandals,
and so forth; and the meditative concentration that brings about the cessation of the suffering pertaining to the miserable states for those beings who have fallen into the realms of misery.
The meditative concentration that emits rays for the sake of providing confidence.
In this regard, what is the pure meditative concentration of a bodhisattva?
It should be understood as being of ten kinds by way of mundane purity.

Pure meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is that which is untasted. It is purified by means of supramundane purity (*lokottara-śuddhi*), being free from affliction (*akliṣṭa*). It is purified by the purity of the preliminary application (*prayoga-śuddhi*), and it is purified by the purity of the fundamental [attainment] (*maula-śuddhi*), as well as by the excellence of the fundamental [attainment].

Dhyāna is pure through purity. Dhyāna is pure through the purity of mastery over entering, abiding, and emerging. Furthermore, it is pure through the purity of mastery over the withdrawal from dhyāna and its re-attainment.
Dhyāna purified by mastery over the miraculous transformations of the superknowledges;
dhyāna purified by the removal of all views.

210/03/. Dhyāna. And there is pure dhyāna through the purification that consists in the abandonment of the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations. This dhyāna of the bodhisattvas is immeasurable and has great enlightenment as its fruit, depending upon which the bodhisattvas—

Having fulfilled the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), they have awakened to, are awakening to, and will awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
210/11/. In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the Foundation (*ādhāra-yoga-sthāna*), the thirteenth—
Chapter 210/12: The Section on Quiescence (Śamatha) in the Chapter on Dhyāna.
The summary (uddāna) should be understood as previously stated.
212/02. In that regard, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a bodhisattva’s wisdom (*prajñā*)?

It is the discernment (*pravicaya*) of phenomena which functions by taking the five fields of knowledge (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*) as its object, for the purpose of entering into all that is to be known (*sarva-jñeya*) and having already entered into all that is to be known. 212/03–04. And it is that which proceeds by taking the five fields of knowledge as its objective support.
The inner science, the science of logic, the science of medicine, the science of grammar,
and the science of arts and crafts— this should be understood as the intrinsic nature of the wisdom of bodhisattvas.
212/08. In that regard, what is the entirety of the wisdom of bodhisattvas? 212/09. It should be seen as being of two kinds: mundane and supramundane.
Furthermore, it should be understood as being, in brief, of three kinds: [wisdom] regarding the realization of reality with respect to the objects of knowledge...

Having established [this], it is for the sake of cultivating skill in the five fields of knowledge as previously described, in the three categories, and for the sake of performing deeds for the benefit of sentient beings— [all] concerning the ineffable selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) of the bodhisattvas.
Whether for the sake of awakening to the truths, at the time of awakening to the truths, or subsequent to the perfect awakening to the truths,
wisdom is that which is accompanied by supreme tranquility,
is non-conceptual, is free from all conceptual proliferation, and has attained equality regarding all phenomena.
This wisdom of the bodhisattvas, which has entered into the great universal characteristic, which has reached the limit of the knowable,
which is free from the two extremes of superimposition and denial, and which follows the middle way,
serves for the realization and penetration of reality.

It should be understood that skill in the five fields of knowledge is to be understood in detail as previously explained, namely, in the "Chapter on Powers and Lineages. Furthermore, there are three aggregates: the aggregate of phenomena associated with the goal, the [aggregate of] phenomena not associated with the goal, and the aggregate of phenomena associated with neither.
The heap of phenomena associated with the goal, the heap of phenomena neither associated with the goal nor not associated with the goal,
and the heap of phenomena not associated with the goal— skill in wisdom regarding these eight points constitutes a great [attainment].
He fulfills the unsurpassed accumulation of wisdom for the sake of unexcelled perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, the performance of the welfare of sentient beings is as described previously.
It should be understood as being of exactly eleven types. That wisdom which exists in those very same stations should be understood as the wisdom for performing the welfare of sentient beings.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s difficult-to-perform wisdom? It is threefold.
It should be understood that [this] is difficult for the sake of knowing the profound selflessness of phenomena;
it is difficult for the sake of knowing the means for disciplining sentient beings; and it is difficult for the sake of knowing the knowledge that is unobstructed regarding all objects of knowledge.

213/08/. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s all-encompassing (*sarvato-mukhā*) wisdom? It should be understood as being fourfold: the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), based upon the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Wisdom (*prajñā*). It is the wisdom comprised by the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*) regarding the engagement in what is to be done by a bodhisattva and the desisting from what is not to be done;
and it is the immeasurable wisdom of the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmikā*) comprised by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*).
213/14. Wisdom.

213/15. In this regard, what is the wisdom of a bodhisattva, a true person (*satpuruṣa*), which is the wisdom of a true person? It should be understood as being of five kinds. [The first is] the true Dharma...
It is thoroughly ascertained by means of hearing, accompanied by individual internal wise attention,
and accompanied by the means for accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others, concerning the unerring stability and systematic arrangement of phenomena.
Wisdom that abandons the afflictions is wisdom. Another formulation is: it is subtle because it enters into the knowable by way of its mode of being (yathāvad-bhāvikatayā);
it is skillful because it enters into the knowable by way of its full extent (yāvad-bhāvikatayā); it is innate [wisdom] due to the previous accumulation of knowledge.

It is endowed with realization because it is the grasping and retaining of the meaning of the Dharma as proclaimed by the Buddhas and by those Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*) and are possessed of the scriptures. It is endowed with attainment from the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*) onwards.
213/26. Up until the attainment of the stage of final consummation.
213/27. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s wisdom in all its aspects? It is as follows:

The sixfold and sevenfold [knowledges], when condensed together, should be understood as being thirteenfold. Among the [Four] Truths, there is the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of the path, and at the culmination, the knowledge of exhaustion.

Knowledge is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). This, first of all, is the sixfold wisdom (*prajñā*). Furthermore, it is sevenfold: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of the superknowledges (*abhijñā-jñāna*), and knowledge of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-jñāna*).
Knowledge preceded by the ten powers, and knowledge of the principles regarding the four principles.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s wisdom concerning those who seek relief from distress? It is as follows:

It should be understood as being eightfold, beginning with the knowledge of the synonyms of phenomena (*dharma-paryāya-jñāna*): this is the bodhisattva’s analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvit*). Beginning with the knowledge of the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa-jñāna*): this is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvit*). [Beginning with] the etymological definitions of phenomena (*nirvacana*)...

The analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) is based on knowledge. The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is based on the distinctions between the types and words of phenomena (*dharma*).
The wisdom of a bodhisattva is for the sake of subduing all opposing disputants; it is [the wisdom] that... all [obstacles].

Wisdom is for the purpose of establishing and maintaining debate; wisdom is for the correct administration of the household system and for the prosperity of the family; and it is the decisive wisdom of the bodhisattva regarding royal policy and worldly conventions of conduct.

214/19. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s wisdom that brings happiness in this world and the next? It should be seen as being of nine kinds: wisdom that is thoroughly purified and well-established in the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*); [wisdom] in the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*); and in the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*).

Wisdom that is well-purified in the science of grammar and in the science of worldly arts and crafts, yet not firmly established; relying upon those very five kinds of well-purified sciences, [there arises] that which belongs to a bodhisattva for others...

Wisdom is that which, respectively for those to be trained who are deluded, negligent, despondent, and those who have correctly entered the path, is the means of demonstrating, the means of instigating, the means of inciting, and the means of gladdening.
In that regard, what is the pure wisdom of a bodhisattva? Briefly stated, it should be understood as being of ten kinds. Regarding the meaning of reality, it is twofold.
Because of the grasping of the reality of things through their full extent (*yāvad-bhāvikatā*) and their mode of existence (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*);
because of the twofold grasping of the object of engagement by way of both cause and fruit;
and because of the twofold [grasping] regarding the object of appropriation, namely, error and non-error.

Through thorough knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*). Regarding the meaning of skillful means (*upāya*), there are two kinds [of thorough knowledge], because of the thorough knowledge as it truly is of all that is to be done and all that is not to be done. Regarding the meaning of the culmination (*niṣṭhā*), there are two kinds, through [the thorough knowledge] of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) as affliction and of purification (*vyavadāna*) as purification, as it truly is.
215/08/. Through the thorough knowledge of reality (bhūta-parijñāna), this fivefold wisdom of bodhisattvas, with its ten subdivisions, should be understood as purified by the supreme purity. 215/10/.
Thus, this wisdom of the bodhisattvas is both well-determined and immeasurable.
Wisdom has great enlightenment as its fruit; relying upon it, bodhisattvas fulfill the perfection of wisdom and awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

This should be understood as a concise summary of the six perfections taught by the Blessed One in various scattered discourses (*sūtrāntara*). In whichever discourse spoken by the Tathāgata [the perfection of] giving—
Whether it be a perfection, up to and including the perfection of wisdom,

that comes under exposition or detailed explanation, it should be introduced as giving by way of its intrinsic nature, up to and including giving by way of purification; and its inclusion [within the perfections] should be understood according to what is appropriate.
It should be understood that in this same way, the entry into and the inclusion of the other [perfections], beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*) and ending with wisdom (*prajñā*),
as they have been described, should be understood according to their respective application. And those [births] of the Tathāgatas which arise from the conduct of a Bodhisattva—
The Jātaka tales concerning difficult practices that are to be measured—all of these are associated with giving; they should be understood as being preceded by giving.
Just as it is with giving, so it is with ethical discipline, patience, and vigor.

215/26/. Dhyāna associated with all forms of wisdom (*prajñā*) should be understood as being undertaken on the basis of wisdom. Some [discourses] are undertaken solely on the basis of giving (*dāna*), while others range up to [the other perfections].

216/02/. With reference to wisdom alone, some [teachings] are mixed with two [perfections], some with three, some with four, and some with five; some are to be understood as referring to all six perfections. By means of these—

Bodhisattvas who are fully realizing unexcelled, perfect enlightenment through the six perfections are called "great oceans of pure white dharmas" and "great seas of pure white dharmas" for the sake of all sentient beings.

They are called great jewel-lakes that are the cause for the perfection of all aspects. Furthermore, for this immeasurable accumulation and realization of merit and wisdom, there is no other fruit more appropriate than this.
Just as [it is said], "only unexcelled perfect enlightenment."
In the *Yogasthāna* on the Foundation, the fourteenth chapter is the "Section on Wisdom" (*Prajñāpaṭala*).
The summary (*uddāna*) should be understood as before.
217/02. In this regard, what is the nature of the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas?

217/03. Here, a bodhisattva utters toward sentient beings speech that is pleasing, truthful, in accordance with the Dharma, and beneficial. This is the [nature] of the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas.
In brief, this is the nature of agreeable speech (*priyavāditā*).

Among these, what is the bodhisattva’s complete agreeable speech? It should be understood as being threefold. Here, it refers to whatever speech of the bodhisattva is for the purpose of causing joy...
217/08/. By whatever speech a bodhisattva— free from frowning, speaking first,
with a bright countenance, preceded by a smile— inquires after [another's] security and well-being, or inquires after the equilibrium of the elements, or [inquires after their] happiness...

By inquiring after their welfare day and night, or by saying "Welcome," and through such modes as these, he greets sentient beings while conforming to worldly conduct and the ways of a citizen. And as for that speech...

217/14. By means of speech that brings joy to a bodhisattva, when a bodhisattva sees the increase of his sons, the increase of his wife, the increase of his kinsmen, the increase of his wealth, or the increase of his grain—
[he speaks] to those beings who have not themselves perceived their own increase.

By announcing [the virtues] of others, he gladdens them; or again, he gladdens them through the increase of faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Furthermore, whatever speech the bodhisattva possesses that is connected with the teaching of the Dharma endowed with qualities in every respect for sentient beings—
Constantly and continuously present for the sake of welfare and happiness, acting as a benefactor through the highest form of assistance—
this should be understood as the full classification of the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas.

217/23. In that regard, what is the brief summary of all the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas? It should be seen as twofold: that which conforms to worldly conduct and that which conforms to the teaching of the true Dharma. Among these, that which is pleasing speech...
And this delightful course of worldly conduct should be understood as follows: therein,
that speech which is beneficial is present through its supreme benefit.
This has been explained; it should be understood as being in accordance with the correct teaching of the Dharma.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s difficult-to-practice pleasant speech? It should be seen as threefold: namely, when a bodhisattva [speaks pleasantly] toward assassins and adversaries...
With a mind that is perfectly pure and stainless toward adversaries,
he reflects and utters speech that is conciliatory, gladdening,
or beneficial. This is the first difficult practice of agreeable speech by a bodhisattva.
It should be understood as follows: furthermore, when a bodhisattva,
without becoming weary, deliberately delivers a discourse on the Dharma to beings who are extremely deluded and of dull faculties.
Having accepted weariness, he causes [beings] to grasp the righteous, wholesome Dharma. This is the second difficult-to-practice kind of pleasant speech of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva [acts toward] beings who are deceitful and fraudulent... [as a teacher...]
When those who deceive their preceptors, teachers, and those worthy of offerings engage in wrong conduct,
a bodhisattva— without a mind of malice, yet with a mind of resentment— utters words that are pleasing, gratifying, or helpful. This is [the transgression] of a bodhisattva.
The third kind of agreeable speech should be understood as difficult to practice.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s agreeable speech that faces in all directions?
It should be seen as fourfold: [agreeable speech] for the abandonment of hindrances, for proceeding to a happy rebirth, ...

This teaching of the Dharma is not for those who have previously failed to practice; rather, it is for one whose hindrances have departed and whose mind is healthy— a sublime teaching of the Dharma connected with the Four Noble Truths, [addressed] to heedless beings, both householders and...

The correct exhortation of those who have gone forth is for the purpose of rousing them from heedless conduct and establishing them in heedful conduct; it is the teaching of the Dharma for the removal of whatever doubts may arise one after another. This is [the first wheel].
218/26/. The performance of the determination of what is to be said.
In that regard, what is the [discourse] of the bodhisattvas, the true persons (*satpuruṣa*), concerning true persons?

219/02. Kindly speech (*priyavāditā*). It should be understood as being of five kinds. Here, Bodhisattvas who have become [true] Bodhisattvas and those who have become Tathāgatas teach the Dharma to those to be trained (*vineya*) precisely with its cause (*sanidāna*), with its means of escape (*saniḥsaraṇa*), and with its antidote (*sapratipakṣa*).

They establish the rules of training (śikṣāpada) in a manner that is accompanied by conflict, accompanied by valor, and accompanied by miracles; they establish them in a proper place and with their origin story. Therefore, their Dharma is "with its cause" (sanidāna). And for those who have undertaken the training, there is the rising from an offense once it has been committed.
They do not designate it as such. Therefore, their Dharma possesses an escape.
By means of the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*), they establish a practice within this Dharma and Vinaya that is free from error.
Therefore, their Dharma is accompanied by reliance; they fully proclaim the path that leads out of all suffering, which is irreversible.
Therefore, their Dharma is accompanied by valor; [it is] threefold—
And by means of the three miracles (*prātihārya*), they make their entire teaching fruitful. Therefore, their Dharma is accompanied by miracles.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ agreeable speech in all its aspects?

That [speech] is of six kinds and seven kinds; when condensed together, it should be understood as being of thirteen kinds: namely, speaking kindly when granting permission regarding things that should be permitted, and [speaking firmly] when prohibiting things that should be prohibited.
Loving speech is that which elucidates the doctrinal formulations of phenomena;
it elucidates the characteristics of phenomena without error; it elucidates the etymological definitions of phenomena without error;
and it elucidates the various distinctions among the categories of words for phenomena.

219/23. Pleasant speech that brings joy; pleasant speech that brings delight. 219/24. Pleasant speech that consists of being free from excessive concern regarding all the requisites for others, and being free from excessive concern regarding the correct engagement in all their tasks. 219/25. Pleasant speech that consists of clear and open invitation. Regarding various...

And pleasant speech that provides consolation to those who are afraid in times of fear; pleasant speech comprised of instruction in the proper method; and [pleasant speech] that causes one to rise up from unwholesome states.

220/02/. Loving speech for the purpose of establishing others in a wholesome state consists of exhortation, admonition, and censure regarding what has been correctly seen and heard; it is loving speech offered by requesting another who possesses the requisite power. It should be understood as being of all possible forms.
220/05. In that regard, what is the agreeable speech of bodhisattvas directed toward those who are distressed and seeking help?
220/06. It should be understood as being of eight kinds. It is that which a bodhisattva, relying upon the fourfold purity of speech, applies to the eight noble modes of discourse.
220/08/. This speech is called the agreeable speech of Bodhisattvas directed toward those who seek relief from their afflictions.
220/09/. In this regard, there is this fourfold purity of speech: abstaining from false speech; 220/10/. abstaining from malicious speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter. Among these:

There are eight noble conventions: speaking of what has been seen as having been seen; speaking of what has been heard, thought, or cognized as having been heard, thought, or cognized; and speaking of what has not been seen as not having been seen; speaking of what has not been heard, thought, or cognized as not having been heard, thought, or cognized.

220/14. In this regard, what is the agreeable speech (*priyavāditā*) of bodhisattvas that brings happiness in this world and the next? It should be understood as being of nine kinds: agreeable speech for the sake of abandoning the sorrow of loss of kinsmen; agreeable speech for the sake of abandoning the sorrow of loss of wealth; [and agreeable speech] for the sake of health...

Affectionate speech for the sake of abandoning calamity and sorrow; affectionate speech for the sake of abandoning calamity regarding ethical discipline, and for the sake of abandoning calamity regarding views;
and that which is affectionate speech for the sake of the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of view, the perfection of conduct, and the perfection of livelihood.

220/20. The teaching of the true Dharma. 220/21. In that regard, what is the pure agreeable speech of a bodhisattva? It should be understood as being of twenty kinds. It is that which, through twenty aspects, [teaches] the Dharma—
220/23. Teaching (*deśanā*). This, moreover, should be understood as previously explained, namely, in the chapter on the Powers (*bala*) and the Lineage (*gotra*). 220/24–25.
Therein, the practice for the sake of others (*arthacaryā*) and agreeable speech (*priyavāditā*) are to be understood in detail in exactly the same manner.
It should be understood that I shall now describe another form of purposeful conduct (*arthacaryā*) that is superior to this.
For in every way, the Bodhisattva [proceeds] with pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*).

In each respective case, he acts for the sake of leading sentient beings toward that very goal. In this regard, what is the nature of the beneficial conduct (*artha-caryā*) of Bodhisattvas? It is as follows: having shown them logical reasoning through pleasant speech, he accordingly establishes sentient beings in the trainings.

In the practice of purposeful conduct and the practice of conforming to the Dharma, having established a mind of compassion, there is the encouragement, training, introduction, and establishment [of others] with a mind free from worldly motives. This is "purposeful conduct."
221/07. A brief explanation of the nature of conduct.

221/08. In that regard, what is all the beneficial conduct of Bodhisattvas? That too should be seen as twofold: [the ripening] of immature sentient beings and... 221/09. ...the ripening of those who are not yet matured.
221/10. The ripening of immature sentient beings and the liberation of those who are already matured.
Furthermore, that [activity] should be understood through three gateways: instigating them toward goals pertaining to the present life;
instigating them toward goals pertaining to future lives; and [instigating them toward goals pertaining to] both the present life and future lives.

221/13/. Encouraging others toward their own welfare. In that regard, encouraging others toward welfare pertaining to the present life should be understood as the correct encouragement regarding the acquisition, protection, increase, and proper management of enjoyments through qualities of action consistent with the Dharma. Those who—

He does not receive praise from others, yet he dwells in happiness in this very life, sustained by the comfort of his requisites. Therein, having renounced worldly enjoyments, he lives in dependence upon the livelihood of a mendicant, bound to the life of one who has gone forth.

221/19. Encouragement (*samādāpanā*) should be understood as encouragement toward the welfare of future lives (*sāṃparāyika-artha*). By means of this, one certainly becomes happy in the next life, though not necessarily in the present life (*dṛṣṭe dharme*). In that regard, whether for a householder or for one who has gone forth (*pravrajita*), the gradual...

The exhortation to attain complete detachment is to be understood as an exhortation regarding the welfare pertaining to both the present life and future lives, by which one becomes pliant in body and pliant in mind, and experiences happiness in this very life.
He dwells in comfort, and in the future life he is reborn among the pure gods;
he attains final nirvana in the realm of nirvana without remainder.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ difficult practice for the sake of others? It is as follows:

It should be understood as being threefold. Among these, the practice of purposeful conduct (*arthacaryā*) by Bodhisattvas toward those who possess previously cultivated roots of virtue is difficult to perform.

For it is thus: they are difficult to lead toward the undertaking of suffering for the sake of what is wholesome. When sentient beings abide in great abundance of wealth and are possessed by attachment to it, the practice of purposeful conduct (*artha-caryā*) by Bodhisattvas is difficult. For it is thus: they [are attached] to that great...

They abide in states of negligence and in the grounds of negligence. Among those outsiders, among the non-Buddhist heretics, and among those beings who previously followed the views and conduct of heretics, the bodhisattvas’ practice for their benefit is difficult to perform; for they are themselves deluded.
222/09/. And they are firmly established in this Dharma and Vinaya.
222/10/. In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ beneficial conduct directed toward all quarters?
It should be understood as being fourfold. Here, a bodhisattva [inspires] one who lacks faith to have faith...

He encourages others in the perfection of concentration until he establishes them in it. He encourages one who is immoral in the perfection of morality; one who is lacking in wisdom in the perfection of wisdom; and one who is stingy in the perfection of generosity, until he establishes them in it.

222/15. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s practice for the sake of true persons? It should be seen as fivefold. Here, a bodhisattva encourages sentient beings toward a genuine purpose; he encourages them at the proper time; [he encourages them] toward that which is connected with benefit.
He encourages others toward the goal. He encourages them gently. He encourages them with a mind of loving-kindness.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ beneficial conduct in all its forms?

This [discipline] is of six kinds and seven kinds; when condensed together, it should be understood as being of thirteen kinds. Herein, a bodhisattva correctly gathers those beings who are to be gathered, and [correctly restrains] those beings who are to be restrained.

He correctly restrains them. He removes the hostility of those beings who are antagonistic toward the teaching. He causes neutral beings to enter this teaching, and those who have entered, he correctly establishes in the three vehicles.

He brings [beings] to maturity; he liberates those beings who have reached maturity; and he establishes some among them in the preservation and accumulation of the provisions [for enlightenment]. That which...

Or else, it concerns the departure via the Hīnayāna or the departure via the Mahāyāna. Just as [there is application] regarding the preservation and increase of cyclic existence, so too [it concerns] seclusion, one-pointedness of mind, the purification of hindrances, and the cultivation of mental application.

He establishes them [in their respective paths]. Those belonging to the lineage of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he establishes in the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Those belonging to the lineage of the Tathāgatas, he establishes in the vehicle of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

223/08. In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ beneficial conduct for those who are distressed and seeking aid? It should be understood as being of eight kinds. [It consists in] [acting toward] sentient beings who are obsessed by the obsession of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) regarding matters for which one ought to feel shame.

One dispels and removes the outburst of obsession (*paryavasthāna*). Just as with the outburst of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), so too with the outburst of lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) regarding things that should inspire dread, the outburst of torpor (*middha*), and the outburst of restlessness (*auddhatya*).
In these situations, he dispels and removes the obsession of regret, the obsession of envy, and the obsession of stinginess.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s beneficial conduct that brings happiness in this world and the next?

This [purification] is to be understood as ninefold, beginning with the purification of the bodily action of other sentient beings: (1) causing others to undertake the complete abstention from taking life in all its forms;
(2) causing others to undertake the complete abstention from taking what is not given in all its forms...
Furthermore, it consists of: (1) the encouragement of all forms of abstaining from sexual misconduct;

(2) the encouragement of all forms of abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants that cause negligence; and, with respect to the purification of vocal action, all forms [of such encouragement].

223/23/. Encouraging others to undertake the abstention from false speech; encouraging others in every way to undertake the abstention from malicious speech; encouraging others in every way to undertake the abstention from harsh speech; encouraging others in every way to undertake the abstention from frivolous chatter;

223/26/. Causing others to give. With reference to the purification of mental action, it is the instigation of others to undertake the complete abstention from covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view in all their aspects. 224/01/. 224/01/. 224/02. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s pure conduct for the sake of others?
It should be understood as being of ten kinds: five kinds based on external purity, and five kinds based on internal purity. Based on external purity—

224/05. Furthermore, there are five kinds of beneficial conduct toward sentient beings for Bodhisattvas. 224/06. What are they? They are: irreproachable, irreversible, successive, all-pervading, and according to what is appropriate.

In this case, a bodhisattva does not engage sentient beings in conduct that is mixed with misconduct, preceded by misconduct, blameworthy, afflicted, and unwholesome. This is his blameless beneficial conduct toward sentient beings.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not lead sentient beings to believe that liberation exists in a state that is not liberation or is not exclusively pure, nor does he lead them to believe that this [state] is liberation or that it is exclusively pure. This is his non-reversing beneficial conduct toward sentient beings.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva first provides a clear exposition of the Dharma for those beings of dull intelligence; he sets forth clear instruction and admonition for them. [Then he does so] for those of middling intelligence...

Having understood them to be of middling capacity, he proceeds to deliver a middling teaching of the Dharma and middling instruction and admonition. And having understood those of vast wisdom, he delivers a profound teaching of the Dharma and subtle instruction.
He imparts instruction for the gradual accumulation of the side of wholesome qualities.
This is his gradual beneficial conduct toward sentient beings.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva [acts] toward the four castes up to the gods...

He practices for the benefit of human beings and all sentient beings according to their capacity and strength; he seeks their welfare and happiness, and he encourages them to undertake that very same [practice]. This is his universally pervasive beneficial conduct toward sentient beings.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva is able to encourage those sentient beings who are capable of being inspired toward any wholesome purpose— whether it be minor, middling, or superior.

Furthermore, by whatever means they are capable of being encouraged to adopt [virtue], he encourages them accordingly in those matters. This, first of all, is the fivefold externally pure beneficial conduct of Bodhisattvas toward sentient beings.

225/04. In that regard, what is the fivefold internally pure beneficial conduct of bodhisattvas toward sentient beings? Here, a bodhisattva practices for the benefit [of others] by being established in an extensive intention of compassion toward sentient beings. Furthermore, the bo[dhisattva...]

225/07/. A bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, remains with a mind free from weariness even through all sufferings and labors; indeed, he acts for the benefit of sentient beings with great joy. Furthermore, even when [encountering] the most excellent and supreme...

While abiding in prosperity, he acts for the sake of sentient beings with a humble mind— like a slave, a servant, a submissive son, or a lowly child— having set aside pride, conceit, and egoism. Furthermore, the bodhisattva, with a non-material [motivation]...

He acts for the benefit of sentient beings with both artificial and supreme affection. Furthermore, the bodhisattva acts for the benefit of sentient beings with a mind of loving-kindness that is ultimate and irreversible.

This delight is to be understood as the fivefold bodhisattva’s practice of purposeful conduct (*arthacaryā*) that is pure internally toward sentient beings. As for the fivefold [conduct] that is pure externally and the fivefold [conduct] that is pure internally— all of that together, taken as one— should be known as such.
In brief, the tenfold pure purposeful conduct of bodhisattvas is thus described.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s commonality of purpose (*samānārthatā*)? Here, the bodhisattva—
When a being encourages others toward a certain purpose or a certain root of virtue,
he himself trains in that same purpose or that same virtue, whether it be equal to or greater than his previous undertaking. This is what constitutes awakening—
A sentient being’s having the same purpose as others is called "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*).
When other disciples perceive this common purpose in the Bodhisattvas,
they become firm in their resolve and irreversible in that regard toward the wholesome.
In the undertaking of the root [vow]. Why is that? Because it occurs to them:
"Surely this is for our benefit, this is for our happiness, wherein this awakening—"
226/03. This being has encouraged us. For this Bodhisattva, in whatever he enjoins us, that very thing he himself practices.
In that regard, knowing it to be harmful and unpleasant, he would not practice it himself.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, other speakers do not address this bodhisattva who shares the same purpose in such a way: "Since you yourself do not even abide by undertaking what is wholesome, why do you urge others so excessively to undertake what is wholesome?"
"You should be spoken to, you should be instructed, and you should be exhorted;
indeed, you yourself must first be spoken to, instructed, and exhorted by others. There is a bodhisattva who, while living in common purpose with others, [is thus addressed].
He does not display that to others. There is one who, while lacking common purpose, displays as if he had common purpose; there is one who, having common purpose, displays his common purpose;
and there is one who has neither common purpose nor displays common purpose.

226/15/. It does not demonstrate the actual state of affairs. In that regard, the first alternative refers to a bodhisattva of equal virtue and power who has accepted the role of a teacher (*ācāryatva*) for other bodhisattvas on the bodhisattva path who possess equal virtue and power.
By virtue of concealing his own goodness, he does not display his qualities or power.
This is the second alternative: for those beings of inferior inclination who are terrified by profound matters, the Bodhisattva, having reflected upon them, [does not display these things].

In this way, for the sake of disciplining sentient beings through that means, he manifests himself as a fellow practitioner of the Dharma. And intentionally desiring to act for the benefit of those down to the outcastes and even dogs, and desiring to pacify their afflictions and discipline them—

226/24. He is born among the commonality of those as low as the caṇḍālas or even dogs. 226/25. The third alternative is that, for the sake of stabilizing those disciples who have undertaken unstable roots of merit, the Bodhisattva—possessing the same purpose or a superior purpose—is [born there].
He demonstrates the nature of pride. The fourth alternative is one who, being himself negligent, neglects the welfare of others.
In this regard, that which has been taught as the various kinds of giving,
and that which is ethical discipline in detail, up to and including common purpose— therein, through the perfections,
there is the internal ripening of the Buddha-qualities and the [application of] the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
The ripening of all sentient beings by means of material things should be understood as the collective activity of a bodhisattva’s wholesome dharmas. In this regard,
there is the gift of many kinds— as previously described— up to and including consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*).
The practice of these many kinds of immeasurable wholesome factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣika) should be understood as occurring through three causes;
their excellence should be understood through two causes, and [their superiority] through three causes.
227/12. Through these, purification is to be understood.
227/13. Conduct by way of body, speech, and mind is to be understood;
because of its loftiness and its lack of affliction, it is supreme and unsurpassed.

And its uncommon nature should be understood. In that regard, its magnanimity should be understood by way of the non-differentiation of sentient beings, the non-differentiation of things, and the non-differentiation of time. Therein, the non-differentiation of sentient beings is when a bodhisattva, having taken all sentient beings as his basis, [acts for] all...

227/18/. He practices those roots of virtue, such as giving and the rest, with reference to sentient beings, and not for the sake of himself alone. In that regard, there is no differentiation of the object when a bodhisattva [practices] all those roots of virtue in all their aspects, beginning with giving—
Having undertaken these various [practices], he proceeds. In this regard, there is no distinction in time when a bodhisattva,
being constant and continuous, does not abandon his application and does not cast off his burden— whether by night or by day, or in the present life,
or for that same reason in future lives.

He also practices those roots of virtue, such as giving and the rest. In this regard, non-affliction should be understood through four aspects. Here, a bodhisattva, with a joyful mind, cultivates those wholesome qualities; he is neither suffering nor dejected.
On that account, he becomes free from remorse. Furthermore, a bodhisattva,
having not harmed another and not being attached to dogmatic views, [is free from remorse] regarding his misconduct.
228/02/. He practices those mixed roots of virtue, such as giving and so forth.

228/03/. Furthermore, the bodhisattva, with reverence and with his whole being, perceives only virtues in them, perceives their essence, perceives their tranquility; he is well-settled, independent of others, and—
Furthermore, the bodhisattva, having undertaken those wholesome qualities such as giving and so forth,

continues to practice them; yet he does not expect the ripening result (*vipāka*) of those wholesome qualities of giving and the rest, nor does he desire [to become] a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).
Whether it be the state of a *tīrthika*, or the state of Śakra, or the state of Māra, or the state of Brahmā;
nor does he hope for recompense from others, nor does he rely upon them, nor upon all gain, honor, or fame. Nor...
Finally, one becomes dependent even upon body and life. Thus, by these modes,
[one practices] the wholesome qualities beginning with giving and ending with common purpose, accompanied by clarity and joy, impartially, respectfully, and dependently.
The manifestation of phenomena is what is called their state of being undefiled.
Purity, brilliance, immovability, and perfect purity are to be understood [as its characteristics].
In that regard, for a bodhisattva who has entered the stage of pure resolute intention (*adhyāśaya-śuddhi-bhūmi*), [the following applies]:

These roots of virtue become heated and immovable. In this regard, "heatedness" means that for a bodhisattva whose intention is pure, all those virtuous qualities become such that they do not require further deliberation. In this regard:

228/20/. Immovability is when a bodhisattva, having purified his intention, does not fall away from the wholesome dharmas as they have been attained and as they have been accumulated. 228/21/. He is no longer subject to falling away in the future, except for those [dharmas]...
With the passing of nights and days and the transcending of those stages of self-existence,
as the bright fortnight of the moon arrives, the Bodhisattva indeed increases in wholesome qualities and does not decline, reaching the stage of ultimate consummation.

Furthermore, for a bodhisattva who is established [in the final stage], whether bound to one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) or in his final existence (*caramabhavika*), these wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) are thoroughly purified.

It should be understood that for those [practitioners], there is no further state of even greater purity on the bodhisattva stages. Thus, by three causes, there is the manifestation of these wholesome dharmas;
by two causes, their excellence; and by three [further causes].
229/05/. Through these causes, the complete purity of the [perfections] beginning with generosity and ending with common purpose (samānārthatā) should be understood. 229/06/.
In that regard, [there is the purity] of all generosity and all ethical discipline, and so on in detail up to all— 229/07/.
When concordance in purpose (*samānārthatā*) is cultivated, thoroughly purified, and made entirely complete,

it brings about as its fruit unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyaksaṃbodhi*), a body with the essence of a diamond (*vajra-sāra-śarīratā*), and the long endurance of the True Dharma (*saddharma-cirasthitikatā*).

In that regard, through the practice, thorough purification, and cultivation of difficult giving, difficult morality, and so forth, up to the state of having difficult meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
the fruit is the Tathāgata’s possession of the peerless and marvelous qualities of conduct.
It is accomplished therein through universal giving,
universal morality, and so on in detail up to universal consistency of purpose;
thus, by the Tathāgata, among all beings— whether gods or humans— he is preeminent in every respect.
The fruit that is produced is the state of being worthy of worship. In this regard, for the gift of a true person,
the morality of a true person, and so on up to the shared purpose of a true person—
whatever beings there may be, whether footless, two-footed, or four-footed, [who honor] the Tathāgata...

All these immeasurables are called the bodhisattva’s compassion (*anukampā*).
Therefore, Bodhisattvas who are endowed with these are called "compassionate."

In this regard, observing one hundred and ten aspects of suffering within the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*), bodhisattvas cultivate compassion for those beings. What are these one hundred and ten aspects of suffering? One type of suffering is—

243/06. Generally speaking, with reference to the suffering of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti-duḥkha*), all sentient beings have fallen into cyclic existence and are suffering. There are two kinds of suffering: that rooted in desire (*chanda-mūlaka*) which arises from the transformation and alteration of those things one holds dear; [and the other kind].

From existence, suffering arises; and there is the suffering that is the ripening of delusion. When one is touched by intense physical sensations, being utterly deluded regarding that personal existence with the notions of "I" or "mine," one grieves excessively.
By means of which one experiences a twofold arrow of sensation, both physical and mental.

There are three kinds of suffering: by way of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). There are also four kinds of suffering.
The suffering of separation is that which arises from being dissociated from those who are dear.

The suffering of annihilation is that which arises from death, through the casting off of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*). The suffering of continuity is the birth of one who has died in a subsequent state.

That which arises through a continuous succession— namely, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādāna-skandha*) of those sentient beings who are subject to ultimate suffering and lack the nature of final nirvana—
is fivefold suffering. [The first is] the obsession of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-paryavasthāna*).
The condition [of suffering] consists of the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of ill-will, lethargy, torpor, restlessness,
regret, and doubt;
and there is the sixfold suffering, which is the suffering of the cause— the cause for rebirth in the lower realms (*apāya*).

From frequenting [unwholesome objects], there is the suffering of the fruit arising from rebirth in the miserable states (apāya). Or, with reference to enjoyments (bhoga), there is the suffering of seeking them, the suffering of guarding them, the suffering of lack of contentment, and the suffering of their loss. Summing all this up:
Suffering is sixfold; suffering is sevenfold:
birth is suffering, aging, illness, death, association with the unpleasant, and separation from the pleasant.

244/03. Separation from what is desired is also suffering; furthermore, not obtaining what one seeks even while searching for it is also suffering. All suffering, great suffering, suffering from every direction, suffering of misconduct, suffering of cyclic engagement, suffering of being forced against one's will,

And suffering: therein, all suffering is that which has arisen from past causes and that which has arisen from present conditions. Therein, great suffering is that which is long-lasting, intense, and manifold.

to the animal realm, to the world of hungry ghosts, and to those included within the happy destinies.

Furthermore, among these, the suffering of misconduct is that which one experiences or brings about in the present life through transgressing against others or inflicting harm upon them. It is also the suffering born from an imbalance of the elements caused by the consumption of unwholesome food.
He brings it forth. Or, by departing from the suffering in this very life through an improper method, he brings forth self-inflicted suffering.

One experiences the suffering of remaining [in saṃsāra]. Furthermore, due to an abundance of misconduct of body, speech, and mind, one experiences the suffering of the miserable states in the future. As one wanders through saṃsāra, birth occurs [in various states]. Due to the lack of certainty regarding one's own physical existence (*ātmabhāva*), having been a king, one becomes a minister or a pauper. Due to the lack of certainty regarding parents, the lack of certainty regarding sons and wives, and the lack of certainty regarding female and male slaves, laborers, and servants, [there is likewise no certainty regarding] friends...
Because there is no fixed rule regarding mothers, maternal relatives, and blood kin: having been one's mother or father,
and so on in detail up to having been a friend, minister, maternal relative,

An adversary. Furthermore, due to the instability of enjoyments, one who has wandered through cyclic existence having been very wealthy may, at a later time, become extremely poor. In that regard, there is the suffering of acting against one's will for one who desires long life.

One is born against one's will due to a short lifespan; for one who desires beauty, it occurs against their will through ugliness; for one who desires birth in a high family, it occurs against their will through birth in a low family; and for one who desires sovereignty, it occurs against their will through the onset of poverty.

245/24/. Furthermore, for one who desires great strength, it arises through the unwanted onset of weakness; 245/25/. and for one who desires to know the object of knowledge, it arises through unwanted delusion.

It arises from the manifestation of knowledge. That suffering which arises from the affliction of narrow entrances, congested spaces, and obstacles; that suffering which arises from a livelihood dependent on others; and that suffering which arises from the affliction of deficiency or impairment of the limbs and minor members. And that suffering...

It arises from injuries such as killing, binding, cutting, beating, and banishment. In that regard, there is incidental suffering, which is the suffering found among the eight worldly concerns when that which is subject to destruction has been destroyed, or that which is subject to decay [has decayed].

When that which is subject to decay has decayed; when that which is subject to illness has become ill; when that which is subject to death has died; or furthermore, whatever suffering arises from lack of gain, ill repute, or censure—this is the eightfold [suffering].
The twenty-sixth type of suffering is the suffering of longing.

This is called incidental suffering (*ānuṣaṅgika-duḥkha*). Among these, "suffering in all its forms" refers to the fivefold suffering, which is the opposite of the happiness previously mentioned, as well as causal suffering.
Suffering as felt sensation; suffering as the mere absence of pleasure;

suffering as the non-interruption of felt sensation; and [suffering] as the opposite of the bliss of renunciation, seclusion, tranquility, and awakening—namely, that which belongs to the household life and the realm of desire.
The fifth type of suffering to be experienced is that arising from association with vitarka (discursive thought) and that of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Thus, there are these five kinds of suffering. [Furthermore, there is] that which is not subject to assault, that arising from the deficiency of requisites, that arising from the imbalance of the elements (*dhātu*), and that arising from the loss of what is dear...

247/01/. Summarizing these together, the tenfold suffering is said to be of all aspects (sarvākāra).

By condensing these fifty-five aspects into a single whole, there are one hundred and ten aspects of suffering. This is the objective support for a bodhisattva’s compassion; it is by means of this objective support that compassion arises in bodhisattvas.
It is kindled, it increases, and it reaches the fulfillment of its cultivation.
And from this great mass of suffering, great compassion proceeds, taking nineteen types of suffering as its object. Ekānna-...
What are the twenty types of suffering? They are: suffering that is the maturation of delusion;

Suffering caused by external injury, suffering from the failure of ethical discipline,

All suffering born of misconduct, all suffering of involvement,

In this regard, compassion is called "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā) for four reasons:
it arises having as its object the suffering of sentient beings— which is profound, subtle, and difficult to discern— and it has been cultivated over a long period of time.

It has been practiced for many hundreds of thousands of eons. It proceeds with an intense application toward the object, by means of which application this Bodhisattva, permeated with compassion, effects the removal of suffering from sentient beings.
For the sake of this cause, one would renounce even hundreds of one's own lives, let alone a single life,
and let alone bodily requisites; and one would endure all varieties of painful torments, becoming utterly pure, just as follows:
And by the purification of the bodhisattva stage of those bodhisattvas who have reached the ultimate goal, and by the purification of the tathāgata stage of the tathāgatas.

Indeed, by means of these one hundred and ten aspects, those bodhisattvas who cultivate compassion toward sentient beings cultivate the entirety of a bodhisattva’s compassion. Furthermore, they very quickly [attain] the compassionate disposition...
They attain purity upon entering the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśaya-bhūmi*). Furthermore, they possess minds that are exceedingly affectionate toward sentient beings, minds of love,

Their minds are pliable and their minds are self-controlled. Yet, for the noble disciple who has realized the truth of suffering and has reached the ultimate goal, the mental continuum accompanied by world-weariness does not remain distant.

248/12. It proceeds as follows: when a bodhisattva, with a mind preceded by compassion toward sentient beings, perceives this great mass of suffering consisting of one hundred and ten aspects, 248/13. yet the bodhisattva does not [despair] in this way.

One whose mind is permeated with compassion would not fail to relinquish any internal or external object whatsoever. There is no undertaking of ethical discipline or restraint that such a person would not perform, nor is there any harm inflicted by others that they would not endure.
There is no exertion of vigor that they would not undertake;
there is no meditative concentration that they would not enter; there is no wisdom that they would not penetrate. Therefore, when the Tathāgatas are questioned, where [would they go]?
When answering correctly that "the awakening of a bodhisattva is established," they answer:
"The awakening of a bodhisattva is established in compassion.
In this regard, each one of these, as previously described, is immeasurable.
Through the perfection of honor, the prosperity of the bodhisattva proceeds.
It is the grasper of immeasurable, desired fruits; it proceeds by way of immeasurable aspects that are exclusively wholesome and irreproachable. Thus, it is immeasurable—
Four benefits for a bodhisattva devoted to cultivation should be known. That cultivation of his is supreme from the very beginning.

It leads to dwelling in happiness in the present life; it leads to the acquisition and accumulation of an immeasurable store of merit; and it leads to the firmness of resolve regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. It is—

250/08/. In that regard, what is the sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*) of bodhisattvas?
That should be understood, in brief, as being of two kinds: by way of its essential nature (*svabhāva*) and by way of its basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva recognizes that the manifestation of a fault is unbecoming for himself alone, his sense of shame (*hrī*) is that very shame; and when he feels shame toward others out of fear and respect, that is his sense of dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*).
Moreover, that shame is [the basis] for the bodhisattva...

In a bodhisattva, this [shame and dread of blame] is intense by its very nature, let alone when it has been practiced; thus should the shame and dread of blame of a bodhisattva be understood in terms of their essential character (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, in brief, their bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*) are fourfold. [The first is] awakening...

The shame felt when one fails to perform what ought to be done for sentient beings is the first basis. Likewise, the shame felt when one performs what ought not to be done by a bodhisattva is the second basis. Likewise, for a bodhisattva...

The shame felt regarding one's own concealed faults is the third basis. Likewise, the shame felt by a bodhisattva when personal remorse has arisen— whether it be based on a point of reliance or incidental— is the fourth.
250/22/. [It is] the basis. Thus it should be understood by way of its basis.

The state of being unshakable through correct application when faced with enmities— whether due to an innate disposition toward courage or through analytical discernment— is this firmness; it should be understood as the essential nature of the empowerment of the power of fortitude (*dhṛti-bala*).
Indeed, this maintenance of the power of fortitude by Bodhisattvas should be understood, in brief,
to have five kinds of bases:

This is to be understood as applying to all the correct applications of the bodhisattvas.
Here, a bodhisattva is by nature strong, whereby he does not become weary. Furthermore, that very state of an untiring mind has been repeatedly practiced by him.

There is that by which one does not become weary. Furthermore, one is engaged in the exertion of vigor embraced by skillful means, whereby—perceiving successive distinctions from beginning to end—one does not become weary. And with intense...

He becomes endowed with the power of knowledge and analytical discernment by which he does not become weary; and this Bodhisattva’s intense mind of compassion and mind of pity toward sentient beings is constantly and continuously present.
That [effort] occurs by which one does not become weary.

In this regard, what is a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the treatises (*śāstrajñatā*)? Here, a bodhisattva, with reference to the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), [studies] the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), the sets of phrases (*padakāya*), and...

252/10. In this regard, what is a bodhisattva’s knowledge of the world? Here, a bodhisattva, with reference to the world of sentient beings, understands it as it truly is:
"Alas, this world has fallen into hardship, in that it is born..."
They age, they die, they pass away, and they are reborn;
yet these beings do not understand, as it truly is, the escape beyond aging and death. Furthermore, this concerns the world of sentient beings itself.

He understands, as it truly is, the time when the defilements (*kaṣāya*) are prevalent, and the time when they are absent or when the defilements are not prevalent; that is to say, with reference to the five defilements:

The defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). For example, at present, the lifespan of human beings is short;

even one who lives long lives for only a hundred years. Furthermore, for example, at present, sentient beings for the most part do not recognize their mothers, do not recognize their fathers, and do not honor ascetics (*śramaṇa*).

They observe the fast but do not abide by undertaking the precepts; for example, as is common nowadays,

Furthermore, various kinds of evil and unwholesome phenomena are observed, comprised of taking up weapons, taking up sticks, quarreling, brawling, conflict, dispute, deceit, trickery, guile, false speech, and false doctrines.
For example, just as at present, for the destruction of the true Dharma and the disappearance of the true Dharma,
many counterfeits of the true Dharma have appeared—

and just as the receptacle-world dissolves and evolves again,

254/04. For the sake of examining the world of phenomena (*kāraloka*) and understanding the ultimate truth of the world (*loka-paramārtha*) as it truly is, he is therefore called "one who knows the world" (*lokajña*). Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees one who is older or more distinguished in virtue... (99a) ...he [acts accordingly].
Or he converses with them properly; having risen from his seat, he invites them to sit;
he performs acts of salutation, prostration, rising to greet, joining the palms in reverence, and respectful service.
