He addresses, converses, and greets others with gentle and sweet words. Furthermore, he does not, out of pride, compare himself to them, whether they are his equals or even those inferior to him in age or in virtues.

Having seen [another], one encourages them by beginning with the instilling of virtues according to one's ability. One magnifies even their slightest genuine virtue and conceals their genuine fault; one does not expose it in such a way that they would become dejected.
He possesses a sense of being. He does not despise him;
nor, having recognized that someone is in need of either the Dharma or material goods, does he turn his face away or knit his brows.
Nor does he mock him for a lapse, nor [despise] one who has fallen into misfortune.

Likewise, he is one who speaks first to all sentient beings— whether inferior, equal, or superior— and is one who says, "Come," "Welcome," and who correctly receives them with both the Dharma and material gifts according to his ability.
He is a gatherer of beings and is neither crooked nor fathomless in his depth toward them;
he is not arrogant on account of any particular eminence. He does not neglect any being he has taken under his care, even if it means using all his resources.
Whether he is ill or healthy, with body and speech actions that are compliant, just as it is toward those who are familiar, so too it is toward those who are unfamiliar; all [of this].

He becomes a friend and a companion free from adversaries. To all sentient beings who are without a protector or a refuge, he performs beneficial actions according to his ability and according to his strength, and not by any other means.

One brings suffering and mental distress upon others, thinking, "May they experience even a moment of unpleasant dwelling. Making this very condition one's motive, one engages in joking with others, even when it is improper.

He engages in jesting, yet not in improper jesting. He does not utter untruths even with close companions who have attained the highest degree of trust and are free from fault. Nor does he remain angry with others for long; even when angry, [he does not harbor resentment].

Furthermore, he does not proclaim the vital vulnerabilities of others. When struck by others—whether by body or by speech—he reflects and either resorts to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) or perceives himself alone as the offender. His mind—

He is steadfast and not fickle; his conduct of body, speech, and mind is stable. He is free from the fourteen impure occupations, covered by the six directions, and has abandoned the four types of evil friends.

He is embraced by the four types of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). All of this should be understood exactly as it is stated in the sūtras. For the sake of benefit in the present life, or concerning the acquisition of wealth, he is endowed with diligence (*utthāna*).
He is endowed with protection, lives in moderation, and has attained skill in worldly arts and crafts. Furthermore, he is free from deceit.

He is free from deceit or the habit of deceiving others. He possesses a sense of shame regarding blameworthy conduct. He is endowed with virtuous behavior, holds such behavior in high regard, and is a protector of that conduct.
Regarding what has been entrusted to him...
Furthermore, he does not act with malice toward the property of others;
he does not default on debts contracted from others; he does not defraud an heir of his inheritance; nor does he deceive one regarding a jewel or what is considered a jewel.

From [the smallest unit] up to even a *kārṣāpaṇa*, he does not deceive those who are deluded by means of such deception. Likewise, he is skillful in worldly conventions and principles that bring benefit to the world; and in those...

When requested by others regarding those matters requiring action, he provides assistance; he does not waver, nor does he evade one thing for another. Furthermore, his undertakings are well-executed, and his actions are never poorly performed.

Furthermore, when exercising sovereignty, he rules according to the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma. He does not take pleasure in punishment. Having turned the great body of people away from immoral conduct, he establishes them in the precepts. Likewise, by means of the noble ones...

He is endowed with eight modes of discourse: by speaking of what was seen as seen, of what was heard as heard, of what was thought as thought, and of what was cognized as cognized; and by speaking of what was not seen as not seen, of what was not heard as not heard, of what was not thought as not thought, and of what was not cognized as not cognized.
Endowed with these and other such qualities, the bodhisattva understands,
as they truly are, everything regarding how he is to be known in the world and how he is to conduct himself in the world; therefore, he is called "one who knows the world."
It is said:
In that regard, how does a bodhisattva apply himself to the four reliances?

257/01. When it is being taught, the bodhisattva, relying on the meaning, listens with respect.
257/02. Furthermore, the bodhisattva understands the provisional teaching (*kālapadeśa*) and the great teaching (*mahāpadeśa*) as they truly are. Understanding them, he relies on reasoning (*yukti*).

[He does not think: "These dharmas were spoken by an elder, or by a person of renown, or by the Tathāgata, or by the Saṃgha"—thus he does not rely on the person. In this way, he relies on the reasoning...

He does not rely on a person, he does not waver from the meaning of reality, and he becomes independent of others regarding the teachings. Furthermore, the bodhisattva has established faith in the Tathāgata, established serene confidence, and is single-mindedly devoted to his word.

One who has full confidence relies upon the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) taught by the Tathāgata, and not those of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). Relying upon the sūtras of definitive meaning, one becomes incapable of being led away from this Dharma and Vinaya; for such is the nature of the sūtras of interpretable meaning.

The differentiation of the various meanings of the diverse approaches becomes indeterminate and causes doubt. Furthermore, if a bodhisattva were not decisive even regarding a sūtra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), he would thus be susceptible to being led astray from this [path].

Furthermore, from the Dharma and Vinaya, a bodhisattva becomes one who perceives the essence in the knowledge of realization (*adhigama-jñāna*), rather than being satisfied with the mere cognition of the meaning of the Dharma through hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*). Whatever is to be known by that knowledge consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-jñāna*), that he [realizes].

Thinking, "It is possible to understand [this] by means of mere wisdom born of hearing," even upon hearing the most profound dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata, he does not reject them nor disparage them. In this way, indeed, is a bodhisattva...

258/05/. Regarding the cognitions: that which is the knowledge consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) concerning all phenomena in all their aspects, in terms of both their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and their mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*), which is unattached and irreversible—this is their "discrimination of phenomena" (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, that knowledge which consists of cultivation regarding all characteristics of all phenomena— both in terms of their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and their mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*)— which is unattached and irreversible: this is their analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, that unattached and irreversible knowledge consisting of cultivation, which pertains to all designations for all phenomena in their full extent (*yāvad-bhāvikatā*) and in accordance with reality (*yathāvad-bhāvikatā*), is their analytical knowledge of etymological interpretation (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, that unattached and irreversible knowledge regarding the existence of all phenomena, in all their various modes of expression, to the extent of their being (yāvadbhāvikatā) and according to their being (yathāvadbhāvikatā)— this is their [knowledge of] reality.

The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*bhāṇa-pratisaṃvid*). Relying upon these four analytical knowledges of a bodhisattva, one should understand the immeasurable skill of bodhisattvas in five areas: skill regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), and skill regarding the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-fields (*āyatana*).

258/20/. Skill in dependent origination and in what is possible and impossible, and by means of these four aspects, all dharmas are both fully realized by the bodhisattva himself and well-expounded to others. Therefore—

Nor does he understand them as they truly are by means of the vehicle-systems— neither by the system of the Śrāvaka-vehicle nor by the system of the Mahāyāna. Therein, he understands as it truly is by means of the Śrāvaka-vehicle, namely, as the Śrāvaka...

Everything as it has been explained regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) should be understood. And how does a bodhisattva, according to the method of the Mahāyāna, understand the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*) as they truly are? Dwelling in the contemplation of the body, he does not conceptualize the body as having the nature of a body, nor does he regard it as being entirely non-existent. Rather, he understands, in accordance with reality, that very body’s true nature as the ineffable intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

This is his ultimate mindfulness-establishment (*smṛty-upasthāna*) regarding the body as the observation of the body within the body. Furthermore, according to the conventional method, the bodhisattva’s mindfulness-establishment regarding the body as the observation of the body within the body is accompanied by the knowledge of the methods for abiding in immeasurable states.

The foundations of mindfulness (smṛty-upasthāna) are to be understood as follows: just as there is the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body in the body, so too are the remaining foundations of mindfulness and the remaining [objects] to be understood.
And the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣyā dharmāḥ) are to be understood in this way. He does not conceptualize the body and so forth as suffering or as its origin;
nor does he conceptualize the abandonment resulting from that as cessation, nor [does he conceptualize] that...
He conceptualizes the cause of attainment through the path. And regarding the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāva*),
he correctly realizes the reality of suffering (*duḥka-dharmatā*), the reality of origination (*samudaya-dharmatā*),
the reality of cessation (*nirodha-dharmatā*), and the reality of the path (*mārga-dharmatā*) as they truly are.

He knows this. This is his cultivation of the truths based upon the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*). Furthermore, from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), the bodhisattva follows the knowledge of the method for establishing the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
In this regard, his cultivation of the objects of the truths is to be seen.

Therein, that non-conceptualization of phenomena by the bodhisattva is to be seen as his *śamatha* (calm abiding), and that knowledge of things as they truly are is to be seen as his *vipaśyanā* (insight).
And that ultimate knowledge which understands the method for establishing the immeasurables regarding phenomena— this is to be regarded as his insight (*vipaśyanā*). In this regard,
the *śamatha* of a bodhisattva is, in brief, of four aspects.
These are to be known.

Preceded by ultimate and conventional knowledge, it is the fruit of ultimate and conventional knowledge; having understood all conceptual proliferation, it proceeds effortlessly with respect to that ineffable reality.

And by means of signlessness alone, through the tranquility of non-conceptual mind, one attains the single flavor of the equality of all phenomena. By these four aspects, the path of calm abiding (*śamatha*) of bodhisattvas proceeds until [the attainment of] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

For the sake of the perfect accomplishment and full realization of the vision of the wisdom of complete enlightenment. In this regard, the insight (vipaśyanā) of bodhisattvas should be understood, in brief, as being of four aspects; and all of these are preceded by the four aspects of calm abiding (śamatha).
Regarding phenomena, they are free from the extreme of false adherence through superimposition, and free from the extreme of false adherence through denial;
they establish the infinite distinctions of phenomena.
And insight is that which conforms to the method. By means of these four aspects,
the path of insight of bodhisattvas proceeds for the sake of the perfection and full realization of the knowledge and vision of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Thus, this has been a brief exposition of the calm abiding and insight of bodhisattvas.
In that regard, what is the skillful means of bodhisattvas? It is as follows:
In brief, it is of twelve aspects: six kinds concerning the internal realization of the Buddha’s qualities, and six kinds concerning the external maturation of sentient beings.
Regarding the internal realization of the Buddha-dharmas, what are the six kinds of skillful means? They are:
the bodhisattva’s regard for all sentient beings accompanied by compassion, and [the regard] for all conditioned phenomena...

The thorough knowledge of things as they truly are regarding those [phenomena], the longing for the knowledge of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, the non-abandonment of cyclic existence based on concern for sentient beings, and the reliance upon the thorough knowledge of conditioned phenomena as they truly are—

His wandering in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is afflicted, yet he maintains ardent vigor based on his longing for the wisdom of a Buddha. This should be understood as the sixfold skill in means (*upāya-kauśalya*) concerning the internal realization of the qualities of a Buddha.

He brings even small roots of merit to the state of immeasurable fruit. Likewise, with little difficulty, he causes vast and immeasurable roots of merit to arise and gather. Likewise, in the teaching of the Buddha—
He removes the hostility of beings who are hostile; he causes those who are indifferent to enter [the path]; he brings to maturity those who have entered; and he liberates those who are matured.

One dedicates it toward perfect enlightenment. Thus, although that root of virtue is small both in terms of its substance and its field, by the power of dedication, it is brought to the state of having immeasurable fruit.

There exists a basis (*vastu*) depending upon which verbal expressions (*abhilāpa*) proceed. Even that [basis] which is expressed by those verbal expressions as having a certain intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), does not, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), possess that intrinsic nature. Therefore, they are said to be "without a basis" (*nirvastuka*).

In the end, this being so, those expressible intrinsic natures of phenomena do not exist at all in any way from the very beginning. How could they arise or cease? Therefore, they are unarisen and unceasing.
...are so called. For example, just as in space various and abundant forms (rūpa) and the activities of form (rūpa-karman) are perceived,

and when that form and those forms—
When the karmas have been removed, then only the utterly pure space, whose nature is the mere absence of form, appears. In this same way,
regarding that ineffable reality which stands in the place of space, the various perceptions produced by diverse verbal expressions—

Conceptual constructions (vikalpa), accompanied by attachment to conceptual proliferation (prapañca), proceed as the basis for form and karma. And all those conceptualizations of perception (saṃjñā-vikalpa) produced by verbal expression,
which are accompanied by attachment to conceptual proliferation, [result in] diverse forms and karma.

For those who abide therein, that ineffable reality— which is like space— provides room. Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas, by means of noble gnosis, [eliminate] those false conceptualizations and discursive proliferations (*prapañca*) arisen from verbal expression, [they realize it].
When all that follows from conceptual attachment has been removed in every respect,
then for those supreme noble Bodhisattvas, by means of that noble gnosis,
that ineffable reality is merely the absence of any nature that can be expressed through words.

It appears pure, like space. And they do not seek any other intrinsic nature (svabhāva) for it beyond that. Therefore, phenomena are said to be equal to space. For example, an illusion does not exist in the way that it appears.

It exists; yet, it is not the case that what is produced by illusion does not exist at all in every respect. In the same way, these phenomena do not exist for fools exactly as they appear through the power of verbal expression and habitual familiarity; nor, however, [do they not exist at all].
In every respect, they do not exist at all by way of their ultimate, ineffable nature. And through this entry into the method, they are neither existent nor non-existent;
thus they are non-dual, like an illusion. Therefore, they are said to be "like an illusion. Thus...
For a bodhisattva does not remove anything from the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), nor does he reject anything; he does not diminish it, nor does he augment it;

For a bodhisattva who is practicing [the path], though not from his own intention,
other [tasks] must be performed for the sake of abandoning evil.
And for the purpose of inducing them to take up the *śālamūla* (root-of-śāla) vow:
those beings who neither seek anything from the bodhisattva, nor are in distress,
nor even— detailed as before— are afflicted by illness, yet are his acquaintances and well-disposed toward him.

The Bodhisattva also causes those very people to be established in that same root of virtue; that is to say, in knowing how to respect their mothers, and so on in detail up to the undertaking and following of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Thus, by the Bodhisattva, they are [established].

If those being exhorted do not comply because of wavering, the bodhisattva displays internal anger toward them out of a desire for their welfare; yet he does not become angry in his underlying intention (*āśaya*). In his activities...

He demonstrates the primary [benefit] out of a desire for their welfare; yet he does not turn away from his underlying intention. Even if he brings about some minor worldly disadvantage for them, it is out of a desire for their welfare and not because he desires their harm.
There arises a sense of dissimilarity in that bodhisattva toward those beings;
such is his intention regarding that activity, and by means of it, he establishes those beings in the abandonment of evil and the undertaking of what is wholesome.
Therefore, this skillful means for disciplining sentient beings is called the bodhisattva’s uncommon intention (*viśeṣāśaya*).
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s skillful means born of firm resolve (*avaṣṭambhaja*)? Here—
Whether he has become his own master, or has become a king, or has attained sovereign power, a bodhisattva correctly instructs his own retinue or his own realm thus:
"Even those who are my retinue or my realm who are not filial toward their mothers..."
There will be, in detail, as far as [the point where] one lives having undertaken immoral conduct. In that case, I shall cut off his appropriate food and clothing.
"I shall restrain him," or "I shall strike him," or "I shall deprive him of all his property," or "I shall banish him entirely from everything. And in that matter, he employs human agents; they—
And because those beings are terrified of that great act of punishment, they abandon evil and abide having undertaken what is wholesome.
Even against their will, they are constrained by that forceful compulsion and established in the wholesome.
By this means, those beings [are benefited]. Therefore, this is called the "method born of support.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s method of returning a favor?

270/10. Here, a bodhisattva has previously performed a small or great service for certain sentient beings, whether by means of giving, by rescuing them from calamity, by rescuing them from fear, or by [consoling them] regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant—
Either by means of bringing about union or separation, or by means of pacifying diseases;
from those who are grateful, mindful of what has been done for them, and desirous of returning the favor,
the bodhisattva accepts only the undertaking of wholesome qualities as the repayment.
He requests and accepts nothing else but worldly material goods,
and says this:
"This alone will be a great service to me from you, if you yourselves become filial toward your mothers."
270/19/. Recognizing their parents, they act extensively [in accordance with their wishes] up to the point that they undertake and abide in ethical discipline (*śīla*).

270/20/. Having performed a service for others, they expect a return in the form of another undertaking of virtue (*kuśala-samādāna*). By that very means, they cause others to undertake that same virtue. Therefore—
This is called the method of "requital for what has been done.
In this regard, what is the bodhisattva’s pure method? Here—

A bodhisattva who has reached the final stage and abides on the bodhisattva ground, having thoroughly purified the bodhisattva path, is reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods. Such-and-such a bodhisattva has been reborn in the Tuṣita host of gods.

Before long, he will now attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in Jambūdvīpa. We must not cause him to lose his passion [for the world], nor should we cause him to become dispassionate; rather, our birth shall be in the presence of that Bodhisattva.

[It is said] "may it be so" for the purpose of generating right aspiration in immeasurable sentient beings and for the purpose of cultivating that aspiration extensively. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva,
having passed away from the Tuṣita host of gods, [is reborn] in a high or noble family.

He is born, that is to say, either in a royal family or in the family of a domestic priest. Likewise, having renounced sublime sensual pleasures, he goes forth into homelessness in order to inspire great respect in sentient beings; furthermore, he undertakes the practice of austerities.
In order to dissuade those beings who are devoted to difficult practices,
he further awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
so that other beings may attain the commonality of awakening and liberation.

For the sake of causing [beings] to thirst [for the Dharma], he awaits the entreaty of Brahmā even after having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; he does not yet teach the Dharma to those beings. For those beings, the Dharma—

In order to inspire reverence [in the minds of the gods], [the Blessed One thought]: "This proclamation of the Dharma will not be a mere minor matter, that now Brahmā himself should entreat the Blessed One for the teaching of the Dharma. Furthermore, with the Buddha-eye...

He surveys the world. Out of reverence for Brahmā, he taught the Dharma when requested by Brahmā; it was not out of his own initiative, nor out of a mind of compassion for sentient beings, nor because it was appropriate for himself alone.
"Having understood"— that is, for the sake of abandoning such false grasping on the part of certain beings, he once again turned the Wheel of Dharma.

He sets in motion in the world that which has not been set in motion before. In this way, he teaches the Dharma and proclaims the rules of training (śikṣāpada). This is called the bodhisattva’s pure means; for there is no other means than this means.
272/05/. And there is nothing further, more transcendent, or more sublime than this.

272/06/. Thus, these six kinds of skill in means (upāya-kauśalya) of the bodhisattvas, through their concise and detailed exposition, [serve] for the removal of the obstructions of obstructed beings. 272/07/. [End of section].

For the removal of heat for those who are neutral, for the entry of those who have not yet entered, for the ripening of those who have entered, and for the liberation of those who are ripened. Thus, there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this. This is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the bodhisattvas.

272/12/. In that regard, what is the dhāraṇī of the bodhisattvas? Briefly stated, it should be seen as fourfold: the dhāraṇī of the Dharma, the dhāraṇī of the meaning, the dhāraṇī of the mantra, and—

272/15. Among these, what is the dhāraṇī of the Dharma (*dharma-dhāraṇī*)? Here, a bodhisattva attains a certain kind of reinforcement of the power of mindfulness and wisdom (*smṛti-prajñā-bala*), by means of which [he retains] what has been heard...

Merely by means of [his] memory, he retains for an immeasurable time immeasurable texts— those not previously studied, those not familiarized through speech, comprised of collections of names, phrases, and syllables, arranged in sequence, properly composed in sequence, and vast in extent.

272/20. Therein, what is the dhāraṇī of meaning? It is as before. Therein, this is the distinction: one retains for an immeasurable period of time the immeasurable meaning of those very same dharmas, which is unknown and unmastered by the mind.

273/03/. The mantra-dhāraṇī of reality.
273/04/. In that regard, what is the dhāraṇī for a bodhisattva to attain the patience of a bodhisattva? Here, a bodhisattva has himself previously practiced intense causes.

Possessing wisdom, dwelling in seclusion, not uttering even a word, not entering even the path of sight with anyone, eating in such a measure, eating without mixing [foods], eating only one kind of food, and absorbed in meditation—
273/09/. Sleeping little at night and staying awake much from others, 273/10/.
these mantra-words spoken by the Tathāgata for the sake of attaining the patience of a bodhisattva are as follows: *iṭi miṭi kiṭi bhikṣāṃti*.

He reflects upon, weighs, and examines the meaning of these mantra-words, beginning with "pada" and "svāhā. Having thus correctly entered into the meaning of these mantra-words in this way, he [understands] that very meaning by himself, even without having heard it from anyone else.
He understands it thus: "For instance, there is no established meaning whatsoever in these mantra-words;
they are indeed devoid of meaning. And this very thing is their meaning, namely, meaninglessness. Furthermore, beyond that..."

He does not seek any other meaning. To this extent, the meaning of those mantra-words has been thoroughly penetrated by him. Having correctly penetrated the meaning of those mantra-words, through that very [penetration] of the meaning...
By means of the essence, one correctly penetrates the meaning of all phenomena even without hearing it from another; and furthermore, one penetrates this meaning as follows:
by means of all verbal expressions, the meaning of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena—
Perfection is that which is the ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāvatā*) of these [phenomena].
This is their meaning of intrinsic nature. Having thus correctly realized the meaning of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, [one realizes] the ultimate reality beyond that.
He does not seek further, and because he has penetrated that noble meaning, he attains joy and rapture. That bodhisattva, having attained it...
Based upon those words of the dhāraṇī, the patience of a bodhisattva is to be described.
Through the attainment of that [patience], that bodhisattva, before long, attains purity of resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*). In the highest degree of resolute belief...
It abides in the patience regarding the three types of conduct. This should be understood as the dhāraṇī for a bodhisattva to attain the patience of a bodhisattva.
In that regard, [it consists of] the dhāraṇī of the Dharma and the dhāraṇī of the meaning. Regarding the bodhisattva...
At the end of the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), having entered the stage of pure resolute intention (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*), one attains that which is certain,

Or [it may arise] by relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). However, it is not certain, not stable, and not sublime. Just as the dhāraṇī of the meaning of the Dharma is to be understood, so too is the dhāraṇī of mantras; yet, this dhāraṇī is for the sake of attaining the patience (*kṣānti*) of a bodhisattva.
Just as they have been explained, so too are they obtained.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva who is endowed with four qualities obtains all these dhāraṇīs, but not if he is deficient in even one of them. Which four?

By these [qualities], one is not attached to sensual pleasures; one does not give rise to envy toward the excellence of others and remains free from envy; one is a giver of everything requested and gives without regret; and one delights in the Dharma.
Delighting in the Dharma, the bodhisattva takes delight in the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, specifically in the Mātṛkā of the Piṭakas.
What is the bodhisattva’s bodhisattva-vow? It is as follows:
In brief, it should be seen as fivefold: the aspiration for the arising of the thought [of awakening],
the aspiration for rebirth, the aspiration for the sphere of activity, the right aspiration, and the great aspiration.
In that regard, the first production of the thought of awakening by a bodhisattva toward unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment is called the "vow of the production of the thought."

The bodhisattva’s aspiration for rebirth is said to be the vow for birth in happy destinies that is conducive to the welfare of sentient beings in the future. The vow for the correct discernment of phenomena consists of the immeasurables and so forth.

The aspiration of a bodhisattva regarding the cultivation of wholesome qualities as its object is called the "aspiration for the sphere of activity. It is for the sake of gathering all the wholesome qualities of a bodhisattva in the future. All—
Furthermore, the vow made by a bodhisattva, whether in brief or in detail, for the sake of gathering virtuous qualities, is called a "right vow" (samyak-praṇidhāna).
Moreover, the great vows of a bodhisattva arise from this very [vow].

It should be understood from right aspiration. That, moreover, is of ten kinds. First, the aspiration for the sake of performing all forms of immeasurable worship and service to the Tathāgatas in the future.
This is called the great vow (*mahā-praṇidhāna*) of the Bodhisattvas. Furthermore,
for the sake of upholding and protecting the true Dharma of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
and for the sake of maintaining the guidance of the Dharma, there is the great vow [of remaining] in Tuṣita.
Based on dwelling in the stage of cultivation, as previously described, up to the great vow for parinirvāṇa; the great vow for practicing the correct conduct of a bodhisattva in all its aspects;
[and] the great vow for the maturation of all sentient beings.
The great vow: the great vow to manifest all world-systems;
the great vow to purify the Buddha-fields;

One perceives all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, because that very ineffable entity has not been fully understood in its true nature, its arising and passing away are perceived as having causes that have not been fully understood. [One perceives] all conditioned phenomena as having an ineffable intrinsic nature (*nirabhilāpya-svabhāva*).

He contemplates conditioned phenomena as impermanent. He contemplates past conditioned phenomena as having arisen and ceased; he perceives neither their cause nor their intrinsic nature. Therefore, they do not exist by way of a cause.
Nor does he perceive their existence by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Rather, he perceives those [dharmas] of the present as having arisen and not yet ceased; he perceives their cause.

One does not perceive [them] because their fruit has already been given; yet one perceives their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) because it is unceased. Therefore, one regards them as existing by way of intrinsic nature, but not by way of a cause. [He likewise regards] future conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) as unarisen...

He perceives them as ceased by wisdom. He apprehends their cause because their fruit has not yet been given; however, he does not apprehend their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) because they have not yet arisen.
Therefore, the bodhisattva perceives their existence from the perspective of the cause, but not from the perspective of intrinsic nature.

Thus, seeing the continuity of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-saṃtati) proceeding uninterrupted throughout the three times, he perceives the three characteristics of the conditioned within each individual moment of a conditioned phenomenon. Beyond that moment—

He perceives the fourth characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*). In that regard, immediately after the destruction of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the preceding momentary formation (*saṃskārakṣaṇa*), there is the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of a previously non-existent momentary formation; this is called "birth" (*jāti*).
He perceives that which is the non-disappearance at that very moment of what has arisen as "stability.
He perceives that the distinctness or alteration of that which has arisen, in relation to the nature of the previously ceased momentary conditioned formation, is [change].

He perceives that as aging. Therefore, he perceives that the intrinsic destruction of that very momentary conditioned factor (*saṃskāra*) which has arisen subsequent to the moment of birth is "decay. He perceives it as having precisely that intrinsic nature which it possessed when it arose.
He perceives the momentary nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). He perceives their very own nature as birth, duration, and decay, and does not perceive them as having any other nature.
And beyond that moment, whatever that momentary conditioned phenomenon...

The departure of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)— that very [departure] of those [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth— is how one sees them as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*). These four conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*),
when taken together, manifest the two states of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in brief.
These are characterized by existence and characterized by non-existence. Therein, that which is existence according to the Blessed One is one characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

That which is non-existence is established as the second characteristic, characterized by equality. And since that existence of those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is manifested through their persistence and transformation, it is established as the third.
The characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) have been established. In that regard, the bodhisattva,
having set aside mere formations (*saṃskāra-mātra*), does not [perceive] their birth, nor their duration, nor their decay,
nor their impermanence as a substantially existent intrinsic nature (*dravya-svabhāva*) at any time.

Having fallen [into contemplation], he sees. Why is that? He perceives only formations (*saṃskāra*) as they arise; he does not perceive for them any other birth, nor duration, nor aging, nor impermanence. And it is only formations that abide and age.
When it is perishing, one perceives neither its birth, nor its duration, nor its aging, nor its impermanence.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva investigates this through reasoning, he does not perceive these factors, such as birth and so forth, as substantial entities. And thus, while investigating in this manner—

One does not perceive [it]. If there were another phenomenon of birth distinct from the conditioned factors such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, then just as the conditioned factors such as form arise by way of their own nature, that [phenomenon] too would likewise arise; if this were the case, there would be two [births].
There would be two types of birth: that which is the birth of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and that which is the birth of birth (*jāti*).
In this regard, the birth of formative forces would either be non-different from that birth of birth, or it would be different. If, first of all, they were non-different, then in that case—

The conceptualization of birth as a substantial entity is meaningless. It is not tenable to say that birth is something other than a substance. Furthermore, if it were so, birth would not be the arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-janma*);
thus, it is not tenable to call it "the birth that is the arising of conditioned phenomena."
Just as with birth, so too should duration, aging, and destruction be understood in detail.

If that which is called destruction were a phenomenon established by way of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then it would arise or cease for this [entity]. And when destruction has arisen, [the entity would necessarily cease].
In that case, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would have to be ceased.
This being so, with little difficulty, the mind— just like that of one who has entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)— would [be stilled].

There would be a non-occurrence of mental factors (caitasika-dharma). Furthermore, because that destruction has ceased through cessation, those conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), even though they have already ceased, would have to arise once again, on the grounds that their destruction does not exist. Therefore, [there is no such thing as] destruction.
It is not tenable that [anything] arises and ceases. Furthermore,

for a son of good family or a daughter of good family who perceives both the existence at all times of things that exist substantially (*dravyasat*) and the perfection of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-pariniṣpatti*) of things that exist as designations (*prajñaptisat*), [it is not tenable].

Disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation are appropriate; conversely, they are inappropriate [otherwise]. Through these aspects, a bodhisattva understands, in accordance with reality, that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.
Furthermore, as those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) thus proceed in a continuous stream as impermanent,
the bodhisattva perceives them as being characterized by the three types of suffering (*duḥkhatā*), specifically the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
[He understands] the suffering of change and the suffering of suffering. In this way,
the bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering."
Furthermore, the bodhisattva understands, as it truly is, the two kinds of selflessness of all phenomena—both conditioned and unconditioned:
namely, the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). In this regard, it is as follows:

280/21/. The selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) is as follows: those existing phenomena (*dharmas*) are not themselves the person, nor does there exist another person distinct from the existing phenomena. In this regard, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is that which [applies] to all [phenomena]. 280/22–23. [This applies to] all... in all... abhi-...
Among all things that can be expressed, no phenomenon possessing the intrinsic nature of verbal expression exists. In this way, the bodhisattva [realizes] that all phenomena are without self.
One understands it as it truly is.

Furthermore, regarding these very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), when their prior causes have been severed and they subsequently cease without remainder, and there is the absolute non-arising of others [similar to them]— this is [the cessation].
Non-arising and non-manifestation: this is called nirvāṇa. And that should be understood as peaceful because of the subsiding of the afflictions and the subsiding of suffering.
Thus, first of all, a bodhisattva whose resolute intention is not yet purified has not [yet] seen—

Or, a true follower of the Śrāvaka vehicle may be inclined toward nirvāṇa and declare, "Nirvāṇa is peace. Yet, he does not possess a realization of that nirvāṇa as it truly is, nor the vision of knowledge according to reality.

In this regard, there exists such appropriate mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*). For example, suppose there were the son of a king or the son of a householder who had been raised within the inner apartments by the king or the householder. And while he was still young, being in the state of a youth—
That king or householder might have prepared artificial chariots made of deer,
or chariots made of oxen, horses, or elephants.
And that prince or householder’s son, playing and delighting himself with them, [might say]:

While amusing himself with those very artificial deer, he might have the perception of them as deer; or with those artificial oxen, horses, and elephants, he might have the perception of them as elephants.
Then, at one time, that king or householder [might speak] to his own son...

Due to the increase and maturation of the sense faculties of living beings, he would describe the appearance of wild animals; he would describe the appearance of living beings, up to and including elephants. Furthermore, for that son of a king or son of a householder...
Upon hearing that praise, it would occur to them:
"This king or householder is speaking in praise of our deer-chariots, up to and including our elephant-chariots. Then, at another time, that king or householder—
Or, having banished his own son from the house, he might show him real wild animals,
even unto real elephants.
He should lie down. Upon seeing that [vision], at that moment, a personal realization of things as they truly are would arise in him:
"These are those actual deer-carts, and so on in detail up to elephant-carts, for which there is no..."
"For what reason has my father for a long time spoken in praise [of this]?
It is because our own resolve has proceeded toward an object that is not as it truly is—an object that is merely a semblance, a mere reflection, and a mere appearance. By that, previously—

By what kind of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) would they be able to cross over? In the same way, for those Bodhisattvas who have grown up within the house of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), whose intentions (*āśaya*) are not yet pure, and for the Śrāvakas— who are like sons and whom [the Bodhisattvas] regard as fathers— [the Tathāgata acts as a father].

282/11. By the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages and who perceive Nirvāṇa directly, the praise of Nirvāṇa as it has been seen was spoken in the presence of those Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas. And by them...
That nirvāṇa has been adhered to for a long time by an intellect that follows mere sound according to its qualities; however,
when,
through the subsequent development of the maturation of their accumulations, those bodhisattvas who possess a disposition of faith—
In those Arhats and Śrāvakas who have seen the truths, direct knowledge regarding Nirvāṇa arises. At that time, a realization of things as they truly are (yathābhūta) also arises for them:
"This is Nirvāṇa," for all Śrāvakas.

Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas whose praise has been spoken by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: previously, due to our immature wisdom, we did not have faith in them according to reality. However, there does exist a semblance of such [a state], and it does exist.
It is merely an appearance. By means of that former resolve, he [attains] this second [stage]. Relying upon that latter resolve which accords with reality, it is as follows:
suppose there were a certain sick man and a certain great physician for him.
For the sake of pacifying a present illness, one should attend to it with appropriate medicines;
yet that sick person has been afflicted for a long time.

He would have faith in those medicines alone; he would find delight in them and perceive their essence in them alone. Then, for that sick man, his former illness [would be cured] by the application of those medicines.
When [the first illness] has subsided, another illness that must be treated with a different medicine might arise. Then, that great physician,
having observed the cessation of the previous illness and the emergence of the subsequent one, [prescribes] another medicine...
Having recognized that [the illness] is incurable and having understood that previous application of medicine,
he should reject it and prescribe another medicine that is suitable. The foolish sick man, however, remains attached to his former medicine.

He perceives those very [medicines] as wholesome. Even though he is told by that great physician, "These former medicines were prescribed for you previously," that he now perceives them directly as unwholesome.
One should not place confidence in the statement that "medicines are for a future illness," nor should one believe his words. In this very same way,
those foolish bodhisattvas and śrāvakas who are afflicted by illness are to be understood as being like that.
Like a man seized by afflictions, [he receives] from the Great Physician, the Tathāgata, that which is higher than the high, most high, and highest; clearer than the clear, clearer, and clearest;
deeper than the deep, deeper, and deepest; and more sublime than the lowly.
They do not enter into, nor do they have faith in, the more exalted or most exalted teaching of the Dharma, the designation of the path, and the instruction and admonition.
In cases where they do not practice in accordance with the Dharma,
a faithful bodhisattva or śrāvaka does not give rise to doubt or uncertainty regarding that which was spoken by the Tathāgata. Furthermore, he [remains] complete in all his faculties...

Having mounted that Dharma-chariot— which is like a noble chariot well-yoked with horses and is impelled by the Tathāgata— one proceeds, like a skillful charioteer, to whatever ground is to be traversed and reached; that [ground] one swiftly—
One becomes a swift traveler, not being slow.

285/04. These five marvelous and wonderful qualities of a bodhisattva are to be known as belonging to one training in the unsurpassed vehicle of perfect enlightenment. What are the five? They are:
(1) spontaneous affection toward all sentient beings; [and] for the sake of sentient beings alone...

These five marvelous and wonderful qualities of bodhisattvas are not shared by any other sentient beings.
There are these five things that are not marvelous for a bodhisattva, endowed with which—

It is said that the Bodhisattva has gone forth endowed with marvelous and extraordinary qualities. What are these five? That the Bodhisattva, although by nature happy, undergoes all suffering for the sake of the welfare of others, solely for the purpose of benefiting others.
He accepts suffering that has a cause. This is the first non-marvel of a bodhisattva;
endowed with which, a bodhisattva is said to be "endowed with marvelous and extraordinary qualities."

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva, while knowing the defects of cyclic existence and knowing the virtues of liberation, loves the purification of sentient beings and finds his very essence in that happiness, he takes the purification of sentient beings as his primary objective.

He accepts cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). This is the second non-marvelous quality of a bodhisattva, as previously described. Furthermore, when a bodhisattva, while being one who knows only the flavor of the bliss of silence, [exerts himself for] the purification of sentient beings—
And because he is dear to them, being composed of happiness, he makes the purification of sentient beings his primary objective and applies himself to teaching the Dharma to sentient beings. This—

The third non-marvel of a bodhisattva is as before. Furthermore, when a bodhisattva— being himself composed of happiness— desires the purification of sentient beings, he [dedicates] the roots of virtue accumulated through the six perfections toward that very purification of sentient beings.
Making wisdom alone his sovereign authority, he renounces everything for the sake of the disposition of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, he does not seek the ripening of that renunciation as a reward.
This is the fourth non-marvel of the bodhisattva, as previously described.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva considers the welfare of others to be his own welfare and is seen to perform all activities for the sake of others' welfare— this is the fifth non-marvelous quality of a bodhisattva, endowed with which a bodhisattva...
He is said to be "endowed with marvelous and extraordinary qualities.

288/03. By means of momentary application; by means of faultless application; by means of the power of analytical reflection; by means of application through the purity of resolute intention; and by means of application that is certain and fixed.
In this regard, by means of the application of guarding, the bodhisattva protects his intelligence (*medhā*),

through which innate knowledge (*sahaja-jñāna*) he very swiftly grasps the teachings (*dharma*). He protects his mindfulness (*smṛti*), by means of which mindfulness he [retains] the teachings already grasped.
