303/06/. There is nothing further beyond this.
303/07/. These five bases of a bodhisattva’s fortitude are to be known.
What are the five? By means of these very five aspects, a bodhisattva—

In the *Pakṣyapaṭala*, the maintenance of the power of fortitude (*dhṛti-balādhānatā*) for bodhisattvas has been explained. Those very things should be understood as the bases of a bodhisattva’s heroism (*vairya-adhiṣṭhāna*); by means of those bases and objects of focus, a bodhisattva’s heroism proceeds.
There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
These five are the bases for a bodhisattva’s open-handedness.
What are the five? Frequent giving and joyful giving.
Giving with reverence, giving without affliction, and giving without dependence. Furthermore, their detailed classification should be understood as it is in the "Chapter on Giving" (*Dānapaṭala*).
By means of these bases and these objects, the [giving] of Bodhisattvas is liberated...
303/18/. [The teaching] proceeds from the hand. There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
303/19/. These five are the bases for a bodhisattva’s unraveling of the knots of profound meaning. What are the five? They are those which the Tathāgata—
The discourses spoken by the Tathāgata that are profound, appearing profound, connected with emptiness,
and in accordance with specific conditionality and dependent origination—
this is the first basis. Furthermore, in the Vinaya, regarding an offense...
Skillfulness and skillfulness regarding emergence from transgressions—this is the second basis.
Furthermore, in the *mātṛkā*, the non-erroneous establishment of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*)—this is the third basis. By these...

The elucidation of the meaning of the conventional designations for phenomena that are generally hidden; this is the fourth basis. And [the elucidation] of the meaning of the phenomena of all phenomena—
304/03/. The classification of the modes of etymological explanation (*nirvacana*). This is the fifth basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
By means of this basis and objective support (*ālambana*), the bodhisattvas' liberation of the intended meaning (*saṃdhi*) of the scriptures proceeds. Not [otherwise].
304/06. Nothing more than this.
304/07. A bodhisattva’s compassion toward sentient beings, from the very beginning, leads to the abandonment of enmity. Thus, a bodhisattva who is compassionate...

He applies himself with an undaunted mind to all activities for the benefit of sentient beings, and he does not become weary in that application. Furthermore, his frequent abiding in compassion serves both for his own dwelling in blameless happiness in the present life and for the sake of favoring others.

And it also conduces [to this]. Furthermore, those benefits of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) spoken of by the Blessed One—such as "poison does not affect his body, nor does a weapon"—all these are to be understood as belonging to the compassionate Bodhisattva. This is [the point].
The fruit and benefit of the compassion of Bodhisattvas is to be seen as follows:
a Bodhisattva who speaks kindly abandons the fourfold fault of speech in this very life— namely, false speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.

And [he avoids] idle chatter. Furthermore, his speech proceeds for his own benefit and for the benefit of others, both in the present life and in the future. A Bodhisattva who speaks kindly becomes one whose words are authoritative and whose words are accepted.
"304/21. No. This should be understood as the fruit and benefit of a bodhisattva’s pleasant speech. 304/22.
First of all, in this very life, the steadfast bodhisattva [attains] everything in every respect... 304/23."
Free from sloth and indolence, he becomes one whose mind is joyful and undertakes the vows of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline. Having undertaken them, he does not despair;
through patience, he benefits both himself and others in the future.
And in all undertakings of the duties of a bodhisattva, he is by nature firm in his exertion; he does not turn back without having accomplished them. Thus, these are the [qualities] of a bodhisattva—
The benefits of the fruit of heroism for those who possess such qualities should be understood.
Furthermore, the benefits of the fruit of being open-handed and of unraveling the knots of profound meanings should be understood. For example:
In the chapter on existence (*bhāva-paṭala*), regarding the power of generosity and the power of wisdom:
this is the fruit and benefit of these marks of a bodhisattva.
And what is their sequence? First, the bodhisattva...

Out of compassion, he favors sentient beings; he regards them with concern and desires their welfare. Therefore, in order to cause them to rise from unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states, he speaks of the proper method, causes them to grasp it, and explains it.

305/12. When beings have entered [the path], and when there are various forms of misconduct among beings caused by the afflictions, he becomes one who endures all kinds of conflict, because he does not abandon those beings who abide in such conduct and misconduct. Thus is that steadfast one.

He brings some beings to maturity through the gathering of material things; some through the gathering of the Dharma; and some through both of these, the gatherings of both the Dharma and material things. This is the [function] of these five types of bodhisattvas...
The sequence of the marks of a sentient being (*sattva-liṅga*) should be understood as follows:
these five marks of a bodhisattva are the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). Among these six perfections, by which perfection is which mark [of a bodhisattva] [established]?

The characteristic of a sentient being is subsumed [by the perfection of generosity]. Compassion is subsumed by the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). Pleasant speech is subsumed by the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Fortitude is subsumed by the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) and the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

That [generosity] is subsumed by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*). Open-handedness is subsumed by the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) alone. The unraveling of the intentional terminology (*saṃdhi*) of profound meaning is subsumed by both the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) and the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).
Thus, these five marks of a bodhisattva are to be understood through five reversals;
their intrinsic nature is established by way of its basis.
By way of the benefits of the fruit, by way of the sequence, and by way of the summary— thus,
in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the practice of the secondary dharmas (*anudharma-yoga-sthāna*) under the heading of the foundation (*ādhāra*).
Chapter 306/06: The First Chapter on the Marks of a Bodhisattva.
307/01: Summary Verse (Uddāna).
307/02/. Bringing good actions to completion, embracing skillfulness, and dedication;
307/03/. this is the last [factor].
307/04/. Whether abiding in the faction of householders or the faction of those who have gone forth, for one who [strives for] awakening—

In brief, four qualities of a being should be understood, training in which— whether as a householder or one who has gone forth— a bodhisattva quickly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. What are the four?
307/08/. Well-performed action, skillfulness, benefiting others, and dedication.

307/09/. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s well-performed action? It is that which consists in acting with certainty regarding the perfections, acting with proficiency, acting constantly, and acting without [interruption]...

307/11. And acting immediately. How does a bodhisattva become one who acts with certainty regarding giving? (116b) Here, when a gift is available and a petitioner has properly approached—even if that petitioner is a wrongdoer or a benefactor—the bodhisattva...
Whether the recipient be virtuous or flawed, he gives inevitably. No human or non-human, no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, nor anyone else in the world, is able to cause his mind of giving to waver.

307/17/. In accordance with the Dharma. How does a bodhisattva act skillfully regarding generosity? 307/18/. Here, when a gift to be given is available and a petitioner has properly presented himself, the bodhisattva gives everything; nor...

307/20/. There is nothing whatsoever that he would not relinquish for the sake of sentient beings, even internal things, let alone external ones. And how does a bodhisattva become one who acts constantly—that is, in giving? Here, a bodhisattva [Tib.]:
307/23/. [160b] Without becoming weary of giving, he gives at all times, constantly and continuously, whatever gift arises. And how does the bodhisattva—

308/02/. He becomes one who acts irreproachably, namely, in giving. Here, a bodhisattva, having avoided that defiled giving which was described in the Chapter on Giving, gives undefiled giving. Thus...

For a bodhisattva is one who acts well, namely, in giving. Just as it is with giving, so it should be understood that these same four modes apply, as appropriate, to the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they consist in acting with certainty.

308/08. Skillful performance, constant performance, and blameless performance. 308/09. In that regard, the skill of a bodhisattva who has acted [skillfully] should be understood, in brief, as being of ten kinds. [The first is: toward sentient beings who are hostile, the removal of hostility...
Skill in means for the removal of suffering; skill in means for introducing those who are neutral;
skill in means for maturing those who have been introduced; and skill in means for liberating those who have been matured. Skill in all worldly treatises. Awakening—
Skill in examining lapses in the undertaking of the restraint of the ethical discipline of sentient beings; skill in right aspiration; skill in the Śrāvaka vehicle;
skill in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and skill in the Mahāyāna. This—

308/17. In all these skillful means (*kauśala*), as previously stated, their specific distinctions should be understood according to their respective applications within this very Bodhisattva stage (*bodhisattvabhūmi*). Furthermore, these ten skillful means of a bodhisattva perform five functions.

They act thus. By means of the four previous types of skillfulness, the bodhisattva establishes sentient beings in their own welfare. Through skillfulness in all worldly treatises, the bodhisattva overcomes all the doctrines of others. [Tibetan]
Through skill in reflecting upon lapses regarding the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara-samādāna*), a bodhisattva either does not incur an offense,
or if one is incurred, he remedies it according to the Dharma; thus his ethical discipline is perfectly pure.
Through skill in right aspiration, the bodhisattva draws forth the undertaking of the excellent [vows] and, in the future, brings to fulfillment all desired aims.

309/01/. He attains [this]. Through skill in the three vehicles, the bodhisattva teaches the Dharma that corresponds to their respective lineages, faculties, and inclinations, and points out the appropriate reasoning. In this very way, by these...
Through ten skillful means, a bodhisattva performs five tasks;
by these five tasks, all his duties are fulfilled with respect to both the present life and the future.

309/07. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s assistance to others? Here, a bodhisattva, relying upon the four bases of sympathy—namely, generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and consistency in purpose (*samānārthatā*)—[assists] some of them...

He brings about the welfare of sentient beings; he brings about their happiness; he brings about both their welfare and happiness. This is a concise explanation of the bodhisattvas' assistance to others. [The detailed explanation follows:]
Furthermore, that should be understood as before, namely, as in the chapter on the welfare of oneself and others (*svaparārthapaṭala*).
In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dedication (*pariṇāmanā*)? Here, the bodhi—

Whatever root of merit has been accumulated by a sentient being through these three doors— by means of skillfulness in the completion of well-performed deeds and by way of benefiting others— all that, whether past, future, or present, [is dedicated] to unexcelled [enlightenment].
He dedicates [the roots of merit] toward perfect enlightenment with a profound and intense faith.
He does not desire any other ripening of the fruit for those roots of merit,
except for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment itself.
And whatever training dharmas have been taught by the Blessed One for bodhisattvas, whether householders or those who have gone forth— all of these are contained within these very [perfections].

310/01. One should understand that there are four types of gathering: in the state of having well-performed actions, in skillfulness, in benefiting others, and in dedication. Therefore, for a Bodhisattva who has thus well-performed his actions and is virtuous, [there is] the benefit of others—

For one who has thus entered upon the transformation [of the path], it should be understood that awakening— which is difficult to reach and difficult to attain— is both near and very near. Whatever bodhisattvas there may be in the past, future, or present time, whether belonging to the class of householders or those who have gone forth...

Those training in these [perfections] who have awakened, are awakening, will awaken, and are awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— all of them do so by means of these very four dharmas; there is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
In this way, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, a bodhisattva becomes one who is correctly applied to these four dharmas. Nevertheless,
there is a very great distinction between a householder bodhisattva and a bodhisattva who has gone forth.

A very great distinction should be understood [between these two]. For instance, a bodhisattva who has gone forth is, from the very beginning, liberated from the fault of attachment to a household, such as mother, father, children, wife, and so forth; whereas one who has not gone forth is not so liberated.

One should know that he is a householder. Furthermore, a bodhisattva who has gone forth is liberated from the afflictions and the suffering of distraction associated with the pursuit of that very same possession—such as agriculture, commerce, and royal service; however, he is not yet liberated [from all things].
The householder is to be understood as such. Furthermore, a renunciant bodhisattva is able to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in its absolute purity, whereas a householder bodhisattva is not.
Moreover, a renunciant bodhisattva [is superior] in all aspects of awakening—
Regarding the qualities conducive to enlightenment, he attains swift superknowledge.
Whatever wholesome practice he undertakes, in each and every case he very quickly reaches its culmination.
A householder bodhisattva does not do so; furthermore, [this applies even more to] one who has gone forth.
Because a bodhisattva abides in the vows and observances for the sake of others, his words become authoritative;
a householder bodhisattva, however, is not so. Such is the category [of this].
310/03/. By means of those qualities, one should understand the very great difference between a lay bodhisattva and one who has gone forth into homelessness.
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the Foundation (*ādhāra*) and the Section on Practice in Accordance with the Dharma (*anudharmayogasthāna*),
this is the second chapter: the Chapter on the Side (*pakṣapaṭala*).
Summary verse:
The wise possess sevenfold affection toward all sentient beings.
Of those, fifteen are intentions, and ten are considered to be performers of tasks.
A sevenfold affection for sentient beings proceeds from Bodhisattvas;
endowed with which affection, Bodhisattvas possess virtuous intentions.
They are said to possess a delightful and virtuous intention (*kalyāṇāśaya*). What is the sevenfold affection (*vātsalya*)? It is:
fearlessness, propriety, tirelessness, being unsolicited, being non-materialistic, extensiveness, and equanimity. For a bodhisattva does not [act] toward anyone...

Furthermore, he is affectionate; he conducts himself toward them with compliant actions of body, speech, and mind that are pleasing and conducive to their welfare and happiness. Moreover, a bodhisattva’s affection for sentient beings is not improperly applied.

312/12/. That is to say, for the purpose of instigating others toward what is not the Dharma, what is not the Vinaya, improper conduct, and what is inappropriate. And yet, the Bodhisattva remains affectionate toward sentient beings, such that through all his endeavors he does not become weary for their sake.
312/15. He is compassionate toward sentient beings even without being asked;
he is not made compassionate by anyone requesting him. He is compassionate with a mind free from worldly motives (*anāmiṣa-citta*), and not out of a desire for a reciprocal favor from others.

Or by one hoping for a desirable maturation; thus the bodhisattva is affectionate toward sentient beings without cause. And that affection of the bodhisattva toward sentient beings is vast, not limited; and likewise, it is vast—
It is as follows: from these sentient beings, the bodhisattva,
while receiving [offerings] in every form, does not reject them.

Bodhisattvas who possess a virtuous intention (*kalyāṇāśaya*)— an intention that is supremely virtuous— are said to be endowed with seven aspects of the arrow of wind regarding themselves and their own bodies.

In this context, the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), comprehension, and certainty that a bodhisattva has regarding the qualities of a Buddha— preceded by faith and preceded by the discernment of phenomena (*dharmavicaya*)—
is called "resolute intention" (*adhyāśaya*). Furthermore, those resolute intentions...
In brief, fifteen [types of] intentions of a bodhisattva are to be known. What are the fifteen? They are:

the intention of excellence, the intention of vows, the intention of the perfections, the intention of the welfare of others, the intention of power, the intention of benefit, the intention of happiness, and the intention of liberation...

313/10/. One whose intention is liberated, one whose intention is firm, one whose intention is non-deceptive, one whose intention is impure, one whose intention is pure, one whose intention is perfectly pure, one whose intention is restrained, one whose intention is innate. In that regard, [the one who possesses] the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha—
The resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) toward these bodhisattvas is called the "supreme intention.

The resolute intention regarding the undertaking of the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline and restraint (*śīla-saṃvara-samādāna*) is called the "intention of the vow" (*vrata-āśaya*). [This applies to] generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

The resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the sake of full realization is called the "intention regarding the perfections" (*pāramitā-āśaya*). The resolute intention regarding the selflessness of phenomena and persons, the ultimate truth, and the profound reality of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is the "intention regarding the meaning of reality" (*tattvārtha-āśaya*).

It is called "aspiration" (*āśaya*). It is that superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) toward the inconceivable power of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or toward their innate power.
This is [the first].

The desire for power is called the *prabhāvāśaya*. The desire to bring about the wholesome among sentient beings is called the *hitāśaya*. The desire to bring about assistance to sentient beings is called the *sukhāśaya*. [Furthermore,] toward sentient beings alone, a mind free from worldly motives (*nirāmiṣa-citta*)...
Regarding that desirable maturation, the state of having an unimpeded mind is called "the liberated intention.

That which is the one-pointedness of mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is called "the firm intention. [This applies] to the means for the welfare of sentient beings and the means for enlightenment.
The resolve accompanied by non-erroneous knowledge is called the "intention that is non-deceptive.

That superior intention (adhyāśaya) of the bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through conviction (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi) is called the "impure intention. [This continues until] the stage of pure intention (śuddhāśaya-bhūmi).

From the stage of reliance up to the stage of certain conduct, the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) of bodhisattvas is called "pure resolute intention" (*śuddhāśaya*). On the stage of reaching the culmination,
the resolute intention of bodhisattvas is called "thoroughly pure resolute intention" (*suśuddhāśaya*).

In this regard, that which is of impure resolute intention (*aśuddhādhyāśaya*) is said to be "restrained" (*nigṛhīta*) because it must be subjected to analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*). Furthermore, that which is of pure and thoroughly purified resolute intention is called "innate intention" (*sahajāśaya*), by virtue of its natural state (*prakṛti*).
314/16/. By way of its essential nature and by way of being well-established in the basis.
314/17/. Thus, by means of these fifteen virtuous superior intentions (*adhyāśaya*) pertaining to all stages, Bodhisattvas, in brief, perform ten tasks.

They offer [these]. What are the ten? With the supreme intention (*agryāśaya*), they perform all forms of worship to the Jewels, which constitute the most excellent of all the accumulations for enlightenment (*bodhi-saṃbhāra*). With the intention of the vow (*vratāśaya*), they undertake the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline and restraint (*śīla-saṃvara-samādāna*).

Even for the sake of their lives, they do not intentionally commit an offense; and having committed one, they confess it with the utmost haste, possessing the intention of the perfections (*pāramitā*).

Through the continuous practice of cultivating wholesome dharmas, they dwell in heedfulness and abide in supreme heedfulness. With a resolute intention toward the ultimate reality, they remain undefiled while wandering through saṃsāra for the sake of sentient beings.
They possess an aspiration for nirvāṇa that is never relinquished. Through their aspiration for its power, they experience a profound flavor of serene confidence in the teaching.
Regarding spiritual cultivation, they perceive it as essential and, having conceived a longing for it, they dwell extensively therein.

They do not rest content with mere hearing or mere reflection. With a disposition for benefit, a disposition for happiness, and a disposition for liberation, they apply themselves to all forms of activities for the welfare of sentient beings; and having applied themselves, they do not become weary, being firm—

With resolute intention, they exert refined vigor and vast vigor; they apply themselves with diligence, neither with lax application nor with interrupted application. Through their resolute intention of non-deception, they quickly attain the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) in each of those respective [tasks].

In the accomplishment of wholesome dharmas, they do not find satisfaction in a mere slight, inferior, or low attainment of distinction. With a restrained resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), they draw forth the innate resolute intention; with the innate [intention], they...
Furthermore, through his resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), he swiftly awakens to unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment for the sake, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. In that regard, whatever [teachings] were spoken by the Blessed One concerning the bodhisattvas...

Those high resolves (adhyāśaya) have been declared, designated, and revealed in various contexts; it should be understood that all of them are subsumed within these very fifteen high resolves. Therefore, [regarding] the past, future, and present—
In the past ages, those bodhisattvas who, with noble resolute intentions,
have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and—
They will emerge and attain perfect awakening; all of them do so by means of these very fifteen superior intentions (*adhyāśaya*). There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this.
Thus, these fifteen superior intentions of a bodhisattva yield great fruit.
316/04/. Praises. Therefore, by relying upon them, a bodhisattva shall attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. 316/05/.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the Superior Intention, within the section on Yoga in Accordance with the Dharma, in the Foundation [section] of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Summary verse:
Lineage, as well as resolute belief, the Joyous [ground], higher ethics, and—
The three [types of] mind, the two types of wisdom, the two signless states— the non-enjoyment and the non-apprehension—
and the analytical knowledges, as well as the supreme state, constitute the dwelling of the Tathāgata.

317/06. Thus, based on the perfection of the lineage (*gotra*), for those training in the aforementioned bodhisattva training and for those in whom the aforementioned marks of a bodhisattva are observed, [there is] the application belonging to the side of the bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, for those Bodhisattvas who are correctly applied and who purify their Bodhisattva resolute intentions (*adhyāśaya*) as previously described, there are, in brief, twelve Bodhisattva stages (*vihāra*). By means of these Bodhisattva stages...
It should be understood that all the conduct of a bodhisattva is subsumed within the twelve [stages] and the thirteenth,
which is the dwelling of a Tathāgata— the unsurpassed dwelling consisting of his perfect awakening. Among these, what are the twelve bodhisattva dwellings?
My [stages] are: the stage of the lineage (*gotra-vihāra*), the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), the stage of joy (*pramudita-vihāra*),

the stage of higher ethics (*adhiśīla-vihāra*), the stage of higher mind (*adhicitta-vihāra*), and the three stages of higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-vihāra*) associated with the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*) and associated with the truths (*satya*).
317/18. It is endowed with the arising and cessation associated with dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).

Thus, by means of that [knowledge], a bodhisattva perceives reality (tattva), and as for that reality which he perceives—due to ignorance of that reality, there is the way in which [suffering] proceeds. 317/20. [And] suffering...

Furthermore, through the knowledge of emptiness, the suffering of sentient beings ceases to arise. As the Bodhisattva investigates with wisdom by means of these three gateways, there come to be for him three abidings in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-vihāra*).
The dwelling that is with effort and with application, which carries the path without interruption and is without conceptualization;
and the dwelling that is without effort and without application, which carries the path without conceptualization.
The dwelling in signs itself, the dwelling in the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the supreme,
perfectly accomplished dwelling of a bodhisattva— these are the twelve kinds of bodhisattva dwellings by which all the dwellings of these [bodhisattvas] are [encompassed].
318.05. This is the compendium; it is the compendium of all the practices of bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the dwelling of a Tathāgata is the dwelling of one who has fully awakened to enlightenment after having transcended all the dwellings of bodhisattvas. In that regard, the Tathāgata—
In the final section on the establishment and application of the last dwelling (vihāra),
there will be a complete exposition. Furthermore, regarding the twelve bodhisattva-dwellings, according to their [respective] order—

There will be an abiding; I shall explain it accordingly. And what is the bodhisattva’s abiding in the lineage (*gotra-vihāra*)? How does a bodhisattva dwelling in the lineage abide? Here, a bodhisattva who abides in the lineage—
Because his mental continuum is naturally virtuous, he is by nature endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva and the wholesome dharmas appropriate for a bodhisattva;
and he is seen to manifest them in practice, precisely because of that natural goodness. It is not [by means of effort].

Through forceful yoga (*haṭha-yoga*), he proceeds toward that which is wholesome; moreover, by way of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), it becomes restrained and accumulated. And the bodhisattva who dwells in the lineage (*gotra*) of all the Buddha-qualities is a bearer of the seed.

All the seeds of all the Buddha-dharmas exist within his own being and within his basis. Furthermore, the bodhisattva dwelling in the lineage (gotra-vihārī) is free from gross defilements; he is incapable of [falling back] from that.

In order to bring into manifestation a form of defilement and obsession (*saṃkleśa-paryavasthāna*), by means of which obsession he, being obsessed, commits one of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).

He would neither practice the roots of virtue nor cut them off. Furthermore, whatever procedure was prescribed for one established in the lineage (*gotra*) in the "Chapter on Lineage" should be understood in detail as applying to the bodhisattva who has abandoned the lineage. This is what is called...
319/04. These are the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the lineage (*gotra-vihāra*).

319/05. In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the practice of resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*)? Here, based on the bodhisattva’s first production of the thought of awakening (*prathama-cittotpāda*), [there is] the impure resolve... 319/06. ...upādāyāśuddhādhyā-

Whatever bodhisattva practice there may be for one who is thus situated, this is called his "dwelling in the practice of resolute belief" (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*). In that regard, the bodhisattva dwelling in the lineage (*gotra-vihārī*) is [the basis] for all the other eleven bodhisattva dwellings.
And for one who has entered this dwelling, it proceeds as a mere cause through the grasping of that cause;
yet, by means of it, no other bodhisattva-dwelling whatsoever has been undertaken, attained, or purified. How much less, then, could there be [any such thing] in the case of the Tathāgata...

The stage of having gone. Furthermore, for a bodhisattva dwelling in the stage of conduct through resolute belief, all the bodhisattva stages and the stage of the Tathāgata have been undertaken; however, they have not yet been attained, nor have they been purified.

However, that very stage of the practice of resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*) has been attained. And he has now set out for the purification of that very stage; once the stage of the practice of resolute belief is completely purified, the previously commenced stage of joy (*pramudita-vihāra*) [is entered].
He attains it in this very way. And he becomes one who has set out for the purification of that very [attainment].

When the Dwelling of Joy (*pramuditavihāra*) is completely purified, he attains the Dwelling of Higher Ethics (*adhiśīlavihāra*), which had already been commenced. And he becomes one who has set out for the purification of that very [dwelling].

He has entered [the state]. In this way, it should be understood in detail up until the supreme, perfected bodhisattva dwelling. When the supreme, perfected bodhisattva dwelling is completely purified, immediately thereafter, of that which was previously undertaken...
The simultaneous attainment and purification of the Tathāgata’s dwelling should be understood as what distinguishes this Tathāgata-dwelling from the dwellings of the bodhisattvas.
The distinction is to be understood.
Among those, what is the Bodhisattva’s stage of Joy (pramuditā-vihāra)? It is the stage of a Bodhisattva whose resolute intention (adhyāśaya) is pure. Among those, what is...

The dwelling characterized by the discernment of the cessation of the object [of meditation]. In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ signless dwelling with application and effort?
It is that which takes as its sovereign those very three types of dwellings in higher wisdom.

Having performed [this] with volitional effort and mental application, it is a dwelling accompanied by the cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom regarding the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, which is seamless and uninterrupted.
In that regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ dwelling of non-apprehension?

320/25. The dwelling of effortless and signless mental formation (*anābhoga-nirnimitta-vihāra*). This arises from the frequent cultivation of that very same aforementioned signless dwelling. 321/01. By virtue of its own...

321/03. In this regard, what is the bodhisattvas’ dwelling of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*)? It is that which, relying upon that very same perfectly pure and immovable concentration of wisdom (*prajñā-samādhi*),...

For one who has attained the vastness of great intelligence, there is the dwelling in the discernment of the distinctions, meanings, etymologies, and definitive conclusions of phenomena, beginning with the unsurpassed exposition of the Dharma for others. In that regard, what is the [dwelling] of a bodhisattva?

This is his supreme dwelling. Abiding therein, the bodhisattva has reached the culmination of the bodhisattva path; having attained the great dharma-consecration for unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he becomes either one bound by only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*) or a *caramabhavika*.

Or it is definitive. In that dwelling of the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), immediately following which, having attained unexcelled perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*) in close succession, one performs all the activities of a Buddha.
A bodhisattva may be one who practices the cultivation of a bodhisattva only to a limited extent, practicing with interruptions, or practicing inconsistently due to the loss of what has been gained.
In the state of joyful abiding (*pramuditavihāra*), the bodhisattva [remains] in that very cultivation of a bodhisattva...
That which one practices extensively, without flaw, and with certainty,
because of not falling away from what has been attained. Just as it is in the Dwelling of Delight,
so it is up through the three dwellings of higher wisdom, beginning with the first, the Signless Dwelling.

From the [stage] based upon [the first] up to the supreme bodhisattva dwelling, the bodhisattva becomes one who practices the bodhisattva cultivation immeasurably, flawlessly, and with certainty. The undertaking of the cultivation of the signless (*nirnimitta-bhāvanā*) should be understood [to begin] there. It should be understood that in the dwelling of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and in the supreme dwelling,

What are the aspects, what are the signs, and what are the marks of a bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief?
A bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief is... [pratisaṃvid...]

He becomes powerful in manifestation. In the application of the bodhisattva’s duties, he applies himself through wisdom after careful deliberation, but not by way of natural disposition or inherent nature. [Tib. 167a] Of the firm and irreversible bodhisattva—

He is one who has not attained meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). There are [five fears]: fear of lack of livelihood, fear of ill repute, fear of death, fear of an evil rebirth, and fear of timidity before an assembly. Yet, through discernment, he applies himself to the welfare of sentient beings, rather than out of natural compassion.
Out of affection, he sometimes behaves wrongly toward sentient beings through body, speech, or mind; at other times, he becomes attached to sense objects;
at other times, he is seen even to be grasping at material requisites; yet he remains one who follows through faith.
This occurs for others— the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— but one does not personally become a knower of reality (tattvajña) regarding the Tathāgata,
or the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, or the meaning of reality, or the awakening of a Buddha.
Whether it be the power of sentient beings, the cause, the fruit, that which is to be attained,
the purpose, the means for attainment, or the sphere of activity— [one] possesses limited knowledge consisting of what is heard and what is reflected upon, but not immeasurable [knowledge].

Furthermore, that [attainment] is sometimes forgotten by him, and it is of a nature subject to forgetfulness. He is endowed with the bodhisattva path that is difficult and slow in its direct knowledge, yet he does not possess intense desire [for awakening].
He does not apply himself to great awakening; his vigor is not ardent, nor is his serene confidence deeply established. Furthermore, he is deluded and lacks mindfulness regarding three points.
In the case of objects— whether pleasant or unpleasant, consisting of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena— there is at times a state of inverted mind; and regarding rebirth,
for one who has been born again and again in various other personal existences from a previous personal existence...
Because of forgetfulness regarding the teachings that have been indicated and mastered;
and because of occasional forgetfulness of what was done long ago or spoken long ago.
Thus, in these three instances, one becomes one whose mindfulness is lost. And at other times...

He is intelligent and capable of grasping, retaining, and penetrating the meaning of the teachings (*dharma*). At times he is not so; at times he possesses mindfulness, while at other times he is of a nature characterized by lost mindfulness. And [he does not [know] beings as they truly are...]

He is devoid of the practice of great compassion toward sentient beings. He attends to sentient beings by providing only a small measure of benefit and happiness, rather than a vast and immeasurable one; nor does he fulfill it in all respects.

In the wandering through saṃsāra, he is not yet endowed with the blazing and immovable wholesome factors that constitute the qualities of enlightenment. These are the signs, marks, and characteristics of such a nature belonging to one who dwells in the stage of conduct through resolute belief.
These should be understood as pertaining to a bodhisattva who is currently abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*).

there is an intensity (*adhimātratā*) of these aforementioned aspects, signs, and marks.
It should be understood that for one abiding in medium patience, there is a state of mediocrity.
For a bodhisattva abiding in superior patience,
these modes, signs, and marks are mild and attenuated.

there is the complete abandonment of these aspects, signs, and marks without remainder, and immediately thereafter,

By way of attainment, for one who dwells in this Stage of Joy (pramuditā-vihāra), all these phenomena do not exist in any way whatsoever. Those which [were previously]—adhi... [325]... [are no longer perceived].

They are said to be those who dwell in the stage of practice for liberation. Conversely, all the factors belonging to the side of purity (śukla-pakṣya) are found therein. Endowed with these, a bodhisattva is called one of pure high resolve (śuddhādhyāśaya). What [are they]?

Furthermore, even for a bodhisattva abiding in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-vihāra*), there is a progressively higher purification of resolute belief by way of its weak, medium, and intense degrees; however, this is not called "purity of superior intention" (*adhyāśaya-śuddhi*). That is so because...

For what reason? Because such resolute conviction proceeds when it is defiled by these various secondary afflictions; however, for a bodhisattva who abides in the stage of "Joyful Conduct" (pramuditavihāra), all such resolute convictions—
Through the abandonment of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), a pure resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) free from secondary afflictions proceeds.
In that regard, for the bodhisattva abiding in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*):

What are the aspects, what are the signs, and what are the marks that should be known? Here, a bodhisattva, entering from the stage of the practice of resolute belief into the stage of joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*),
[fulfills] his previous bodhisattva vow...

Regarding the state of unexcelled perfect enlightenment, having for the most part abandoned that which is poorly penetrated, poorly understood, and poorly understood as to the means— being dependent on others and lacking certainty— one [attains] another, fresh [realization] through six aspects. Well...
Having attained certainty within himself, he generates a bodhisattva vow consisting of cultivation that transcends all other white vows;

It transcends the entire sphere of the world and, because it is accompanied by the protection of sentient beings from suffering, it is not shared with any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; for even when that resolve has arisen for a mere single moment, it is so.
Such is the nature of phenomena (dharma-prakṛti) that it yields immeasurable, desired fruits of pure qualities for bodhisattvas; and that aspiration (praṇidhāna) is unchanging.
It is inexhaustible. Once it has been attained, no decline or alteration whatsoever can be perceived through any means or in any manner. It partakes of distinction;
it extends to the furthest limit of the future and culminates in great enlightenment. Furthermore—

This well-ascertained vow of a bodhisattva is called the "production of the thought of enlightenment" (*cittotpāda*). Furthermore, this production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva should be understood, in brief, by way of four aspects. What are these four? [Tib.]

The thought of those bodhisattvas who have set out upon the bodhisattva course arises [with the aspiration]: "In the future, may there be the swift and perfect fulfillment of all the accumulations for enlightenment,

It is conducive to all modes of the entire equipment for enlightenment; it is conducive to all modes of the bodhisattva’s activities toward sentient beings; it is conducive to the attainment of the self-arisen knowledge of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; [it is conducive to] all modes of the Buddha—

That mind arises as conducive to the performance of what is to be done. Through the arising of that mind, the bodhisattva transcends the stage of the foolish bodhisattvas who are ordinary worldlings and enters the certainty of the reality of awakening.
He is born into the family of the Tathāgata; he becomes a son from the breast of the Tathāgata,

He becomes fixed. Having become thus, he attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) and becomes abundant in joy. He is free from agitation, violence, and anger, and [acts] toward others in every way for the sake of sentient beings as a bodhisattva.
Having described the final activity in all its aspects, the fulfillment of the equipment for enlightenment, the sūtras and the kārikās,
enlightenment, the Buddha-qualities, and the empowerment of the Buddha’s deeds,
one should take these as objects with a pure resolute intention and become convinced of them.
When pride enters [the mind], one perceives that this is conducive to the swift attainment of these dharmas;
seeing and realizing this for oneself, one becomes full of great joy through virtue that is sublime and associated with renunciation. Nirā-...
Through an incomparable pretext, with a joy that benefits both body and mind,
I am endowed with these ardent wholesome qualities;
I have drawn near to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and am purified.

"Furthermore, my resolute intention is set upon great enlightenment, and all my fears have departed. For this reason also, he becomes full of joy; for indeed, five fears do not arise in that bodhisattva who has generated a mind so well-determined.

They are abandoned. For one whose knowledge of selflessness is thoroughly cultivated, even the perception of a self does not arise; how much less, then, could there be either attachment to a self or attachment to the requisites for life? Thus, his livelihood—
There is no fear, nor does he expect anything from others. He has this desire: "I myself must provide for all the needs of these sentient beings. Therefore, he has no fear of ill repute.

"There will be certainty. Thus he becomes certain. Therefore, he has no fear of the miserable destinies, nor [fear] regarding himself in the entire world.
He perceives through his intention that there is no one equal to him, let alone anyone superior. Therefore, he has no fear of intimidation before an assembly.
Thus, being free from all fear, [he teaches] all the profound instructions.

Free from fear, free from the arrogance and pride of all exaltation, free from hatred toward all injuries and misconducts committed by others, and free from the joy of all worldly pleasures; because he is undefiled, unimpaired, and ardent, he is not of the common sort.

With a resolute intention (*āśaya*) for the full realization of all wholesome qualities (*sarva-kuśala-dharma*), he exerts every form of bodhisattva vigor (*vīrya*) regarding the present Dharma, preceded by the predominance of faith (*śraddhādhipati*). Furthermore, regarding those [qualities] in the future...

The ten great vows have been explained in the Chapter on the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment (bodhipakṣya-paṭala). Having accomplished those in this Stage of Joy (pramudita-vihāra), by virtue of the purity of his intention,
he performs worship of the Supreme Being, the Recipient of Offerings, the Teacher, and the Lord of Dharma.
328/14. That which is the great vow for the upholding of that sublime True Dharma;

and for the sake of realizing unexcelled perfect enlightenment and performing the deeds of a Buddha.

He brings forth the tenth great vow: that as long as the realm of sentient beings is not exhausted, and as long as the worldly dharmas are not exhausted, may these great vows of mine continue in every birth.
From birth until reaching the culmination of enlightenment,
may there be non-decline, non-forgetfulness, and non-separation; thus, the mind is rightly directed.

He makes a vow. It should be understood that the vow regarding the object previously intended to be vowed for is the fundamental vow. Taking these very great vows as the primary ones, for that bodhisattva—
One hundred thousand times ten million incalculable vows arise simultaneously.
For one who thus possesses such vows for the future and in the present life, [the result follows].

329/09/. For me, who have initiated vigor, ten qualities that purify the dwelling lead to the purification of the dwelling of joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*). One has faith in all the Buddha-dharmas. By way of the application of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), [one understands] how...

Compassion (*karuṇā*) arises for one who perceives the emergence of the mass of suffering (*duḥkha-skandha*) of sentient beings. Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) arises for one who perceives: "I must liberate these sentient beings from this entire mass of suffering. [This applies to] all suffering...

The disregard for oneself by one whose intention is to provide protection; the relinquishment of internal and external things to sentient beings by one who disregards those [things]; and, for the sake of those very same sentient beings, the [bestowal of] mundane and supramundane dharmas from others.

Knowledge of the world (*loka-jñatā*). Regarding those very same applications, it is the practice of propriety concerning time, occasion, measure, and so forth, based on a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpyatā*). Regarding those very same applications, it is the maintenance of steadfastness and the acquisition of strength through non-retrogression. [Regarding] gain and honor...

330/01. Perfect compassion, loving-kindness, renunciation, weariness [with cyclic existence], knowledge of the treatises, knowledge of the world,

abides in them and cultivates them extensively. Furthermore, he investigates all aspects of the virtues and faults of the path regarding the other nine bodhisattva dwellings, beginning with the dwelling of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).

330/07. From the presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he possesses those superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and has not lost his way. In this regard, the Buddhas appear within his range of vision, as well as those [teachings] which he has heard in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. And those...

To a still greater degree they become purified by means of honoring and upholding the Tathāgatas, the Saṅgha, and the Dharma; by means of the articles of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*) for the sake of maturing sentient beings; and by means of dedicating their roots of virtue toward awakening, and so forth.

For many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. For example, just as gold remaining in its natural state becomes increasingly purified the more it is cast into the fire by a skilled smith, so too—
The roots of virtue of this bodhisattva, whose intention is pure, become even more purified by those causes of purification. Abiding therein,
he is for the most part born as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) throughout his successive lives.
In his birth, he becomes the lord of Jambūdvīpa, free from the stain of all miserliness,

It is devoid of mental attentions regarding the attainment of enlightenment in all its aspects as a jewel. Desiring, "May I become the foremost of all sentient beings and the refuge for all their goals," he exerts such vigor accordingly.
331/22/. That which consists in renouncing all dwellings, wives, and enjoyments, and having gone forth into the teaching of the Tathāgata,

He causes [the earth] to tremble; likewise, he traverses it with his body. Having pervaded [the world] with his radiance, he displays it to others. He brings to maturity a hundred beings to be trained by means of a hundred emanations. And if he so desires, he remains for even a hundred eons.

He establishes his abode. Through the vision of knowledge, he penetrates a hundred eons from the past limit to the future limit. And he investigates a hundred gateways of the Dharma, such as the gateways of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields.

Through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions [of eons], this stage of the Bodhisattvas called the "Joyful" (*pramuditā-vihāra*) is thus well-determined by way of the arising of the four aspects of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), and by the accomplishment of the undertaking of right vows and vigor (*samyak-praṇidhāna-vīryārambha*). Regarding the perfection of this stage...

It should be understood through a summary presentation by way of purification, by way of the cultivation of other dwellings, by way of the purification of the roots of virtue, by way of arising, and by way of power.

These stages are to be understood as proceeding in sequence from the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*) up to the Ultimate Stage (*parama-vihāra*). Thus it is said.
In that regard, what are the modes of the bodhisattvas’ dwelling in higher ethical discipline?

The intention of non-deception; the intention of dwelling in the joy and harmony of fellow bodhisattvas who share the same Dharma; the intention of mastering one's own mind through overcoming all afflictions, secondary afflictions, and the works of Māra; [and] the perception of defects in all conditioned phenomena.

Furthermore, this penetration of the meaning of reality is of two kinds: that which is characterized by conceptualization and that which is free from conceptualization. Furthermore, the penetration of the meaning of reality is also of two kinds: that which is with remainder and that which is without remainder. Therein, the penetration of the meaning of reality with remainder is the realization of the meaning of reality while the aggregates still remain. Whether in the middle or in old age, or this [present state]—these are the six types of conduct that follow upon the eight bases of legal procedure (*vyavahāra-pada*). There is no basis of legal procedure nor any such conduct beyond these. Therefore, it is only this much that is to be followed.

390/08/. He dies and is born again. In that regard, the modes of conduct in worldly convention (*vyavahāra-carita*) are the aspects (*ākāra*); the terms of worldly convention (*vyavahāra-pada*) are the designations (*uddeśa*). Because he recollects those, it is said that "he recollects with their aspects and designations. In that context, the divine abiding (*divyo vihāraḥ*) consists of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
It is called "constant" because that eye depends upon it, because it is its fruit, and because it is sustained by it; thus, the eye is said to be twofold.
Because it is the fruit of perfectly complete and pure meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), it is "utterly pure."

Thus it is said. Because they differ from humans at least in name, they are called "beyond the human" (*atikrānta-mānuṣyaka*). Furthermore, among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), there exists even that divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) which is acquired by birth.
That name follows after similarity; moreover, even that does not exist for humans. Sentient beings who are dying are said to be "passing away" (vyayamāna) in the intermediate state.

Those who are about to arise in a state of existence are said to be "arising. For those whose destiny is darkness, this kind of mind-made intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is produced by two factors; for example, like a black woolen blanket.

The appearance [of the intermediate state] is like the pitch-black darkness of a night; therefore, they are called "ill-colored" (durvarṇa). However, for those who depart by means of light in two ways, their mind-made intermediate state (antarābhava) is of such a form.
It is produced, just as [the color] of moonlit night or of a fine cloth from Vārāṇasī. Therefore, they are called "excellent gold. In that regard:
Those who are ill-favored in color are inferior; those who are well-favored in color are superior. Those who are inferior go to an evil destination; those who are superior go to a happy destination.
Through the failure of ethical discipline, together with its origination, there is misconduct of body, speech, and mind.

They are called "slanderers. By means of that false view, they adhere to a false cause and a false result. With that as a condition, they perform false karmic formations;
performing false karmic formations, [they produce] this which is dharma—

The karma of wrong view is said to be for the sake of undertaking [unwholesome] dharmas.

Even though one is endowed with many various other wholesome dharmas, because of that very [wrong view], one goes to an evil rebirth; thus, by reason of that and with that as the condition, [it is so called].

Thus it is said. Because of the mutual separation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it is called "the dissolution of the body. Because this death is the most inferior among all deaths, it is called "supreme death" (*paramamaraṇa*). This is due to the manifestation of the designation of the hells.

They are called the states of woe, the miserable destinies, and the precipices. By way of analyzing their intrinsic nature, their bodies, and their objective entities, they are called hells. ...they exist. Because they are like a precipice, because one utters great, distressed, piteous, and wretched lamentations and outcries,
and because they produce an intense sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), they are called "downfalls" (*vinipāta*).
These are called the hells themselves. And that which those born there experience, and furthermore,
whatever other most extreme suffering they bring about by their own actions as a result of that experience— all this is elucidated by these designations.
By the reversal of this, the entire white side (śukla-pakṣa) should be understood according to its application.
In this regard, there is this distinction: a destiny preceded by good conduct is called a "good destiny" (sugati);
because it is characterized by the enjoyment of happiness, it is called the "heavenly world" (svarga-loka).

Due to the abandonment of all outflows (*āsava*) together with their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) without remainder, that untainted (*anāsrava*) mind which is their antidote, as well as the untainted wisdom (*prajñā*)— comprised within supreme higher mind (*adhicitta*) and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*)—
is the untainted liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*) resulting from the destruction of the outflows.
Liberation is called liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
Furthermore, that liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*) and liberation through wisdom, in that very last existence,
are realized within oneself by means of the sixth higher knowledge (*abhijñā*) on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

By means of reliance—that is, by relying on the path of cultivation—they realize their own realization as it truly is; and desiring to benefit others, they announce that realization to those who seek it. Therefore, in this very life, by themselves—
It is said that they "realize, attain, and declare" by means of direct knowledge (*abhijñā*).
One should understand the various distinctions among such phrases as "birth is exhausted for me," and so forth, just as they are presented in the *Paryāyasaṃgrahaṇī*.
Summary verse (uddāna):
Its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), its classification (prabheda), its uniqueness (kaivalya), and likewise its equality (samatā);
its activity (karma), its performance (kriyā), its sequence (anukrama), and finally, its distinction (viśeṣa).

Furthermore, regarding these ten powers of a Tathāgata, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should be understood; their differentiation (*prabheda*) should be understood; their exclusivity (*kaivalya*) should be understood;

The sequence should be understood; the distinction should be understood. Thus, in brief, the ten powers of a Tathāgata should be understood through these seven aspects.

In this regard, what is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? These have the five faculties as their intrinsic nature; however, because wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant, they are said to have wisdom as their intrinsic nature. For it is thus stated: "the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible" (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*).
But it is not called the power of faith, nor any other power.
Just as the power of knowing what is possible and impossible is [defined], so should the remaining powers be understood.

Because of this penetration. Thus, by means of these three distinctions, the immeasurability of these ten powers of a Tathāgata is to be understood.
This is their distinction.

In this regard, what is their exclusivity? These ten powers belong exclusively and uniquely to the Tathāgata alone; they do not belong to any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. This is called their exclusivity.
These powers of all the Tathāgatas are equal and without distinction;
