he surveys the class of those who have gone forth: "Is there anyone in this class of those who have gone forth who has emerged from suffering and who teaches the path for the sake of emerging from suffering?"

"Is he sleeping? Or is it that he does not exist? Having understood that he does not exist, and beholding the entire world as being without protection and without refuge, he gives rise to great compassion and surveys the entire world with the Buddha-eye. While surveying it, he...

Having brought into presence the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties, he understands: "There are beings born in this world who, as they grow, possess dull faculties, middling faculties, or sharp faculties. Having known this, he teaches the Dharma to them.
The mind proceeds toward the future. Thereafter, as before, the entire sequence for all other powers—beginning with the various liberations and so forth—is to be understood.
This is the second alternative sequence of the powers.

Another formulation: First, immediately upon his full awakening, the Tathāgata, by means of the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), examines the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) as dependently originated. Thereafter, [he examines] karma—

By the power of his own knowledge, he investigates the notion of a "sentient being" and the realm of sentient beings within those dependently originated phenomena. He discerns: "These sentient beings [experience] such a result from such self-performed karma."

"Experiencing the fruit": having correctly discerned the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) through the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*), [the Buddha] correctly [establishes] those very sentient beings for liberation from suffering.
He instructs by means of the three miracles. Having instructed as before, he proceeds in due order;
having understood the faculties and so forth through the remaining powers, he establishes them on the path.
He liberates those beings from suffering. This is the third sequence of the powers.
In that regard, [the function] of the power of knowing what is possible and impossible is the knowledge of the individuality of karma.

And what is the distinction of power? It is that the desirable or undesirable fruit of wholesome or unwholesome karma is produced; this is due to the power of knowledge regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna-bala*).
Furthermore, it is that whoever performs wholesome or unwholesome karma, he alone [experiences] that [result].

One experiences the desired or undesired fruit [of one's actions] by virtue of the power of the knowledge that [each being] has their own karma (*karma-svakajñāna-bala*). To begin with, those [meditative attainments] such as the dhyānas and liberations belong only to the one who has entered them, and not to anyone else. This is [the power of] karma.

By the power of his own knowledge. Furthermore, when he relies on those very same meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and so forth to instruct those to be trained through the three miracles (*prātihārya*), this is by the power of his knowledge of the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*). As for that which is faith—

The mind apprehends [the object] as conjoined with the innate [factors] beginning with *dhātu*. This is by virtue of the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*). Furthermore, those very faculties [are distinguished] according to their grades, such as weak, medium, and superior.
By this he analyzes. This is by the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñāna-bala*).

First, that which apprehends the disposition (*āśaya*) toward various phenomena based on the faculties is by the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties. Furthermore, that very disposition—

That which distinguishes various [dispositions] is due to the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*). Furthermore, that intention (*āśaya*) should be understood as being analyzed, in brief, by way of six aspects. First, there is the non-liberating intention; for example, that which is separate...

The intention of those who are devoted to Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, the world-systems, and so forth, is the *naiṛyāṇika* (non-leaving) intention; for example, as it is with those who are devoted to the three vehicles. The intention that is far from purification is, for example, [the intention] of those at the stage of weak or middling maturation.
For those who are established [in their respective stages], the intention is close to purification,
as in the case of those established in the highest degree of maturation; it is the intention to attain nirvāṇa in this very life, such as through the vehicle of the śrāvakas.

For those who have attained resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), there is the aspiration for the attainment of nirvāṇa in the future. For example, this refers to those who have attained resolute conviction in the attainment of nirvāṇa by means of the Mahāyāna. That which...
First, one grasps a seed similar to that [object], which is produced by resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

This is due to the power of the knowledge of various convictions (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*). Furthermore, when one grasps that very same seed by distinguishing it into many varieties, this is due to the power of the knowledge of various elements (*nānādhātu-jñāna*).
401/06. By force. Furthermore, that classification of elements (*dhātu*) should be understood, in brief, as having four aspects:

the seed abiding in its own nature (*prakṛtistha-bīja*), the seed arisen from previous practice (*pūrvābhyāsa-samutthita-bīja*), the seed to be purified (*viśodhya-bīja*), and the seed [of those] whose nature is parinirvāṇa (*parinirvāṇa-dharma*). 401/08. Just so... [the seed of those whose nature is parinirvāṇa].
401/09. [The seeds] of those who are one-eyed, and the seed that cannot be purified—such as that of those whose nature is not to attain parinirvāṇa.
To the extent that he understands the entry into the path according to the corresponding realms, this is by virtue of the power of knowledge of the various elements (nānā-dhātu-jñāna-bala).
Furthermore, when one discerns that very same path in all its aspects—
[knowing] "this path leads to affliction," "this leads to purification," "this leads to ultimate purification," and "this does not lead to ultimate purification"— this is [the wisdom of the path].

By virtue of the power of the knowledge of the path leading everywhere: to the extent that, recollecting the past, he understands, as it truly is, the causes of all destinies associated with the past— this is by virtue of the power of the knowledge of the path leading everywhere.

Furthermore, having analyzed it as before, he understands the sixfold conduct associated with worldly conventions (vyavahāra). This is by means of the power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of former abodes (pūrvenivāsānusmṛtijñānabala), which begins from the past limit (pūrvānta) regarding the passing away of sentient beings.

He understands the passing away and rebirth [of beings]. This is by virtue of the power of the knowledge that recollects past abodes (*pūrve-nivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*). Furthermore, when he perceives the ultimate passing away and rebirth of sentient beings, this is by virtue of the power of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapatti-jñāna-bala*). As for that which—

He knows the rebirth and the reconnection at the future limit of sentient beings who have perfected their own welfare; this is due to the power of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapatti-jñāna-bala*).
Furthermore, regarding those who have perfected their own welfare and whose minds are well-liberated...

He understands the attainment of nirvana in this very life. This is due to the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*). This is [the first] among these ten powers of a Tathāgata.
The distinction and non-distinction of the various modes of birth (yoni) should be understood.
The four grounds of self-confidence (vaiśāradya) should be understood according to the text of the sūtra itself. In that regard, these four points were [attained] by the Tathāgatas in the assembly.
These are the points to be asserted: the complete awakening to all aspects of all phenomena through liberation from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) not shared with the Śrāvakas.
This is the first point; and that which is shared with the Śrāvakas...

Liberation from the obscuration of afflictions: this is the second point. And for those beings who desire liberation, the path leading to definitive exit (*nairyāṇika-mārga*) for the sake of transcending suffering: this is the third point. And of that very [path]... the mar...

Those obstructive factors which act as hindrances to attainment must be avoided. This is the fourth point. And the Tathāgata possesses knowledge of these four points exactly as they are. Therefore, his claim—
In the first two positions, there is a deficiency in the activities of body, speech, and mind;
in the latter two positions, there is a deficiency in the vow.
Furthermore, for others, there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows, as well as a fallacy of illogicality regarding the divine [powers].
And for those with vision— whether divine or non-divine— and for those who know the minds of others and those who do not,
when there is an exhortation by way of countering their positions and assertions,
he does not perceive any sign by which these [beings] might be intimidated; thus he is fearless.

With a mind free from dejection, without hesitation or fear, he makes this declaration: "This much is to be declared by the Teacher—that is to say, the complete accomplishment of one's own welfare and the welfare of others. In this regard, by means of the two preceding [qualities]...
Through the first two points, one's own practice for self-benefit is declared to be fulfilled;
through the latter two points, one's practice for the benefit of others is declared to be fulfilled. In that regard, of oneself...

Because of his perfect awakening to all phenomena, the Tathāgata, with reference to the bodhisattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna, declares himself to be a perfectly awakened one (samyaksaṃbuddha).
Furthermore, he declares that the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) pertains to those beings who have set out in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
[he declares] the path leading to liberation, the obstructive factors, and both of these.
With reference to this, he makes this declaration: "In this way, this scriptural passage was taught by the Tathāgata:
'Whatever path leading to liberation has been taught by me for the bodhisattvas and the śrāvakas,'" and so forth. And that is the designation "bodhisattva."

The compilers of the *Saṃgīti* excluded it from the section concerning the *Śrāvaka-piṭaka*. In the *Bodhisattva-piṭaka*, however, it is recited solely under the designation of "bodhisattva. Regarding the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they are exactly as in the sūtra according to the text.

These [teachings] should be proclaimed. For a long time, the Tathāgata has had this desire: "May those to be trained abide correctly in the practice of the Dharma well-taught by me. And for one who has long held that desire, the Dharma—
The Master, the leader of the group, is characterized by being free from affliction through the three applications of mindfulness, whether that request succeeds or fails.

Furthermore, these are established as three by way of the distinction between the three assemblies. What are the three assemblies? One that practices correctly and entirely—all of it—is one assembly. [The second is] one that practices correctly and entirely... [text breaks off].
All practice wrongly; this is the second assembly. The third assembly, moreover, is that in which some practice correctly and some practice wrongly.

The three things that need no protection should be understood according to the text of the sūtra itself. In brief, they consist in the abandonment of concealing any form of misdeed. This is what is elucidated by the Tathāgata through these three things that need no protection.
Even for an Arhat, there may occasionally and at some time be some slight, indeterminate misdeed resulting from a lapse of mindfulness; that too is likewise [to be understood].

For one who has departed, there is absolutely nothing whatsoever; thus the Tathāgata is as he is known. Such is his intrinsic nature. Having repeatedly restrained the disciples, he speaks; having repeatedly overpowered them, he causes some among them to despair.

He banishes some of them; moreover, he treats them harshly. No protective concern arises in him toward them, thinking: "Lest my disciples, through the course of living together with me, come to have impure conduct of body, speech, and mind."
Having understood that, they will, being displeased and dissatisfied with that matter,
either reproach [him] themselves or report it to others.
In this regard, the great compassion of the Tathāgatas is of every aspect, just as previously described.

The worship and service previously described should be understood as occurring in the chapter on the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). Furthermore, that [worship] should be understood as immeasurable, unsurpassed, and pertaining to the Tathāgata.
In that regard, it concerns both what is to be performed by the Tathāgata and where [it is performed].

It occurs in such a manner, in such a way, and at such a time. Because he correctly carries out [his task] therein, in that manner, and at that time, this is called the Tathāgata’s quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃmoṣa-dharman*).
Thus, regarding all the activities of the Tathāgata in all [respects] therein—
In all places, in all means of action, and at all times, there is the state of non-forgetfulness through mindfulness;
this is the state of ever-present mindfulness. This is to be understood here as the quality of non-forgetfulness.
In that regard, whatever [action] of the Tathāgata occurs—whether in movement, in looking, or in speaking—
Whether in a village or in a monastery, there is an abundance of manifest activity that resembles the actual presence of afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is called the Tathāgata’s "eradication of the latent predispositions" (*vāsanā-samudghāta*).
On the other hand, for Arhats, even though they have abandoned the afflictions, [there remains] what appears to be the actual presence of afflictions.
It indeed exists in gestures, movements, glances, speech, and conduct.
In brief, the Tathāgata has perfectly awakened to three categories of phenomena. Which three? Phenomena associated with meaning.
[There are things] associated with disadvantage, [things] associated neither with advantage nor with disadvantage, and [things] associated with disadvantage.
In that regard, concerning those things associated with disadvantage for the Tathāgata, [there is] neither [advantage...
405... [text fragment].
Knowledge regarding all phenomena that are connected with what is not beneficial—
this is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñāna*). In that regard,
as for that which is the Tathāgata’s [knowledge] concerning all phenomena connected with what is beneficial...
Regarding these, there is knowledge. This is called the "supreme knowledge" (*vara-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata.
In that regard, both the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākāra-jñāna*) and the supreme knowledge, when condensed together into one, are termed the "supreme knowledge of all aspects."
It is said:
Summarizing all of this, there are one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). Among these, the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are—

Furthermore, when he is a bodhisattva in his final existence, these secondary marks (anuvyañjana) become thoroughly purified and attained. When, however, the bodhisattva sits at the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), having fully perfected the path of the equipment for awakening (bodhisambhāramārga)—

In his final existence, while cultivating the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening without a teacher, he— while still in the stage of a learner (śaikṣa)— attains the concentration named "the knowledge of non-obstruction in a single moment."
This belongs to that Bodhisattva who is embraced by the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi).

Immediately thereafter, in the second moment, there is the complete purification of the remaining Buddha-dharmas, beginning with the ten powers (daśabala) and culminating in the supreme knowledge of all modes (sarvākāravara-jñāna).

One attains at once a state that is unsurpassed. Through the attainment of these, there proceeds with respect to all objects of knowledge a wisdom that is unattached, unobstructed, perfectly pure, and stainless, which depends merely upon the act of mental application (*ābhoga*). Pari-...

His resolve is fulfilled; thus his heart's desire is completely realized. Having transcended the conduct of a bodhisattva and the stages of a bodhisattva, he has entered the conduct of a Tathāgata and the stage of a Tathāgata. He has reached the essence.

And because of the abandonment without remainder of the functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the side of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), his basis (*āśraya*) becomes transformed. And this is his unsurpassed transformation of the basis. All other [transformations] are merely supreme abodes (*parama-vihāra*).
The transformations of the basis (āśraya-parivṛtti) of Bodhisattvas, while still being subject to further improvement, are to be understood as having a superior [nature].

In this regard, how is the distinction between the knowledge of a bodhisattva established in the stage of reaching the ultimate limit and that of a Tathāgata to be understood as a difference in knowledge? Here,
for a bodhisattva established in the stage of reaching the ultimate limit:
Just as the sight of forms by one with vision is [perceived] when separated by a thin cloth,
so should his knowledge regarding all that is to be known be understood. Furthermore, just as it is not separated by anything at all, such is the knowledge of the Tathāgata.

It should be viewed as follows: it is like a painting-work complete in all its colors, yet not yet refined by a final, perfectly pure stroke of color; in this way, the gnosis of that bodhisattva is to be viewed.
Just as [the vision] is perfectly purified, so should the gnosis (*jñāna*) of the Tathāgata be regarded.
It is like the perception of forms by a man with clear sight when the darkness is very slight; likewise for the Bodhisattva, as before. Ya-...
Just as [the eye of one who is healthy] is free from all forms of darkness, so should the gnosis of the Tathāgata be viewed.
It is like the sight of forms by one with eyesight from a distance;
likewise for the Bodhisattva as before. As it is when nearby, so it is for the Tathāgata.
As for one who has gone [into the womb], it is as before: just as the perception of forms by one with mild cataracts;
so it is for the Bodhisattva, as before: just as by one with perfectly pure eyes;
so it is for the Tathāgata, as before: just as by the self while still in the womb.

Existence. Thus should the Bodhisattva established on the stage of reaching the ultimate goal be viewed. Just as the personal existence (ātma-bhāva) of one born in a state of rebirth, so should the Tathāgata be viewed. Just as that of an Arhat who has entered the midst of a dream.

The movement of the mind of that bodhisattva who abides on the stage of reaching the ultimate goal should be viewed as being like the movement of the mind of one who has awakened individually; in this same way, the movement of the mind of the Tathāgata is to be viewed. That—
Just as the intrinsic nature of an impure lamp is [impure], so too is the intrinsic nature of the gnosis of a bodhisattva abiding on the stage of reaching the ultimate.
It should be viewed as being like the nature of a perfectly pure lamp.

In this way, the nature of the Tathāgata’s gnosis should be viewed. Therefore, there is a great difference in gnosis, a difference in personal existence, and a difference in thought regarding the Tathāgata.
It should be understood that this applies to both the bodhisattva who stands at the stage of going and the one who stands on the stage.
Thus, having fully awakened to enlightenment, the Tathāgata performs all the deeds of a Buddha in every Buddha-field throughout the ten directions.

407/07/. In that regard, what is the work of a Buddha? In brief, there are these ten tasks of a Tathāgata, duties to be performed by a Tathāgata. And each individual task of a Tathāgata accomplishes the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings.
It exists. There is nothing beyond this, nothing more than this. What are the ten?
First, within his own state as a Great Being, from the very beginning, it produces clarity of mind and generates conviction regarding that state of a Great Being. This is the first.

That which is the work of a Tathāgata is accomplished through the primary marks and secondary signs. The application of instruction in all its aspects for the sake of all sentient beings is the work of a Tathāgata;
that is, what the Tathāgata performs by means of the four kinds of complete purity in all aspects.

He accomplishes this. This is the second task of a Tathāgata. The capacity to perform the welfare of all sentient beings and the capacity to sever all doubts is the third task of a Tathāgata, which the Tathāgata— [Tib. 210a]—[performs].

He accomplishes [this] by means of the ten powers of a Tathāgata. For it is by means of the ten previously mentioned powers that the Tathāgata becomes capable of accomplishing every purpose for all sentient beings. And those which are these ten...
They ask questions concerning the powers of a Tathāgata, just as those things which have been known, seen, understood, and realized by the Tathāgata,
so does the Tathāgata, when questioned by them, explain all [matters] regarding others.

The defeat of opponents in debate and the establishment of one's own doctrine constitute the fourth task of the Tathāgata— that which the Tathāgata accomplishes through his grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*).

The fifth deed of the Tathāgata is the state of an unafflicted mind toward those disciples who abide by the command of the Tathāgata and those who do not. It is that which the Tathāgata brings to perfection through the applications of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*), such that his conduct is exactly as his word.
The sixth deed of a Tathāgata is that the Tathāgata maintains himself with things that require no protection.
The seventh deed of a Tathāgata is that the Tathāgata surveys the entire world day and night with the Buddha-eye. That which the Tathāgata [performs] as a great...

He accomplishes [this] through compassion. The non-deprivation of all activities for the sake of all sentient beings is the eighth deed of a Tathāgata, which the Tathāgata accomplishes by way of his nature of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃmoṣadharmatā*). It is the thorough accordance with the conduct of a Tathāgata as it truly is.

408/10. Turning and non-exertion is the ninth deed of a Tathāgata. That which a Tathāgata accomplishes through the total eradication of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) regarding those phenomena which are connected with what is not beneficial, as well as those which are neither connected with what is beneficial nor connected with what is not beneficial.

Excluding those, the thorough explanation, exposition, and clarification of those phenomena that are conducive to the goal— that is the tenth deed of a Tathāgata, which the Tathāgata performs by means of the excellence of all aspects.

He accomplishes [this] through gnosis. For it is in this way that the Tathāgata, by means of these one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), performs the ten activities of a Tathāgata and carries out all the work of a Buddha. [The detailed account follows.]
Furthermore, if one were to analyze this very activity of a Buddha, it would not be easy to calculate its number, even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
This is the dwelling of the Tathāgata; this is the ground of the Tathāgata; this is the foundation.

Thus it is said. For what reason? Because by relying upon this, by being established in this—upon which Bodhisattvas, desiring its form, train in the Bodhisattva trainings—and even having attained that foundation, they rely upon this very one.
By relying upon these, one accomplishes all the aims of all sentient beings;
therefore, they are called "the foundation.
And all these qualities of a Buddha are exceedingly dedicated to performing the welfare of others.

The banks [of the Buddha's teaching] possess the power of performing the welfare of others for the sake of all beings, whereas that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is not so; therefore, these qualities of his are unique (āveṇika).
Thus they are called. And those Buddha-qualities exist which are not found at all among Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Namely:
great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃmoṣa-dharmatā*), and the eradication of latent predispositions (*vāsanā-samudghāta*).

The knowledge that is supreme in all its aspects: even those things which are perceived by others are not complete in all their aspects; but for the Tathāgata, all things that are perceived are complete in all their aspects, and are far more transcendent and far more sublime.
Therefore, these are called his "unshared" (āveṇika) qualities. The meaning of "unshared" should be understood as the sense of exclusivity (*kaivalya*).
Thus, this is the complete path of training for Bodhisattvas. Śi...

The patience, the path, and the fruit have been revealed. This Bodhisattvabhūmi serves as the foundation for the instruction on every aspect of the path of training of all bodhisattvas, as well as the fruit of that path of training. Indeed, this is the Bodhisattvabhūmi.
It is also called the *Mātṛkā* of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; it is also called the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*; it is also called the *Exposition of the Path of Perishing and Non-perishing*;
and it is also called the *Root of the Purification of Unobstructed Knowledge*.

409/18/. It is said: whoever from this world—including its gods, humans, asuras—whether being a god or a human, or a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, having produced firm resolve toward this bodhisattva stage, shall hear this...
If one shall take it up, retain it, apply oneself to it through the mode of cultivation,
or explain it in detail to others— even down to having it written out and retaining it— and shall offer worship and honor to it, for that person, in brief:

Whatever mass of merit has been described, detailed, explained, established, and revealed by the Blessed One for the act of hearing and so forth this sūtra, which is comprised within the entire Bodhisattva-piṭaka— so great is his mass of merit.
The aggregate (skandha) is to be expected. For what reason?
Because, in this Bodhisattva stage, [it contains] the entirety of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The gateways of summary and detailed exposition have been collected and explained.

Furthermore, whatever Dharma and Vinaya has been extensively revealed in this *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, that [Dharma] is frequently practiced through summary, recitation, and the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharma*).

Through these practices, he will remain firm and shall attain vast increase and expansion. For as long as counterfeit versions of the true Dharma do not become prevalent for the sake of the disappearance of the true Dharma, [he will remain] because of that true Dharma.
In the year 410, imitations will become abundant. Consequently, this True Dharma,
which is endowed with the ultimate reality, will disappear.
In the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, within the section on the Foundation (*ādhāra*) and the Culmination (*niṣṭhā*), the sixth stage of yoga (*yoga-sthāna*).
The fourth chapter, on the Foundation, is completed. (K. adds here:
This was written after seeing it in an ancient manuscript lacking a date, transcribed in ink characters upon palm leaves.)

In this regard, the sequence on the Bodhisattva-bhūmi is as follows: a bodhisattva established in the lineage (gotrastha) generates the mind directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi).

411/03/. Having generated the [awakening] mind, one applies oneself to the welfare of oneself and others. (150b) While applying oneself to the welfare of oneself and others, one obtains the means for non-affliction. Being unafflicted, one obtains the means for non-exhaustion. Being undaunted, [one cultivates] the roots of virtue—

He obtains the means for increase. Increasing through roots of virtue, he awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, regarding the application of the welfare of oneself and others, the means of non-affliction, and the means of indefatigability, [he increases] his roots of virtue.

411/09/. And while practicing the means for increase and the attainment of enlightenment, from the very beginning he establishes resolute faith (*adhimukti*) in the profound and sublime teachings (*dharmas*). Having developed that faith, he seeks those teachings; having sought them, [he seeks] others...

And he teaches them; and he himself accomplishes them through practice. While accomplishing them, he practices by that means, in that place, and for that purpose; by that means, in that place, and for that purpose, he practices.
411/15/. Practicing in such a way that there is an accumulation of merit (*puṇya*) and an accumulation of knowledge (*jñāna*), he practices accordingly.

Having accumulated merit and knowledge, while not abandoning cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), he practices for the sake of [avoiding] the lower realms. Practicing therein within the non-defilement of cyclic existence, [he proceeds].

He practices. Practicing therein, he practices without attachment to his own happiness. Practicing therein, he practices without weariness toward the suffering of *saṃsāra*. Being thus unwearied, [he studies] the treatises.

Having mastered [the teachings], he becomes one who is skilled in all treatises (*śāstra*). Being a knower of treatises, he knows exactly how each thing is to be taught; knowing that, he becomes a knower of the world (*loka-jña*).
Thus, being both a knower of treatises and a knower of the world, he investigates phenomena (*dharma*) in a systematic and thorough manner (*yoniśas*).
411/24/. Thus, while seeking [this], one becomes capable of cutting through all the doubts of all sentient beings. Being thus capable, one cuts through the doubts of others.
Increasing through merit, he will fulfill the accumulation of merit;
and increasing through wisdom, he fulfills the accumulation of wisdom.
While fulfilling them, [he cultivates] the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya*) by way of their aspects (*ākāra*).

He applies himself to the cultivation of the Dharma, yet he does not understand the method of cultivation. Practicing in that manner, he dedicates that cultivation toward the parinirvāṇa of the Mahāyāna,
and not toward the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

In nirvāṇa, he is likewise skilled in means regarding all that is spoken by bodhisattvas. By the power of his cultivation, even those dharmas never heard before appear to him in every form. He is endowed with *dhāraṇī* and eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
One practices for the sake of abandoning all obscurations by means of the three doors of liberation.
While practicing therein, one becomes engaged in the practice for the sake of abandoning the conceit of self-deprecation and the conceit of superiority toward others. This is his [practice].

412/13. Perfection of practice in all its aspects. Having practiced in such a manner, he becomes superior to all sentient beings, even to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, both by virtue of the excellence of his practice and by virtue of the excellence of the benefits of that practice.

412/16. Regarding that, there is a distinction in the excellence of practice: a bodhisattva practices for the benefit of both self and others, and thus his own task is the welfare of others; whereas a śrāvaka and a pratyekabuddha do not have the welfare of others as their own task in that same way. All sentient beings—

Toward these [beings], he maintains a mind of equality with himself. Being of equal mind, he constantly engages in rendering service and does not expect anything in return. Engaged in this way, he constantly aspires for their welfare and happiness.

Thus, possessing the intention for their welfare and happiness, he applies himself to them in a way that is never fruitless. This is the excellence of the quality of practice, brought forth in a progressively ascending manner.
413/01. Regarding the specific qualities of its benefits: there, the bodhisattva receives a prophecy from the Buddhas; neither the śrāvaka nor the pratyekabuddha does so.
Having received the prophecy, he abides on the stage of irreversibility. Abiding therein—

He attains the quality of non-forgetfulness regarding what must necessarily be done and what must be constantly done. By virtue of this quality of non-forgetfulness, he is designated by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as the foremost among all sentient beings in all their undertakings.
And he does not fall away; nor does he fall away through the loss of what has not yet been attained.
Not falling away, he constantly and continuously increases in wholesome qualities. Like the waxing moon, he truly progresses.
He becomes a true Bodhisattva, not a mere semblance.

Being a genuine Bodhisattva, he understands every aspect of all methods for disciplining [beings]. Knowing these, he becomes skilled in all systematic arrangements—that which is to be sought, that which [is sought], and by what means.
And having investigated it, once it has been investigated, this [teaching] is established.
One who is skilled in establishing [the teaching] becomes skilled in instruction. Being skilled in instruction, one attains the King of Samādhis, which has immeasurable objects of focus.
One who has attained that samādhi becomes a teacher of the Dharma who is never fruitless;
he becomes one who has set out by means of the Mahāyāna. Having set out by means of its greatness, he becomes a gatherer of the Mahāyāna for others among those belonging to the Mahāyāna.
In the stage of departure (*niryāṇāvasthā*), he desires any one of the names;
and by means of a name common to all bodhisattvas, he is awakened by the entire world.

He is also attended upon and praised by the sons of the Buddha and the bodhisattvas. Thus, these specific qualities of benefit and virtue are to be understood. The marks of a bodhisattva belonging to one who has such a name are to be understood... even when... (Note: The bracketed portion indicates a lacuna in the source text corresponding to approximately 28 syllables.)
Even when he has departed [from the household life], he accomplishes [the goal] in both states; by accomplishing [it] in both states,
he becomes one whose practice is essential, whose resolute intention is directed toward the exclusively wholesome side,
and whose intention is such that he is embraced by householders.

...remains [in that state] until such time as he so chooses. Thereafter, having reflected, he intentionally takes up rebirth in existence (*bhavopapatti*) where there is an assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the sake of sentient beings; therein, together with those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he dwells constantly—

414/10. Constantly, he experiences the state of attaining excellence in the side of wholesome qualities supported by instruction. Grasping the benefits of that experience, he enters the state of attaining that excellence by way of dwelling [in it]. That state—

With a mind established in ever-higher stages of excellence, one exerts effort in every way until reaching the ultimate goal; this is non-contentment. Exerting oneself in such a manner, one attains the final establishment, beyond which there is nothing further.
One who has attained the unsurpassed does not seek further.
The sequence of the Bodhisattvabhūmi is completed.
And the Bodhisattvabhūmi is finished.
